# Education AI — Market Intelligence


## 🆕 `p769` — **School-estate decarbonisation and energy reporting. All four regions set a cadence — the second consecutive register to manage it — but this is the first register where the duty is a *published figure*, and that changes who buys and what can go wrong. 🔴 The EMEA duty currently exists in EU law and in NO member state's national law: the Commission opened infringement proceedings against all `27` on `15 July 2026`.**

**Every interval, threshold and effective date below is search-sourced and labelled as such. No primary legal text was read this pass (see `intel/open-gaps.md`).**

### 🟢 The duty layer, placed by region

| Region | Instrument | Cadence it sets | Trigger | Competent person |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EMEA — UK** | **Display Energy Certificate** + advisory report, for public buildings `>250 m²` frequently visited by the public | 🟢 **Annual DEC above `1,000 m²`**; a DEC for `250–1,000 m²` reported valid `10` years; advisory report `7` years. Penalties reported at **£500** for no DEC and **£1,000** for no valid advisory report | 🔵 **Floor area.** 🔴 Trading Standards is reported to take a narrower view for buildings used *solely* as a school; community use pulls a school into scope | 🔴 An accredited DEC assessor — **not primary-verified this pass** |
| **EMEA — EU** | **EPBD recast, Directive (EU) 2024/1275** | 🔴 **Transposition was due `29 May 2026` and is not done anywhere.** Renovation-passport schemes also due `29 May 2026`; solar on new public and non-residential `>250 m²` by **`31 Dec 2026`**; national building renovation plans by **`31 Dec 2026`**; **zero-emission standard for all new public buildings from `1 Jan 2028`** (other new buildings `2030`) | 🔵 Building class and floor area | — |
| **North America** | **State and city building performance standards**, with **ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager** as the reporting instrument | 🟢 **Annual benchmarking report** in most jurisdictions. **Washington's Clean Buildings Performance Standard Phase 1 begins `1 June 2026` and is reported to cover K-12 schools explicitly** (`50,000 sq ft`; Phase 2 `20,000 sq ft` in `2028`). California **AB 802** requires benchmarking plus public disclosure; **NYC Local Law 97** and **Maryland BEPS** are reported to cover schools | 🔵 **Floor area, set per jurisdiction** | — |
| **APAC — Japan** | **省エネ法** (Act on the Rational Use of Energy) + **建築物省エネ法** for the building fabric | 🟢 **Annual, and the most precisely dated cadence on the register: エネルギー使用状況届出書 by the end of May; 定期報告書 and 中長期計画書 by the end of July.** Filed electronically through **EEGS** | 🔵 **Energy volume, not floor area: `1,500 kL` crude-oil equivalent per year triggers 特定事業者 designation.** Separately, a `300 m²` threshold for the building-side notification | 🟢 **Named: 文部科学省 (MEXT) is the competent ministry for schools**, and publishes 学校のための省エネガイドブック (令和７年３月 / March 2025) |

| **LATAM — Brazil** | **Resolução CGIEE nº 4/2025** (published `30 Sep 2025`) + **ENCE / PBE Edifica**, enforced by **INMETRO** | 🟢 **A dated ratchet rather than a refresh cycle: federal public buildings at ENCE level `A` from `2027`, NZEB by `2035` (`2040` for Rio Grande do Sul); state and district level `A` reported `2032–2035`, NZEB `2037–2040`; municipalities above `50,000` inhabitants in a final phase to `2040`** | 🔵 Public-building class, by federative level | 🔵 **INMETRO.** 🔴 Schools are not named — they are in scope as public buildings, which is an inference this base labels as one |

🟢 **Second consecutive register with a cadence in all four regions** (`p768` was the first in five). 🔴 **But the *shape* differs for the first time, and the difference is the finding:**

| Shape | Regions | What the artefact is |
|---|---|---|
| 🟢 **A posted label at the entrance** | **EMEA (UK)**, **LATAM (Brazil)** | A certificate the public can see. Two unrelated legal traditions converging on the same artefact |
| 🟢 **An annual filing to an authority** | **APAC (Japan)**, **North America** | A report, submitted and retained |
| 🔵 **A rating programme** | **APAC (Australia)** | A score obtained, with no disclosure duty attached |

### 🔴 `T679` revisited, and sharpened rather than restated

`T679` held that *"North America refuses to set a cadence"*. `p768` found a hard federal cadence for fleet compliance (49 CFR 396.17) and concluded the refusal was a property of estate safety, not of the United States. 🟢 **This register sharpens it further: North America sets a cadence here too, but at STATE and CITY level, with no federal instrument at all.**

🟢 **The predictor that survives both data points: the US legislates federally where the duty rides on interstate commerce (a vehicle crosses state lines) and leaves it to states where the duty rides on a building (which does not).** A fleet duty is federal; a building duty is municipal. **For a studio this is operational, not academic: a North American fleet deliverable has one rule set, and a North American estate deliverable has as many rule sets as the client has jurisdictions** (`T713`).

## Opportunities by region

### North America

🟢 **`p769` — the strongest permissive substrate of any region on this register, and the only one with a published system of record.** `SEED-platform/seed` (BSD-3-Clause, `121★`, pushed `2026-11-11`) is a benchmarking platform built for exactly this duty, with `py-seed` (MIT **and** BSD-3) as its API client; `NatLabRockies/EnergyPlus` and `OpenStudio` (both BSD-3) are the engine and SDK; `LBNL-ETA/EnergyPlus-MCP` (BSD-3, `126★`) already exposes the engine to an agent. 🟢 **The opportunity is jurisdiction multiplication:** Washington's Phase 1 starts `1 June 2026` and covers K-12 explicitly, and a district spanning several jurisdictions needs one data model with per-jurisdiction cadence and threshold rules — which is `P352`. 🔴 **The named risk is the instrument itself:** ENERGY STAR is reported to be moving out of the EPA as of March 2026, with at least `$33M` appropriated for FY2026; **a deliverable that hard-codes Portfolio Manager as its scoring authority is exposed to a programme transfer**, so the score belongs behind an interface (`P353`).

### EMEA

🔴 **`p769` — the largest regulatory opportunity and the largest regulatory uncertainty on this register, and they are the same fact.** The **EPBD recast was due to be transposed by `29 May 2026`, and on `15 July 2026` the Commission opened infringement proceedings against all `27` member states** for failing to transpose it fully; a March 2026 action against `19` member states over draft National Building Renovation Plans preceded it. 🔴 **So an EMEA deliverable today is built against a directive, not against `27` national laws — the national detail a compliance engine needs does not exist yet in most member states.** 🟢 **The correct posture is therefore to build the EU-level obligations that are already dated and will not move (`31 Dec 2026` solar on new public buildings `>250 m²`, `1 Jan 2028` zero-emission new public buildings) and to keep national thresholds as configuration, not code.** 🟢 **The supply side is unusually good here:** `BBSR-GEG-Portal`'s MIT web service and print application are **the German statutory certificate artefact published permissively by the federal institute itself**, `ABC-TransitionBasCarbone/bilan-carbone` is MIT from the body that owns the French method, `energiacte/cteepbd` and `pachi/envolventecte` implement the Spanish CTE, and `jmcaamanog/CE3X-MCP-Server` already wraps the Spanish certification tool as an MCP server.

### APAC

🔵 **`p769` — the clearest duty on the register and the thinnest supply, and the two facts are unrelated.** Japan's 省エネ法 sets the most precisely dated cadence found anywhere this pass (届出 end of May, 定期報告 end of July, EEGS e-filing, **MEXT named as the competent ministry for schools**), and Australia has a schools rating tool plus a three-year public-school rating commitment. 🔴 **And the open-source supply in the region's own languages is nil:** `7` Japanese legs and `3` Korean legs returned **`0`, `0`, `0`, `0`, `0`, `0`, `0`** and **`1`, `1`, `0`**. 🟢 **The opportunity is consequently integration, not assembly:** a Japanese engagement is an **EEGS submission pipeline** over a permissive Western stack — `OpenStudio` for the model, `rrule` for the two statutory dates, and the 1,500 kL threshold as a volume trigger rather than a floor-area one. 🔵 Australia's NABERS commitment is a **rating-production** engagement with a fixed three-year horizon. 🔴 **No verdict is published for Korea or China on the school estate: the targeted search leg returned nothing on Korean or Chinese school energy instruments, and the Chinese-language supply legs are pollution-dominated (see below).**

### LATAM

🟢 **`p769` — the only region whose duty is a dated ratchet, which makes it the easiest to sell and the hardest to fake.** Brazil's **Resolução CGIEE nº 4/2025** puts federal public buildings at ENCE level `A` from `2027` and NZEB by `2035`, states from `2032`, municipalities above `50,000` to `2040`, requires the labels in **public procurement**, and requires the **ENCE to be displayed at the main entrance** of a completed public building. 🟢 **A ratchet with named years is a multi-year engagement with a built-in renewal: the client cannot do it once.** 🔴 **Supply is the weakest of the four regions:** the Portuguese and Spanish legs returned `17`, `8`, `1`, `2` and a `450`-result `huella de carbono` leg that is almost entirely coursework, with **`0` grant-carrying Brazilian or Spanish-American repositories on this register**. 🔵 **`OneBus/OneBus-API` (MIT, LATAM) carried forward from `p768` remains the only LATAM-origin permissive data model on this base's recent registers**, and it is about vehicles, not buildings. 🔴 **Schools are not named in Resolução 4/2025** — their inclusion is an inference from "public building", and a Brazilian engagement should confirm it against the resolution text before it is scoped.

### Global

🔵 **`p769` — the market numbers do not agree on their own base year, and that is the finding to carry into a proposal.** Building energy management software forecasts cluster at **`9–14%` CAGR**: one estimate puts BEMS at **`$46.1B` in 2026 → `$83.77B` by 2032 at `10.43%`**, another puts building-specific software at **`$2.49B` (2025) → `$6.51B` (2032) at `13.9%`**, and broader energy management software estimates for 2026 range from **`$14.29B`** to **`$60.94B`** depending on scope. 🔴 **Carbon accounting software is worse: 2026 base-year estimates in the same search range from `$98.1M` to `$22.27B` to `$27.51B` — a spread of more than `100×` — with CAGRs from `4.01%` to `22.2%`.** 🟢 **A `100×` disagreement is not noise, it is the absence of an agreed market definition**, and a studio quoting any single figure is quoting a scope choice. 🔵 **The defensible framing for a client conversation is the duty, not the market: the dates are fixed (`31 Dec 2026`, `1 Jun 2026`, `1 Jan 2028`, `2027`, `2035`), and the spend follows them.** 🔴 **Regulatory headwind, global:** the CSRD **Omnibus** raised thresholds to **`>1,000` employees and `>€450M` turnover from FY2027**, which one vendor-adjacent source puts at roughly **`85%` of previously covered companies removed from mandatory reporting** — a single-source figure this base does not endorse. **The school estate is largely unaffected, because its duty comes from building law, not from corporate reporting law — which makes the public estate a more durable buyer than the corporate one** (`T714`).

🔴 **The governing commercial finding of this pass is jurisdictional, not technical, and no licence file states it.** On a statutory-compliance register the code is cheap and **the law is the asset**. US federal regulation is a work of the United States government and carries no copyright, so `29 CFR 1910`/`1926` can be ingested and redistributed — which is exactly what the one artefact with no vendor in its data path does (`dtjohnson83/osha-mcp`, MIT, ingests from eCFR). ## Market size — the honest range

| Estimate | Source | Note |
|---|---|---|
| ~$10.6B (2026) → $42.48B (2030), 41.5% CAGR | Market-research summary carried in prior passes | The figure this KB has used since cycle 2. |
| $41.01B by 2030 | Alternative vendor estimate | ~3.5% below the above for the same year. |
| $10–23B for 2026–2027 | Third vendor range | The spread *within one year* is >2×. |
| US segment: $3,280M (2025) → $15,250M (2031) | Ken Research | Country-level, marketing-grade. |
| Sector opportunity $3.37B | Technavio, May 2026 | Smaller scope — "market opportunity", not total market. |

**Read this as: roughly $10B today, consensus on a high-30s-to-low-40s CAGR, and no
agreement beyond that.** The 2030 numbers are extrapolations from an uncertain base.

## Adoption — the firmest numbers available

- **86%** of education organisations use generative AI (Microsoft, 2025) — the highest
  cross-industry adoption rate recorded.
- **66%** institution-wide AI implementation (Technavio, May 2026) — up sharply.
- **95%** of UK undergraduates use AI in at least one way (2026 tracker).
- **Only 45%** of the most-used tools have published research meeting an ESSA evidence tier.
  This is the single most commercially relevant statistic on this page: adoption is near
  universal, **evidence is the bottleneck**, and the market has started paying for proof.

## Structural shift: from policing to pedagogy

The sector has left the "panic phase" of generative AI. The focus has moved from academic
integrity enforcement to cognitive-load optimisation and measurable outcomes. The OECD's
*Digital Education Outlook 2026* (January 2026) frames the constraint precisely: AI helps
learning **only when pedagogy stays in control**.

Fading, per 2026 analyses — worth knowing so a studio does not pitch them: blockchain
credentialing, full-classroom VR, and the undifferentiated chatbot-as-tutor.

Also notable as a demand signal: **Chegg cut 45% of staff (388 roles)** as AI tools eroded
homework-help traffic. The incumbent homework-help business model is being destroyed, not
augmented — which is where displacement work comes from.

## 🆕 `p752` — the education-to-employment register, and a verdict on this page that was `16` months stale

**`2026-11-10`.** 🟢 **The register this pass took is the transition layer — skill extraction, occupational taxonomy, credential-to-job matching: the layer that decides what a learner's record is worth in a labour market.** It is the commercial end of everything this base already holds, because a tutoring agent sells to a faculty and an assessment agent to a registrar, **but a skills agent sells to a ministry of labour, a state workforce agency or an employer consortium — and those buyers procure against a national vocabulary.**

🔴 **The correction this page needs, stated plainly.** `p681` placed this opportunity **under EMEA only** and recorded that *"the measured supply behind it is poor — three permissive ESCO projects were probed and all three are dormant."* Both halves of that need amending:

1. 🟢 **The dormancy measurement was right and remains right** — `3 / 3` of those addresses are still dormant (`T453`). **But the live successors existed the whole time and were never promoted**, and two were pushed the day of this pass. The register is **actively maintained**, not poorly supplied.
2. 🔴 **The EMEA-only placement was wrong**, and it was wrong in the specific way this base is instructed to avoid. **North America has a parallel, active, Apache-2.0 stack** — [`CredentialEngine`](https://github.com/CredentialEngine)'s CTDL registry, OSMT and CLR 2.0 matcher — which sat at **`0`–`4` mentions across `751` passes. An opportunity placed in one region when it exists in two is not a placement; it is a blind spot with a label on it.**

🟢 **The structural finding, and it decides scope before architecture does:** this register has **two national stacks that do not interoperate and are not trying to** — **ESCO/ISCO** in EMEA, **CTDL/RSD/O\*NET** in North America — and they are **asymmetric in opposite directions**:

| | **North America** | **EMEA** |
|---|---|---|
| Platforms (authoring, registry) | 🟢 **Present and Apache-2.0** | 🔴 **Absent** |
| Extraction libraries | 🔴 **Thin** — `onet occupation api` → `2` | 🟢 **Present and MIT** — `162★` and `32★` |

🔵 **So the same capability is two different engagements:** in the US you layer agents onto an existing platform and **write the extraction**; in Europe extraction is nearly free and you **build the authoring and registry surface**. 🔴 **One deck cannot serve both, and a proposal that assumes the European shape in a US engagement under-scopes the hardest part of the work.**

🔴 **A boundary that governs every claim below.** `esco.ec.europa.eu`, `jobtechdev.se` and `www.onetcenter.org` are all unreachable in this session (`3 / 3`, DNS `ENOTFOUND` / `curl 000`). **ESCO's licence terms are therefore not asserted anywhere in this pass**, and the O\*NET grant split recorded below came from search-result text rather than the authoritative page and is marked second-hand. `p747`'s `T396` boundary, reproduced in a second register.

### North America

#### 🆕 `p768` — 🟢 the region that **does** set a cadence, which settles `T679` — and the deliverable flips from justification back to schedule

🟢 **The structural finding this page has carried twice is now bounded.** `T657` (CPSC playgrounds) and `T679` (ANSI A300 / ISA TRAQ trees) both recorded that the US instrument **deliberately sets no inspection interval**, and `p767` generalised it toward *"North America refuses to set a cadence"*. **On school transport fleet compliance the US sets one, federally and without qualification:**

| Instrument | What it sets | Why it matters to the deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| **49 CFR 396.17** | 🟢 a **12-month periodic inspection** against the Appendix A item list | The cadence is a constant, so the product is a **schedule and an evidence trail**, not an authored justification |
| **49 CFR 396.19** | 🟢 the inspector's **training and experience standards** | 🟢 **The first instrument on this page that defines the competent person in regulation** — so the qualification becomes a validated data field (`P347`) |
| Record retention | annual inspection report **`14` months**; DVIRs **`3` months** | Two more recurrence rules, both dated |
| State layer | 🔴 **semi-annual, quarterly and monthly** school-bus requirements are each reported | 🔴 **Unenumerated this pass.** Build the cadence as a per-jurisdiction lookup, never a constant |

🟢 **So `T679` is a property of condition-driven estate safety, not of the United States** (`T688`). Where the asset is a vehicle and the failure mode is mechanical, the US sets a number like every other region.

🔴 **The region's open-source supply is the weakest part of the opportunity.** `FMCSA compliance` returns `51` repositories and `driver qualification file` returns `3`; `electronic logging device` and `hours of service ELD` return `89` each, and ranked by stars the usable ones are nil — the register's `209★` flagship is **PolyForm Noncommercial** (`768-A`). 🔴 **And North America is the one region that sets a cadence without publishing a machine-readable proof**: the DVIR and the annual inspection report are paper or vendor-proprietary, where the EU specifies `.DDD`, Japan a QR-coded certificate and Brazil a public calibration registry (`T699`).

**AI-in-education market context for the region, from this pass's mandated legs:** North America is reported as the **largest** agentic-AI-in-education market (Mordor), against a 2026 regional policy picture of **`134` AI-in-education bills across `31` states**; **Ohio** became the first state to require every K-12 district to adopt a formal AI policy, deadline **`1 July 2026`**; **California AB 1159** prohibits using student data to train AI models; **New York A 9190** restricts classroom AI to grade `9` and above with diagnostic and special-education exceptions; **North Carolina Session Law 2026-41** sets a state model policy by **`31 December 2026`**, local policies by **`30 June 2027`** and teacher training by **`30 June 2028`**. Federal action remains limited — a **K-12 AI Literacy and Readiness Act of 2026** advanced in House committee. 🔵 All bill numbers and dates are **search-sourced and not verified against state legislative sites**.


#### 🆕 `p767` — 🔴 the region that **refuses to set a cadence**, for the second consecutive register — so the product is the justification, not the schedule

🔴 **The structural finding, now holding twice.** `T657` recorded that the CPSC playground handbook deliberately sets no inspection interval. **ANSI A300 Part 9 and the ISA Tree Risk Assessment Qualification do exactly the same for trees.** They specify:

- **method** — risk rated by categorising the likelihood of failure against the severity of its consequences;
- **qualification** — TRAQ, requiring ISA Certified Arborist status plus a course with a field component, a written and a performance-based exam, **retest every seven years**, and it **may not be transferred**;
- **report content** — identification and location of each tree assessed, the methods used, the assessment data, and recommendations for mitigating risk or conducting further evaluation;
- 🔴 **and no frequency at all.**

🔴 **Sources disagree on the standard's own edition**: ANSI A300 consolidated into a single document since **1 January 2024** per one source, Part 9's revision dated **2017** per another. **State the edition as contested on any client deck** (`T679`). 🔴 A TRAQ handbook and several arborist-firm pages are the sources here; **ANSI and ISA were not read directly.**

🟢 **The opportunity, inverted.** With no cadence to encode, the sellable artefact is a **dated, authored, cited justification** of the interval a district chose, bound to proof that each assessment was performed by a currently-qualified person. `P343` builds it. 🔴 **The `competent_person` entity — TRAQ status, award date, seven-year expiry — has no open-source implementation anywhere on this register and must be built** (`T681`).

#### 🆕 p766 — 🔴 the one region where this register's "international instrument" advantage **breaks**: the US instrument deliberately sets **no inspection interval**

**Register: playground-equipment inspection** (`ACTION p765-E`). `p765` nominated this register precisely because EN 1176/1177 is an *international* family, so a deliverable would not need rebuilding per jurisdiction. **In North America that reasoning fails, and the failure is the commercial finding.**

The **CPSC *Public Playground Safety Handbook* (Publication 325)** is the US reference, and in its own wording inspection frequency *depends on the type and age of equipment, the amount of use, and the local climate*. **It sets no fixed interval.** **ASTM F1487** is a *performance specification* — dimensions, entrapment, protrusions, guardrails, use zones, labelling — not an inspection cadence. (A `F1487-25` revision is vendor-reported and **unconfirmed against ASTM**; recorded as unconfirmed.)

🟢 **Why that is an opportunity rather than a dead end.** Where EMEA hands you the interval, North America hands you a **duty to justify the interval you chose**. That is a defensible-reasoning deliverable — equipment type, age, usage volume and climate as inputs, with a written, dated rationale as output — and it is worth more than a calendar, because it is the artefact a district needs when something goes wrong. **No open-source tool produces it:** `CPSC` is `0` on this entire base and `ASTM F1487` is `0` (`T657`, `P338`).

**The permissive supply here is one MCP server:** [`SamuraiBuddha/building-code-mcp`](https://github.com/SamuraiBuddha/building-code-mcp) (`0★`, **MIT**, `1,089 B` · `3a8f258e33c1`, `main`) — ICC/NFPA/local-jurisdiction routing, which is the right shape for a per-district interval policy. [`phredogee/ITAI-1378-Final-SiteGuard-AI`](https://github.com/phredogee/ITAI-1378-Final-SiteGuard-AI) is grant-less.

**Market context, measured this pass:** North America is the largest regional AI-in-education market at a reported **`38%`** of global share, with institution-wide implementation reported at **`66%`**; **at least `15` states** have introduced or passed legislation specifically addressing AI in education (Virginia's S.B. 394 directs the state education agency to issue guidance including teacher training), the US Department of Education's FIPSE awards total **`$169M`** including responsible-AI use, and NTIA has opened an edtech review stating *"the pace and scale of edtech adoption … haven't been matched by serious scrutiny."* 🔴 **Vendor-sourced and mutually inconsistent** — student-use figures of `66%→92%` and adoption of `86%` come from marketing material and are recorded as a range, not a number.


#### 🆕 p765 — the statutory instrument is state-level, the deliverable is a **filed return**, and the regulation corpus is public domain

**Register: school-estate safety and statutory compliance.** The buyer is the district's risk, safety or facilities office, and what it owes is not a dashboard — it is a signed statutory filing with a named signatory and a deadline.

🟢 **Three states specify it precisely enough to build against.**

| Jurisdiction | Instrument | What is owed |
|---|---|---|
| **New York** | NYSED public-school fire-safety manual, 2026 edition | **Every building owned, operated or leased** by a public school district or BOCES must be inspected for fire safety, and school officials must file the annual **Fire and Building Safety Report** |
| **Florida** | Statute **1013.12** (2026) | District fire-safety inspections by persons **certified by the Division of State Fire Marshal**; reports to the local fire authority; **the district certifies completion to the State Fire Marshal** |
| **South Carolina** | Office of School Facilities Policy and Procedures Manual | Fire and smoke protection inspection provisions **effective 16 February 2026** |

🔵 **Search-sourced**: the NYSED manual and the Florida statute are published at `nysed.gov` and `flsenate.gov`; **`www.flsenate.gov` is refused at this tunnel and was not fetched.** Treated as directional on the exact subsection numbers, firm on the shape of the obligation.

🟢 **The opportunity is the cleanest on this register because the corpus is free.** US federal regulation carries no copyright, and `29 CFR 1910` and `1926` are retrievable from the government's own eCFR service. [`dtjohnson83/osha-mcp`](https://github.com/dtjohnson83/osha-mcp) (`1★`, MIT) already does exactly this — `npx tsx scripts/ingest-standards.ts  # Fetch from eCFR` into a self-hosted Supabase, with `get_standard_text` among five tools — **and is therefore the only architecture on this register with no vendor anywhere in the data path** (`T639`).

🔴 **The contrast row is the one to price against.** [`contextkits/osha-compliance-assistant`](https://github.com/contextkits/osha-compliance-assistant) is also MIT, and its MIT grant covers **a thin client against a metered API**: Sandbox `10` calls/day free, Developer **`$79`/mo**, Team **`$199`/mo**, Enterprise **`$499`/mo`**. A proposal that cites "MIT-licensed OSHA tooling" without reading the README has committed the client to a subscription (`T584`'s class).

🔴 **Declared gaps, measured not assumed.** **No federal school requirement for indoor air quality, radon or lead in water surfaced in this pass's searches**, against `0` prior mentions of each on this base. The ASCE `$85B` deferred-maintenance figure circulating in vendor material is **not adopted here**: `p764`'s `$90B` *State of Our Schools* reading stands as this base's figure. **And no open-source artefact produces New York's Fire and Building Safety Report or Florida's State Fire Marshal certification, which is the actual deliverable in both states.**

#### 🆕 p764 — the register with the largest measured unmet need on this base: **`$90` billion a year**, and the engines to address it are published in the same country

**Register: the school estate** — buildings, work orders, the deferred-maintenance backlog, the utility bill and the capital programme.

🟢 **The demand side is quantified by a named primary report.** *State of Our Schools: America's K–12 Facilities 2025*, by the **21st Century School Fund**, the **International WELL Building Institute** and the **National Council on School Facilities**, puts the annual US public K-12 facilities shortfall at **`$90` billion a year**:

| Component | Annual spend | Annual gap |
|---|---|---|
| Capital improvements | **`$82B`** | **`$56B`** |
| Facility operations and maintenance | **`$70B`** | **`$34B`** |
| **Total** | **`$152B`** | **`$90B`** |

- **The benchmark the gap is measured against** is `7 %` of district budgets on facilities — `4 %` capital, `3 %` operations and maintenance. Actual spending falls well short.
- **Who pays**: local districts **`80 %`**, states **`17 %`**, the federal government **`3 %`**. 🔵 **This is the opposite of `p763`'s register**, where a `$28.5M` federal programme set the agenda. Here the buyer is the district and the bond, not the ministry.
- **The trajectory**: `$46B` (2016) → `$85B` (2021) → `$90B` (2025). The 2025 edition reads this as slowing growth, not reversal. Lead author Mary Filardo: districts raised annual facilities spending from **`$95B` in 2016 to more than `$150B` now** and are still falling behind.
- 🔵 **Search-sourced**: figures above are from the report's own summary coverage; the primary PDF is published at `21csf.org` and was **not fetched this pass** (outside this session's allowed domains). The `$80B` and `$85B` variants circulating in October 2026 trade press are earlier or differently-scoped numbers and are **not** used here.
- **`$82B` of K-12 bond activity in 2026** is reported separately as a *surge*, which is the same money seen from the capital-markets side rather than the budget side. 🔵 Trade-press-sourced; treated as directional.

🟢 **The opportunity is unusually clean: the demand and the engines are in the same jurisdiction and have never been joined.** `LBNL-ETA/EnergyPlus-MCP` (Berkeley Lab), the four `NatLabRockies` engines (EnergyPlus, OpenStudio, SAM, ComStock), `VOLTTRON` (Battelle/PNNL) and `wyeworks/nucore-open` (Northwestern) are all North-America-published, all permissive, all byte-read this pass — and **not one of them references a school district as a user.**

🟢 **And the buyer has already learned to ask.** Mendota Township HSD 280 (Illinois) heard a `$95,500` HVAC-optimisation proposal with `$25,027`/year projected savings in December 2025 and **tabled it pending references and verification of incentive guarantees**; Aurora East USD 131 is running a six-school tune-up pilot with ComEd incentives and *will monitor billing afterwards* (June 2026). 🔵 **The deliverable a district will buy is measured, weather-normalised before-and-after — which is an evidence product, not a dashboard.**

Data collection with Deaf-community consent is a budget line, not an assumption (`T471`). Recipe: [`../compose/patterns.md`](../compose/patterns.md) `P268`.

Price accordingly.

🔴 **The data-licence trap, and it is the opposite of the default engineering assumption** (second-hand; `www.onetcenter.org` unreachable here, re-read before quoting): the **O\*NET bulk Database is `CC BY 4.0`** and commercially usable with version-specific attribution, but **Web Services data** reportedly may not be re-shared onward to third parties or modified, and the **Career Exploration Tools are `CC BY-ND 4.0`** — *NoDerivatives*. 🟢 **Ingest the bulk database; do not build a product surface on the convenient API or the career-tools content** (`T463`).

🔵 **Regulatory context for a 2026 proposal.** Activity is overwhelmingly at **state** level: trackers count **`134` AI-in-education bills across `31` states in 2026**, with student-data privacy dominant — **California AB 1159** bars using student data to train AI models and **Idaho SB 1227** requires privacy protections for AI tools in schools. Restrictions are appearing too (**New York A 9190** would limit classroom AI to grade 9 and above; **Illinois HB2400** bars AI from giving direct instruction). Federally, the House Education and Workforce Committee advanced the **K-12 AI Literacy and Readiness Act of 2026**. 🔴 **An April 2026 deadline **[🔴 `p753`: now `2027-04-26` for entities ≥ `50,000`, `2028-04-26` below — `T475`]** for updated ADA web accessibility rules reaches vendor applications** — which lands directly on any learner-facing surface Globant ships. **Canada's AI rules remain workplace-focused rather than school-focused.** 🔵 *State bill statuses move fast; verify against the legislature before quoting.*


#### 🆕 `p751` — the scheduling and assignment register, placed in North America

🔴 **The regulatory hook for this register is placement, and it is already written into district policy.** Of the measures read this pass: **`134` AI-in-education bills were introduced across `31` states in 2026**, and **Idaho, Maryland, Oklahoma and Virginia** enacted education-specific AI measures. 🔴 **Oklahoma's law prohibits AI tools used *solely* for grading, discipline or student promotion**, and board-approved district policies read this pass prohibit AI from being the **sole basis for high-stakes decisions, naming placement explicitly**. Ohio districts had to adopt an AI-use policy by **`2026-07-01`**; New York City runs a one-year moratorium barring students through 8th grade from generative AI; a Florida proposal would require district AI instructional-tool policies by **`2027-07-01`**. There is **no comprehensive federal K-12 AI law**.

🟢 **Why that is an opportunity rather than a wall.** A constraint solver that allocates places or builds a timetable is a *decision-support* system with a human approver by construction — which is precisely the shape these statutes demand. **The sellable artefact in North America is not the optimiser, it is the optimiser plus the audit trail**: why this student got this seat, which constraint bound, and who approved the override.

🟢 **The one hard money number in this register is North American.** Boston's joint school-start-time and bus-routing work (the **BiRD** algorithm, published in *PNAS*) reports **`$5M` in annual savings alongside a `50`-bus fleet reduction** with service quality maintained. ⚠️ **The same literature also reports `530` buses, an `18%` reduction and `$10–15M` in savings — these two figures do not reconcile, and this base does not pick between them.** Quote the `$5M`/`50`-bus pair, which is the one tied directly to the deployed implementation, and say it is a published case rather than a Globant result. 🔴 **The BiRD implementation itself was not found publicly released** — the rebuild is billable.

🔴 **The measured supply gap, and it is the clearest regional asymmetry this pass found.** EMEA has permissive, maintained MCP adapters for four national school portals; **North America has none for any major US SIS** (`PowerSchool`, `Infinite Campus`) — searched and absent. The only US-placed open artefact found is [`jcirni/school-bus-router`](https://github.com/jcirni/school-bus-router) (**MIT** · `1,075 B` · sha256₁₂ `8fb07e0d8f81`, `0★`, pushed `2026-10-22`) — OSM + nearest-neighbour + 2-opt, **one bus per route, with multi-bus splitting declared as unstarted "Phase 2"**. 🟢 **Opportunity:** the SIS adapter layer and district-scale multi-bus routing are both unoccupied and both buildable on `or-tools` + `VROOM` + `OSRM`, all permissive.

#### 🆕 `p750` (2026-11-10) — the wellbeing and safeguarding layer: the gate is consent, it is dated, and it is being enforced this week

🔴 **The single most important datum for any North America wellbeing engagement: parental consent is a
precondition, not a preference.** The US Department of Education's **August 2026** student-privacy
guidance states that for behavioural-health screeners probing emotional or psychological states, schools
must obtain **written parental consent prior to administration**, grounded in **PPRA**, which covers
surveys and screenings touching on *"mental or psychological problems of the student or the student's
family"*.

🔴 **And it is being enforced right now, on exactly the architecture most products ship.** The
Department's Student Privacy Policy Office has **demanded that the Illinois State Board of Education
revise** its guidance on conducting mental-health screenings without parental consent and on holding
results apart from the education record. **ISBE's response deadline is `2026-11-13`.** The stated
federal position is that treating screening results as *"temporary records"*, storing them in separate
repositories, or withholding them from parents **each infringe FERPA parental rights**. 🟢 **For a
proposal this converts the records architecture from an appendix into work package one** (`P252`).

**The other dated instrument:** the amended **COPPA** rule carries a compliance deadline of
**`2026-04-22`**, with separate parental consent required for AI-training uses; a school's consent
covers educational use only, not AI training or third-party sharing. FERPA keeps the district as the
responsible party, and a vendor reaches student records only as a *"school official"* with a
*"legitimate educational interest"*.

🟢 **The commercial opening, and it is the clearest in the register: the incumbent category is under
legal attack on four fronts at once.**

| Pressure | What is on record |
|---|---|
| Federal legislative scrutiny | Senators Markey and Warren opened an investigation into **GoGuardian, Gaggle, Bark and Securly**, reporting *"regulatory and legal gaps"* and recommending federal action. 🔴 **No federal statute specifically regulating student monitoring software has been enacted.** |
| Constitutional litigation | **Nine** current and former students of **Lawrence Public Schools (Kansas)** filed a federal civil-rights suit alleging the district's Gaggle use violates their **First and Fourth Amendment** rights. |
| Transparency litigation | A **Knight First Amendment Institute** suit seeks records on how a district uses monitoring tools. |
| Accuracy | An advocacy-group analysis reports that **roughly two-thirds of `1,200` Gaggle alerts over `10` months** in Lawrence were **false positives**; Gaggle's own published figure is **`6.9` billion student items scanned in 2024–25**. ⚠️ Advocacy-sourced — labelled as such. |

⚠️ **Securly** faced a 2023 California class action alleging collection and onward sale of student
information; **no 2026 ruling was found** this pass. A docket-dated commentary (August 2026) states
there is **no landmark class action or student-privacy verdict against GoGuardian** — a patchwork
including a Texas public-records case.

🔴 **Measured supply nil for this region's named demand.** `student retention agent llm` returns **`0`**
repositories and `school safety llm agent` returns `2`; the entire open early-warning tier is `7 / 7` at
`0★` (`T429`). 🟢 **So the North America play is a build, and its differentiator is the consent and
evidence architecture that the incumbents are being sued over** — not a better classifier.

**Regional policy context carried from the mandated leg:** more than **4 in 5** teens have used AI tools
with over two-thirds reporting regular use, while roughly **half of their schools have no AI policy at
all**; the PIE Network tracked **nearly 100** state bills this year touching student AI use; Illinois
required guidance by **`2026-07-01`**; a Stanford AI Index 2026 reading reports **only `6%`** of teachers
call their school's AI policy clear. ⚠️ A vendor-blog claim that *"at least 15 states"* have legislated
on AI in education could not be corroborated against a primary source.

#### 🆕 `p749` (2026-11-10) — the alternative-format layer: the deadline moved by one year, the obligation did not, and the agent supply is `0`

🔴 **The single most important datum for any North America accessibility engagement: the ADA Title II
deadline was extended, and most published guidance is now wrong.** DOJ issued an **interim final rule,
effective `2026-04-20`**, moving the web and mobile accessibility compliance dates of its 2024 Title II
rule:

| Covered public entity | Was | 🔴 **Now** |
|---|---|---|
| Total population **`≥ 50,000`** | `2026-04-24` | **`2027-04-26`** |
| Total population **`< 50,000`**, and special district governments | `2027-04-26` | **`2028-04-26`** |

🟢 **What did *not* change, and this is the sales point:** the **technical standard is unchanged —
WCAG 2.1 AA**, and DOJ stated explicitly in the IFR that covered entities **retain their ongoing Title II
obligation** to make digital services accessible. ⚠️ **Public universities, community colleges and school
systems are squarely in scope** as public entities. DOJ accepted comments through **`2026-06-22`** and
signalled a possible separate NPRM for substantive changes. 🔵 The National Federation of the Blind is
reported to have sued to undo the extension; **no ruling found as of `2026-10-12`** — so the dates above
are the planning basis, not a settled one.

🔴 **Read the extension correctly or lose the engagement.** A twelve-month slip on a multi-year
remediation backlog is not relief — for a large university with tens of thousands of untagged PDFs and
thousands of lecture hours, it is the difference between "late" and "very late". 🟢 **It is also the best
possible commercial window: the deadline is far enough out to fund a real programme and close enough to
make it urgent.** Separately, HHS's Section 504 web accessibility deadline in **May 2026** was **not**
extended by this rule, and it reaches federally-funded education and health-professions programmes.

**Supply — 🔴 the gap is severe and it is measured, not asserted.** `alt text generation llm accessibility`
→ **`0`** repositories; `captioning lecture accessibility open source` → **`0`**;
`course accessibility checker lms` → **`1`** at `0★`. The integrated product US institutions actually buy
is **owned by the commercial layer** (Anthology Ally and peers), while every component needed to build it
is permissively licensed (`repos/foundations.md`, `10` rows).

🟢 **The one row with the right provenance for this region is American and academic:**
[`ASUCICREPO/PDF_Accessibility`](https://github.com/ASUCICREPO/PDF_Accessibility) — **MIT**, `137★`,
Arizona State University's Cloud Innovation Center. 🔵 **Lead with it.** It answers the procurement
question "has a peer institution actually done this?" before it is asked, and the licence lets Globant
extend and ship it.

**Market sizing — honest and unflattering.** Digital accessibility *software* is roughly
**`$0.85B`–`$1.0B`** in 2026 across publishers (Mordor `~$0.85B`; Grand View `$886.7M`; Fortune Business
Insights `$0.93B`; Precedence `$0.97B`), with the wider market including services near **`$1.75B`**
(Straits). 🔴 **No publisher found this pass quantifies education-sector remediation spending**; the
closest is a `6.84%` 2026–2035 education-segment CAGR (Market Research Future, a table fragment, thin
evidence) and a `> $320M` 2024 North American enterprise ADA-solutions figure that does not break out
education. ⚠️ **Do not quote an education-accessibility market size to a client — there isn't a credible
one.** Quote the deadline and the backlog instead; both are verifiable and both are more persuasive.

| [`Internet2/grouper`](https://github.com/Internet2/grouper) `103★` | 🟢 **Apache-2.0** (index said `NOASSERTION`) | **The group and entitlement authority US higher education actually runs.** It answers *"is this person allowed?"*, which is the question an agent needs after the IdP has answered *"who is this person?"* |

🔴 **Regulation — the agent-identity standard does not exist yet, and that is the sales position
rather than an obstacle** (`T406`). **NIST CAISI** opened its **AI Agent Standards Initiative in
February 2026** and the **NCCoE** followed with a concept paper; the **Cloud Security Alliance**
published agentic-identity guidance in **September 2026**; there is **no ratified standard**, so
every vendor platform interprets *agent delegation* differently. The control sets institutions are
actually audited against today are the **OWASP Non-Human Identity Top 10** and **NIST CSF 2.0
`PR.AC-4`** (least privilege). ⚠️ Secondary sources (CSA report, CSO opinion, EdTech Magazine,
vendor blogs) — **the CAISI and NCCoE outputs are the primary ones to track.**

🔵 **Why education is more exposed here than the average sector:** an agent acting for a student
touches **FERPA-protected** education records. An agent holding a service account carries the
*institution's* authority; an agent carrying a delegated assertion carries the *student's*. Only the
second is defensible to a regulator — and `P236` builds the first artefact that proves which one you
have.

**Demand — the standing figures, carried and dated.** North America remains the largest regional
market at **~`38%` of global AI-in-education revenue**; one tracker puts the **US market at

credible is structural: **Chegg cut `45%` of staff (`388` roles)** as AI-assisted search displaced

At state level one tracker counts **~`100` bills in `2026`** that could affect K-12 AI use, and at
least **`15` states** have introduced or passed education-specific AI legislation —
**Virginia's S.B. 394** is enacted and directs the state education agency to issue guidance
*including teacher training*. **`USD 169 M` in FIPSE awards** include support for responsible AI
use. ⚠️ Hard regulation remains thin relative to guidance; **NTIA** has opened an ed-tech scrutiny
initiative and rules for minors are described as pending.

🟢 **The opportunity, and it follows from the statute text rather than the market size: the
deliverable is a training record.** Virginia's enacted law names **teacher training** explicitly,
and Panorama Education worked with **four states (Utah, North Carolina, West Virginia, Wisconsin)**
on guiding principles. A district facing ~`100` bills cannot buy a position on each; it can buy
**one auditable record of which staff were trained, on what, against which guidance, and when** —
which is a documentation-and-workflow engagement, not a model engagement. Published as `P187`.
🔵 **Pair it with the US-specific supply this base already holds** — the district MIT stack behind
`P88` — so the pedagogy layer and the compliance record ship together.

🔴 **And the downside case, which is the most useful single data point for a client conversation:**
**Chegg cut `45%` of staff (`388` roles)** and recalled its former CEO as AI assistants and Google
AI Overviews removed its homework-help traffic. 🔵 **Why it belongs in a market section: it prices
the cost of being a content destination rather than a workflow.** The institutions and vendors that
survive this are the ones embedded in assessment, records and compliance workflows — which is
where every pattern on [`../compose/patterns.md`](../compose/patterns.md) deliberately sits.
⚠️ **Gap unchanged: Canada is still absent** — this leg returned no federal position, no Ontario,
no Québec, for the fourth consecutive pass (`p705` gap `(1)`).


#### 🆕 `p734` (2026-11-10) — the volume of state activity is the opportunity, and the deliverable is a training record

🟢 **Volume, measured.** **Nearly `100` state bills** tracked this year that could directly affect
students' use of AI in K-12, and **at least `15` states** have introduced or passed legislation
specifically addressing AI in education (`T293`). Federal executive orders issued between 2025 and
early 2026 produced a national framework with agency action plans and a **K-12 AI instruction task
force**; the White House *Pledge to America's Youth: Investing in AI Education* is the voluntary
track; a **California ballot initiative** announced January 2026 runs a separate child-safety track
on how AI companies may interact with minors.

🔵 **The opportunity, and it is not a model.** Virginia's **S.B. 394** shape — guidance that *must
include teacher training* — makes the sellable artefact **evidence that staff were trained and that
tool use is governed**, per district or per state agency. With ~`100` bills in motion and `15`+
states already legislating, the same artefact resells across jurisdictions with the instrument name
swapped. The US Department of Education's **`$169M`** FIPSE awards include support for responsible
AI use and are a live funding channel.

🟢 **And the supply side is already placed for it.** `p731` measured the North American
institutional publisher tier at **`436` repositories, `268` novel and permissive** — Canvas clients,
LTI scaffolds, SCIM, SAML, data pipelines — with **`0` learning agents** (`T267`). `p734` reproduced
exactly that shape in EMEA (`T290`). **So the North American engagement is governance and
integration over Canvas-and-LTI estates**, which is what the tier publishes and what the statutes
ask for. ⚠️ Named vendors under pressure rather than expansion: Chegg cut **`45 %`** of staff
(`388` roles) as AI search gutted homework-help traffic.

#### 🆕 `p733` (2026-11-10) — guidance has become statute, and the binding obligation is educator capability

🟢 **A named enacted law, which this base has been short of.** Virginia's **S.B. 394** directs the
state education agency to issue guidance explicitly covering **teacher training** — an obligation on
the *institution's workforce*, not on student-facing product. Context: **at least 15 states** have
introduced or passed AI-in-education legislation, one tracker counts **nearly 100 state bills**
touching K-12 student AI use, and the **Education Commission of the States** reports states
embedding **AI-literacy standards in curricula** and attaching **professional-development
requirements for educators**. Four states — **Utah, North Carolina, West Virginia, Wisconsin** —
have published joint **Guiding Principles** via Panorama Education; **Student Privacy Compass**
maintains a state guidance tracker. Federal action remains **executive only**: a national AI-in-
education framework and a K-12 AI instruction task force by executive order, plus **$169M in FIPSE
awards** including responsible-AI use. 🔵 **The opportunity, and it inverts the usual pitch:** what
is becoming enforceable here is *teacher capability and AI-literacy coverage*. A tutoring product
answers no state mandate; an educator-capability programme with evidence answers S.B. 394 directly.
Stage on **`P179`**. 🔴 **Demand-side caution for pricing:** **Chegg cut `45 %` of its staff
(`388` roles)** as AI eroded homework-help traffic, and only **`45 %` of the most-used tools** meet
an **ESSA evidence tier** — a gate US districts may already apply, and therefore a differentiator
(`T285`). ⚠️ Adoption figures remain vendor-sourced and mutually inconsistent (`86 %` of education
organisations using generative AI; `66 %` institution-wide implementation); secondary-only per
`725-F`. ⚠️ **`0` North American repository rows were placed at `p733`** — the prescribed district/
university organisation sweep (`703-G`, `729-B`) has still not been run. **That is a gap, not
coverage.**

#### 🆕 `p732` (2026-11-10) — the regulatory calendar is now the engagement calendar

**Secondary-source; US state legislatures and education agencies.** The pattern across sources is
**state-level binding rules with light federal action**: roughly **`134` AI-in-education bills
across `31` states** in the 2026 session, concentrated on data privacy, classroom-use limits and
curriculum integration rather than mandated adoption.

Dated obligations worth planning against:

- **North Carolina — Session Law 2026-41** sets a hard sequence: **state model policy by
  2026-12-31**, **local school-unit policies by 2027-06-30**, **teacher training by mid-2028**.
- **California** — the CDE AI Working Group published a statewide *Model Policy: Artificial
  Intelligence in Education* on **2026-06-25**. Commentators treat California as a de facto
  national regulator for AI in children's products.
- **Maryland** — requires district AI policies, creates an **AI coordinator** role and a statewide
  collaborative, and **aligns procurement with state guidance**.
- **Washington DC** — a non-mandatory policy for the **2026-27** school year **bars AI from
  grading, discipline, IEP decisions and teacher evaluations**.
- **New York** — a bill would restrict classroom AI to **grade 9 and above**, with diagnostic and
  special-education exceptions.
- **Federal** — the **K-12 AI Literacy and Readiness Act of 2026** advanced in the House Education
  and Workforce Committee. ⚠️ Committee advancement is not enactment.
- ⚠️ **Texas HB2400**, reported as banning AI from *direct classroom instruction*, is carried by a
  single low-authority source and is **not treated as established** here.
- **Canada** — AI rules remain largely workplace-focused (Working for Workers Four Act, 2024)
  rather than education-specific.

🔵 **Opportunity, and it is procurement-shaped rather than product-shaped.** The deadlines above
create a **compliance artefact market with named dates**: model policies, district policy
instruments, procurement alignment and teacher-training programmes. Maryland's procurement-alignment
clause is the commercial detail — it means state guidance becomes a **purchasing precondition**, so
the studio's deliverable is a system that can *evidence* conformance, not merely one that performs.
🔵 **Two DC-style prohibitions are design constraints this base can already satisfy:** where AI is
barred from grading and from IEP and discipline decisions, `P174`'s architecture fits exactly —
machine-checked **state and process** with a frozen rubric and an auditable mastery record, with the
consequential judgement left to a human. 🟢 The strongest NA supply tier remains `p731`'s **`436`
repositories across four institutional publishers**, `275` permissive — integration infrastructure,
which is what these policies actually require.

has APAC overtaking). Canvas is the higher-education incumbent, so Canvas/LTI integration
is the practical delivery surface. Federal money is moving: the US Department of Education
released **$169M in FIPSE awards** including responsible-AI support.

orders between 2025 and early 2026 produced a national framework and a K–12 AI task force.
At state level the PIE Network tracked **~100 state bills** this year; at least **15 states**
have introduced or passed AI-in-education legislation. California's "AI bridge" and
screentime scrutiny are the two live policy fronts.

that 55% of tools lack is directly monetisable against procurement requirements.

products for the collapsing homework-help segment. (4) State-compliance tooling: 50

real statutes say something different.** A secondary roundup states that *"Illinois' Act 964

| Instrument | What it actually does | Date |
|---|---|---|
| **Public Act 104-0399** [105 ILCS 5/2-3.118a] | Requires **ISBE to issue statewide guidelines** on AI use in K–12 — a guidance mandate on the *agency*, not a curriculum mandate on *districts*. ISBE published the guidance **2026-07-09**. | effective 2026-01-01 |
| **Public Act 104-0565 (SB 2909)** | **Prohibits administrators from using AI to assign numerical scores or qualitative ratings in teacher evaluation.** | sources disagree: 2027-01-01 (amendment to §24A-5) vs 2027-07-01 |
| **HB4625** (103rd GA) | *Would* have added AI literacy to the School Code's digital-literacy section. **Introduced only; not law.** | proposed 2024-07-01 |

🔵 The error matters in both directions. A deck citing "Act 964" would be citing nothing,
and an engagement scoped to K–12 *AI-literacy curriculum delivery* in Illinois would be
scoped to a mandate that does not exist. **The real Illinois opportunity is the opposite
shape:** PA 104-0565 bans AI-assigned scores in **teacher evaluation**, which makes

implementing a statute. The bill-count figures remain genuinely contested and are reported as

### EMEA

#### 🆕 `p768` — 🟢 the region whose compliance evidence is a **specified binary file**, with permissive parsers for it — and the register's only duty-adjacent implementation

🟢 **EMEA is the strongest technical case on this register, for a reason that is new on this page: the evidence artefact is named in regulation and is machine-readable by statute.** The `.DDD` download from the vehicle unit and the driver card is a specified format, not a document somebody authors (`T699`).

| Instrument | What it sets | Supply against it |
|---|---|---|
| **Reg (EC) 561/2006** | driving time, breaks and rest periods | 🔴 `EU 561/2006 driving time` returns **`1`** repository; `AETR driving time` returns **`0`** |
| **Reg (EU) 165/2014** + download periods | 🟢 **driver card ≤ `28` days, vehicle unit ≤ `90` days**; retention ≥ `12` months, longer in some member states | 🟢 **`tachograph DDD parser` returns `2` and both are usable** — `way-platform/tachograph-go` (**MIT**) and `traconiq/tachoparser` (**AGPL-3.0**) |
| Smart Tachograph 2 | 🔵 reported required for vans `2.5`–`3.5 t` in international carriage and cabotage **from `1 July 2026`** | 🔴 `smart tachograph gen2` returns **`0`** |
| **Directive 2014/45/EU** periodic roadworthiness | annual testing for buses and coaches | 🔴 **An informed gap: the mandated leg returned nothing on this Directive.** Named so the absence is not read as coverage |

🟢 **The register's closest thing to a duty layer is here and it is MIT:** `flespi-software/TachoBox` (`3★`, pushed `2026-11-10`) computes against **EU 561/2006** from the `.DDD` file. 🔵 It is tiny, so its value is as a **reference implementation to validate against**, not a dependency (`P346`).

🔴 **The German-language leg inverts `p767`'s expectation and the inversion is the finding.** `Fahrtenschreiber` returns `6` repositories, four at `0★`; `Lenkzeiten` returns `4`; `Hauptuntersuchung` returns **`0`**. 🟢 **`p767`'s `Baumkataster` payout of `45` grant-carrying civic-tech repositories does not reproduce here, and the reason is structural: a municipal tree register has a public body as its data owner, while a tachograph record belongs to a private operator** (`T690`). The one German row with a grant is abandoned (`sebastian-tschen/fahrtenschreiber`, Apache-2.0, last pushed `2021-03-18`) — and its only real value turned out to be evidential, proving `T692`.

**AI-in-education regulatory context for the region:** 🟢 **`T686` is corroborated and may now be stated.** The **Digital Omnibus**, reported as **Regulation (EU) 2026/1744**, defers the AI Act's **Annex III** high-risk obligations — **education among them** — to **`2 December 2027`**. Unaffected and still in force: the **Article 5(1)(f)** ban on emotion recognition in education (since **`2 February 2025`**) and the **Article 50** transparency duties (from **`2 August 2026`**). Council of the EU conclusions this year stress **reducing dependency on AI tools developed outside Europe**, including in education and training, and point to the European Digital Education Hub, the European School Education Platform and EPALE; an **OECD/EU AI literacy framework** for primary and secondary education was released in 2026 (`T703`). 🔴 The Official Journal was not read.


#### 🆕 `p767` — 🟢 the region that **hands you all three artefacts**: a published cadence, a competence definition, and a model work instruction — and the register's largest permissive supply cluster, invisible to an English query

🟢 **Germany is the strongest jurisdiction on this entire register** (`T680`). It is the only one where the duty, the technical rule and the operational cadence are three separately published, separately citable artefacts:

| Layer | Artefact | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| Duty | **§ 823 BGB**, as the courts have developed it (*Verkehrssicherungspflicht*) | 🔴 **No legal norm prescribes an inspection interval** |
| Technical rule | **FLL Baumkontrollrichtlinie**, 2020 edition | 🔵 **Not law** — counts as *Stand der Technik*, and requires a professional risk weighting rather than a fixed period |
| Operational instrument | 🟢 **GALK *Musterdienstanweisung für Regelkontrollen von Bäumen***, adapted in 2021 to the 2020 edition | 🟢 A published **model service instruction** for the party carrying the duty |

🔴 **Periods conflict across sources and this base states none as authoritative**: an annual *Regelkontrolle* is cited as the **published *Richtwert*** for frequented urban trees; two-yearly for young trees; up to three-yearly for healthy mature trees with low safety expectation; and one blog's flat "1–2 year minimum for public roads" is uncorroborated. 🔴 **The FLL text is a paid product and was not read.**

🔵 **England is the weaker half of the same region.** The duty arises under health-and-safety and occupiers'-liability law and **no DfE or statutory rule setting a mandatory interval could be found**; frequency is tied to tree condition and failure risk. Competence runs through Arboricultural Association training and the **LANTRA national occupational standard `LANTw31` — *Carry out tree surveys and inspections***. One arboricultural report recommends **18-monthly** survey by a qualified consultant; sources otherwise disagree, and several recommend event-driven staff checks after high winds.

#### 🆕 p766 — 🟢 the region that *hands you the interval*: a three-tier cadence, a named competent person, and a statute corpus under **MIT**

**Register: playground-equipment inspection** (`ACTION p765-E`). EMEA is where this register is strongest, and it is the reason `p765` chose it: **EN 1176** is a multi-part European family with **EN 1176-7** covering installation, inspection and maintenance, and **EN 1177** covering impact-attenuating surfacing. The cadence is tiered — **routine visual → operational → annual main** — the annual main inspection is performed by a certified inspector (**RPII** in UK practice), and the regime therefore specifies all five fields of the duty schema: duty, instrument, interval, competent person, evidence artefact. Collected as data at [`evidence/statutory-intervals.2026-11-11-p766.tsv`](../evidence/statutory-intervals.2026-11-11-p766.tsv). 🔵 **Honest limit: the EN 1176-7 text itself was not read this pass** — it is a paywalled CEN deliverable — so the tier *names* are sourced and the exact periods for the routine and operational tiers are recorded as operator-set, with vendor-reported ranges marked as such.

🟢 **The find of the pass sits in this region: [`legalize-dev/legalize-pt`](https://github.com/legalize-dev/legalize-pt)** (`38★`, **MIT**, `1,002 B` · `309f2212fb92`, `main`) — a Portuguese primary-law corpus that **cites `EN 1176-7`** in a 1998 decree, under a permissive grant. GitHub's index reports `NOASSERTION`. This base has never before placed a permissively-licensed national statute corpus on a safety register (`T653`).

**The register's whole permissive agent supply is also EMEA:** [`cananzeyneppmit-droid/urban-park-green-space-chat`](https://github.com/cananzeyneppmit-droid/urban-park-green-space-chat) (`1★`, **Apache-2.0**, `9,197 B` · `a7d00bfd5452`, `main`, Türkiye) — EN 1176 plus green-space metrics on TypeScript + Ollama, **no vendor in the data path**.

#### 🆕 p765 — the most precisely specified school-estate compliance regime this base has measured, a central return going digital in **autumn 2026**, and a national asbestos register that was **refused**

**Register: school-estate safety and statutory compliance.** England is the reference jurisdiction, and it is unusually legible.

🟢 **The duty and its owner.** The duty holder is the employer — local authority, governing body or academy trust — under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 and the **Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012**.

| Element | What this pass measured |
|---|---|
| **Asbestos presumption** | Any school **built or refurbished before 2000 must be presumed to contain asbestos** until a specialist proves otherwise. A 2019 DfE survey is reported as finding **around four in five schools** do. CAR 2012 requires the duty holder to identify, record location and condition, assess risk and manage it |
| **Condition data** | The DfE's second Condition Data Collection (**CDC2**) covers about **`22,000` school buildings**, added RAAC in 2021, **concludes in 2026**. Responsibility for condition data moves to responsible bodies — academy trusts, local authorities, dioceses — with pilots in **2026–27** and national rollout from **autumn 2027** |
| **The annual return** | 🟢 **From autumn 2026, responsible bodies make a light-touch annual return through a new digital service, *Manage Your Education Estate*, confirming they meet the School Estate Management Standards** |
| **RAAC** | Confirmed in around **`1 %`** of schools and colleges in England |
| **The decisive negative** | 🔴 **A parliamentary committee recommended a national digital asbestos register for schools and the government rejected the recommendations in its April 2026 response**, pointing instead to the existing CAR 2012 duty |

🔵 **Search-sourced, and one source conflicts.** A consultancy blog reports the DfE will conduct **no** future Condition Data Collection surveys, which contradicts the rollout timeline above. **Both readings are recorded; neither is adopted.** `www.hse.gov.uk` and the DfE primary pages are refused at this tunnel, so no statutory interval below is primary-verified. Specifically: one vendor claims `BS 8214` recommends six-monthly professional fire-door surveys for school premises and another says no fixed interval applies and the fire risk assessment sets it; **this pass could not reach the standard to settle it, and `knowledge.bsigroup.com` is refused.** A claimed `BS 8214:2026` publication on 20 March 2026 is **unverified**.

🟢 **The opportunity is structural and specific.** **The compliance *return* is being digitised centrally while the *evidence* behind it stays with thousands of responsible bodies and has no open system of record.** The fire-door log, the asbestos management plan, the legionella sample record and the fixed-wire certificate are the evidence; *Manage Your Education Estate* is the attestation. **A trust with 30 schools must assert compliance annually against evidence held in spreadsheets, PDFs and contractors' portals.** That is the engagement.

🟢 **EMEA also supplies the only agents on this register that address a named national statutory regime**: [`Domera-proptech/mcp-server`](https://github.com/Domera-proptech/mcp-server) (MIT, Sweden) serves **OVK statutory ventilation inspection and energy declarations**; [`Gariknik/FireCodeCheckerAgent`](https://github.com/Gariknik/FireCodeCheckerAgent) audits against **DBN V.1.1-7:2016** (Ukraine, 🔴 no grant); [`OpenGewerk/opengewerk-haustechnik`](https://github.com/OpenGewerk/opengewerk-haustechnik) is an open-source **CAFM** created **1 October 2026** (🔴 AGPL-3.0); and [`DINFO-UniFI/RoofClassify`](https://github.com/DINFO-UniFI/RoofClassify) (University of Florence, 🔴 GPL-2.0) **identifies asbestos roofing from satellite imagery** — the only artefact found anywhere that detects this register's asbestos surface remotely.

🔴 **And the licence facts that decide an EMEA engagement.** The standards bodies are the chokepoint: `buildingSMART/IDS` is **CC BY-ND 4.0**, so a national *profile* of the specification is refused while `.ids` files you author are not (`T637`, confirming `T618`); `1EdTech` has **moved Caliper to private repositories**; BSI's fire-door standard is a paid product. **Every permissive artefact in the EMEA column above is a tool. Every piece of the law it needs is restricted.**

#### 🆕 p764 — the school estate is a **statutory condition return** here, the survey that feeds it completes this year, and nobody has said what replaces it

**Register: the school estate.** 🟢 **EMEA is the region where this register has a dated legal instrument**, in the same way `p763` found the UK's s537A census for the data return.

**England — Condition Data Collection 2 (CDC2):**
- CDC2 **surveyed every government-funded school in England** and is completing in 2026; earlier DfE material gave a completion date of **March 2026**.
- 🟢 **The survey is not a report, it is a funding formula input.** The DfE's *Condition funding methodology and spend guidance* (March 2026) states that CDC2 data is used to calculate **the condition weighting component of School Condition Allocations in 2026-27 where CDC2 reports are available**. CDC2 scores **replace CDC1 condition band grades** for that purpose.
- 🔴 **It redistributes money, visibly**: the transition produced *significant reductions in annual maintenance funding for some multi-academy trusts*. A trust's condition data is now directly its revenue.
- CDC data also informed selection into the **School Rebuilding Programme**.

**The capital programme attached to it:**

| Instrument | Figure |
|---|---|
| School Rebuilding Programme | **almost `£20B`** to 2034-35, **`750+` schools** |
| Capital maintenance | **almost `£3B` per year** by 2034-35 |
| Renewal and Retrofit Programme | **over `£700M`** to 2029-30 |
| RAAC | permanently removed from **`71`** schools and colleges |
| Delivered via SRP | **`51`** schools rebuilt |

🔵 RAAC and SRP counts are from the **February 2026 Education Estates Strategy**; all figures in this block are search-sourced from government and sector reporting, with the primary gov.uk documents not fetched this pass.

🔴 **The open question is the successor.** Sector commentary is explicit that it *remains to be seen whether a further national programme will be announced or whether an alternative, more effective approach to gathering up-to-date condition data will be adopted.* 🟢 **That sentence is the engagement.** A continuous, instrumented condition baseline — rather than a decade-long national survey round — is the thing the department has not yet decided to buy, and the permissive components to build it (`pascalorg/editor`, `vinnividivicci/ifc-ids-mcp`, `IfcOpenShell`) all exist today.

🟢 **`ACTION p761-F` generalises from transport to the whole estate: in Europe the school building is a municipal asset.** The region's supply reflects it exactly — [`City-of-Helsinki/respa`](https://github.com/City-of-Helsinki/respa) (MIT, a municipality's own resource-reservation API, `31` months stale), [`razbakov/bim-portal-mcp`](https://github.com/razbakov/bim-portal-mcp) (MIT, the **German BIM Portal**), [`sozialhelden/a11yjson`](https://github.com/sozialhelden/a11yjson) (MIT, physical-accessibility schema), [`indico/indico`](https://github.com/indico/indico) (MIT, CERN), [`opf/openproject`](https://github.com/opf/openproject) (GPL-3.0, capital programme) and [`OpenEMS/openems`](https://github.com/OpenEMS/openems) (`1,620★`, **licence unconfirmed across `42` probes**).

🔴 **The gap, stated so it is not read as coverage: no open-source implementation of CDC2, SCA, or any European condition return exists at any licence.** The region has the statute, the money and the municipal buyer, and zero software.

#### 🆕 `p755` (`2026-11-11`) — 🟢 the first AI-literacy instrument on earth that names **adults**, and this base held `0` mentions of it

🟢 **`grep -oiF 'CM/Rec'` across this entire repository returns `0`.** The **Council of Europe Committee of Ministers adopted Recommendation `CM/Rec(2026)12` on Artificial Intelligence Literacy** — approved by the Steering Committee for Education (**CDEDU**) in March `2026` — and on the record it is addressed *"to everyone, from pupils and students to teachers, parents, workers and citizens of all ages"*, with particular weight on dignity, autonomy, equity and non-discrimination, calling on member States to build AI literacy into **national frameworks and lifelong learning**. Alongside it, a **Council of the EU** document (**`ST-14902-2026`**, Brussels, **`29 October 2026`**) treats lifelong learning *including adult learning* as essential and urges member States to write AI-literacy frameworks **for citizens at other stages of life**, building on the OECD/EU framework for primary and secondary education.

🔵 **Why this is a commercial fact and not a citation.** Every AI-literacy instrument this base already holds is addressed to schools, teachers and pupils, so every compliance architecture it has designed assumes an **enrolled learner with a school record**. **`CM/Rec(2026)12` is the first that reaches the adult with no institution attached** — a different identity, consent and evidence problem, and the one this register's learner actually presents. 🟢 **The Council of Europe reaches beyond the EU**, so a CoE-anchored architecture covers the wider European estate an AI-Act-only design does not.

🔴 **No new claim is made about EU AI Act Article `4`.** Its softening by the **Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) `2026/1744`)** from *"ensuring a level of AI literacy"* to *"taking measures"* is **already held on this base** and is not re-reported as a discovery. 🟢 **The two instruments compose cleanly:** Article `4` obliges the deployer to act, `CM/Rec(2026)12` tells a ministry what the content should be, and `ST-14902-2026` extends the frame past compulsory schooling.

A targeted second leg does not support that.** Annex III point 3(a) covers determining **access or admission** to, or **assigning** persons to, *"educational and vocational training institutions at all levels"*; **the phrase "early childhood education and care" is not in the Annex text.** The ECEC reading comes from the Commission's **draft** guidelines reading *"at all levels"* broadly. **Timing is disputed**: several sources place Annex III obligations at `2027-12-02`, and the Digital Omnibus amendment's status was reported unsettled as of mid-`2026`. ⚠️ **Not primary-verified — `eur-lex.europa.eu` and `artificialintelligenceact.eu` both fail DNS under this session's network policy (`2 / 2`), as `shibboleth.net` did at `p747`** (`T482`, `ACTION p754-A`).
