🟢 **`T404` is the reusable insight for APAC business development: NREN code is a reuse network, not
a set of national silos.** The AAF's registry runs New Zealand's federation; Japan's national
discovery service is a maintained Swiss derivative, still carrying SWITCH's 2012 grant and pushed
`2026-10-22`. **A platform validated at one NREN is a credible proposal at the next one** — which is
exactly how a regional practice should be sold.

🔴 **The risk to raise in an APAC engagement, measured:** `org:GakuNin` is `5` repositories,
**`5 / 5` indexed `NOASSERTION`**, and of the two byte-probed one has a clean BSD-3-Clause and the
other (`orthros-docs`, pushed `2026-11-06`) has **no grant at `7` probed paths**. `org:AARNet` has
`18` repositories and **no identity estate at all** — its top row is a GitBook of digital skills.
🔵 **Actively maintained and clearly licensed are different properties here, and establishing the
second costs one `curl` per repository.**

**Regulation and demand — new 2026 instruments, mixed sourcing.** 🆕 **The Philippines' DepEd
launched `AGAP.AI` in January 2026**, a nationwide responsible-AI programme targeting **`1.5M`
students, teachers and parents**, alongside a **National Education Plan 2026–2035** that embeds AI
and digital literacy from primary school through university — 🟢 **the clearest ministry-scale buyer
signal in the region this pass found, and it is a programme rather than a guideline.**
⚠️ **EdTech Hub (March 2026)** puts South-East Asian teacher AI use at ~`86%` (primary source
unverified); ⚠️ **Times Higher Education (April 2026)** finds uptake of advanced tools **uneven**
across Asia with connectivity a likely constraint and virtual-tutor use at `30%`; the **Ipsos
Education Monitor 2026** records weaker public support for classroom AI bans across the Asian
markets it covers. 🔵 **Read together: high individual use, low institutional readiness, and at least
one national programme with a budget** — the same shape the identity layer is sold into, because a
`1.5M`-person programme cannot be run on per-service passwords.

#### 🆕 p746 — APAC

**Regulation — APAC now supplies the only *dated and closing* compliance window on this page.**
- 🆕 🟢 **South Korea — the AI Basic Act entered into force `22 January 2026`.** It regulates
  **high-impact** AI, **education included**, and the ministry (MSIT) has indicated that **2026 is
  effectively a pilot/grace period with guidance rather than penalties**.
  🔵 **This is the sharpest commercial read in the region and it is a clock, not a principle:** a
  grace period that is already running is a dated deadline for every education provider operating
  in Korea, and it closes *before* the EU's `2 December 2027`. **The EU is the louder regime; Korea
  is the sooner one.**
- 🆕 **Vietnam — the Law on Artificial Intelligence took effect `1 March 2026`.** It complements
  the instrument this base already holds (`Decision 33/2026/QD-TTg`), which names education —
  **specifically automated assessment and behavioural monitoring** — as high-risk. ⚠️ Sources
  disagree on a separate August 2026 compliance date for identified systems; **the disagreement is
  recorded, not resolved.**
- **China** — Generative AI Services Management Measures and synthetic-content identification rules,
  effective `1 September 2025`; the MoE subject rename for 2026–27 is carried from `p741`.
- **Japan** — principles-based, relying on cooperation and existing law rather than penalties.
  **Singapore** — frameworks and toolkits (`AI Verify`). 🔵 Both are *non-instrument* regimes: the
  deliverable there is evidence of governance, not a filing.
- **Australia** — no AI-specific statute, but **TEQSA requires all higher-education providers to
  file institutional action plans** addressing generative-AI risk (carried). 🔵 The regulator asks
  for a document, which makes the document the deliverable.
- ⚠️ **EU spillover is a real APAC constraint:** APAC providers serving EU learners fall in scope of
  the Annex III regime above.

**Adoption — nil for the fifth consecutive pass, and it is a measured nil.**

#### 🆕 `p745` (2026-11-10) — 🟢 the APAC regulation nil breaks: Vietnam names automated assessment as high-risk, and it is the first APAC instrument this base holds that is *about this tier*

🟢 **`Decision No. 33/2026/QD-TTg`, issued `2 July 2026`, classifies education — naming
automated assessment systems explicitly — among Vietnam's high-risk sectors.** This is the first
*named, dated, assessment-specific* APAC instrument on this base, and it matters out of proportion
to Vietnam's market size for one reason: **it is Annex III's structure appearing outside Europe.**
A studio that builds `P226`/`P227` to the EU shape has built to Vietnam's shape too, and the
reusability of a compliance architecture across jurisdictions is the thing that makes it worth
building once rather than per-engagement.

**The rest of the regional surface, which is general-purpose rather than education-specific:**

- 🔴 **China — the only binding regime of the three majors.** Layered rules over algorithms, deep
  synthesis and generative AI; public-facing services need **security assessment and algorithm

  labelling rule is the operative one: a generated exam item or an AI-written feedback comment is
  labelled content.
- **Japan — the AI Promotion Act is a fundamental law with no penalties**, relying on cooperation
  and existing law. ⚠️ Note the contrast with `p744`'s MEXT guidance finding, which constrains

- **India — no standalone AI law**; stated priority is innovation over regulation. ⚠️ Sources
  conflict on whether India mandates AI content labelling or merely urges notices; **published as
  a conflict, not averaged.**
- **Adoption ordering (general AI, not education):** Singapore leads, then Australia, Korea,
  Taiwan. ⚠️ Two sources disagree on China's position — one places it behind Japan/India, another
  ranks it 12th globally and *ahead* of Australia, Korea, Japan and India. **Unresolved; both recorded.**

| Jurisdiction | Instrument | What it means for a vendor |
|---|---|---|
| **Japan** | **Act on Promotion of R&D and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies**, passed **May 2025** — a *framework* law, promotion-first rather than prohibition-first. Education guidance **explicitly warns against inputting personal or sensitive data** into generative systems; guidelines released with **named pilot schools** while the government decides what to regulate | 🔵 **A data-handling constraint, not an approval gate.** A design that keeps student records out of the model context satisfies it by construction — which is exactly why `P224` starts at the catalogue rather than the student |

2026** (published **January 2026**) cites an **evaluation of Shiksha Copilot**, the AI-assisted
lesson-planning tool used in Indian schools. 🔵 **This is the first *named, evaluated* APAC
deployment this base holds** — and for a studio proposal an evaluated pilot in a comparable
jurisdiction is worth more than a regional adoption percentage, because it names the intervention,
the setting and the measure.

🟢 **Market and players**, secondary: **Embibe** (India, AI explanation of maths and science
concepts); **PhysicsWallah IPO'd at ~`$5B` in November 2025** — the clearest public-market
validation in the region; **TAL** pivoted into **AI learning hardware** after the 2021 tutoring
ban; **ByteDance's Gauth** became a top education app in the US; **Squirrel AI** (carried).
🔵 **Read the regional history as the risk disclosure it is:** China banned a `~$100B` private
tutoring industry almost overnight in July 2021 and India's BYJU'S collapsed into insolvency. **The
hardware and institutional-infrastructure plays survived the policy shock; the consumer tutoring
plays did not.** That is the argument for entering APAC at the institutional layer.

#### 🆕 `p743` (2026-11-10) — the first education-specific instruments, and a measured supply nil in this pass's tier

🟢 **`T370`: APAC now has operative education-AI provisions, not only sentiment.** **Vietnam Decision `33/2026/QD-TTg`** names education among six high-risk sectors and **names automated assessment explicitly** — the most directly usable provision this base holds for the region. **South Korea's AI Basic Act** has been in force since **`22 Jan 2026`**, with enforcement decrees unfinished and a **guidance-first grace period through 2026**. **Australia's TEQSA** requires **every** higher-education provider to file an **institutional action plan** on generative-AI risk.

🔵 **The deliverable is therefore a document, and the regulator has already specified it.** An institutional action plan (AU) and an automated-assessment risk file (VN) are both writable work with a named recipient — the cheapest credible entry into a region where this base has no adoption data. Regional shape for positioning: comprehensive risk-based statutes (South Korea, Vietnam) · targeted regulation (China) · light-touch and principles-based (Japan, Singapore, Australia).

🔴 **Supply nil in this pass's tier, and it was measured rather than assumed.** `org:jpcoar` — Japan's national open-access consortium — returns **`2` repositories (`9★`, `2★`), with no grant on either**. `org:NII-Japan` returns `422`: no such organisation under that name. Against `org:scieloorg`'s **`158`** and `org:lareferencia`'s **`38`**, **LATAM's scholarly infrastructure is on GitHub under reachable organisation names and APAC's is not.** That is a discovery-surface finding, not a claim that the systems do not exist — Japanese and Korean national infrastructure may well be published elsewhere or under names this pass could not reach.

🔴 **Declared gap, third consecutive pass: no APAC classroom or institutional adoption percentages at usable quality.** `p737`'s Ipsos ban-support series (`23 %` Indonesia → `31 %` South Korea, AU/NZ higher) is still the only quantified reading, and **ban-support is not adoption** — the Anglophone APAC markets remain the restrictive ones, which inverts the usual framing.

#### 🆕 `p741` (2026-11-10) — two national curriculum mandates on dated calendars, a regulator that names education high-risk, and `0` promoted rows from the region

🟢 **The demand side is the strongest of the four regions this pass, and it is curriculum
procurement rather than tooling procurement.** **China's Ministry of Education** has formalised the
school subject under a new title — **"Artificial Intelligence and Technology"** — for the
**2026–2027** year, which one analysis reads as long-term infrastructure commitment rather than a
pilot. **India** plans **AI and computational thinking in every school from Grade 3, beginning the
2026–27 academic year**, under NEP 2020. 🔵 **A mandated subject across a national school system is
teacher training, curriculum authoring and assessment at national scale** — the engagement shape
`p693` identified for the UAE, now confirmed in the region's two largest systems.

🔴 **And the regulatory picture is genuinely divergent, so it must be sized per country.** Binding
regimes in **South Korea, China and Vietnam**; **Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia and India**
relying on existing law, guidance and targeted rules. 🔴 **Vietnam lists education among its
high-risk AI sectors explicitly, naming automated assessment and behavioural monitoring** — which
is the most directly product-shaping instrument found in the region to date and lands on exactly
the two features an assessment or engagement-analytics product ships. **India's amended IT Rules
require labels on AI-generated content from `20 February 2026`**, already in force. ⚠️ Sources
disagree on whether India's framework is voluntary guidance or binding; **both readings are
recorded rather than averaged.**

🟡 **The opinion data reproduces `p693`'s inversion and should still size the change-management
line.** Ipsos **Education Monitor 2026** support for *banning* AI in schools: **Indonesia `23%`,
India `26%`, South Korea `31%`** — against New Zealand `47%` and Australia `52%` from the prior
read. 🔵 **The same product is a tailwind sale in Jakarta or Delhi and a headwind sale in
Melbourne.** ⚠️ `ipsos.com` does not resolve here (`P693-I`); secondary throughout.

#### 🆕 `p740` (2026-11-10) — India has put AI on a dated curriculum calendar, and the stack it will run on is MIT

🟢 **Demand leg: the region's firmest calendar in any market this base covers.** India's Ministry
of Education announced (October 2025) that **AI and Computational Thinking will be introduced
progressively from Class 3 in 2026–27**, with **Classes 9 and 10 following in 2027–28**,
coordinated with **CBSE, NCERT, KVS, NVS** and the state and Union Territory authorities. Alongside
it: CBSE already offers a **15-hour AI skills module from Class VI** with AI as an optional subject
for Classes IX–XII, and a **45-hour *AI for Educators* module** runs under SOAR covering AI
pedagogy, classroom tool use, project design and ethics. ⚠️ The curriculum dates come from
practitioner guides rather than the gazette; cite the MoE announcement and the school year, not a
circular number.

🔵 **Why a dated curriculum mandate is a better signal than an adoption percentage.** It names the
year, the grade and the coordinating bodies — so the procurement that follows it is **scheduled**,
not speculative, and teacher-capability work (the `45`-hour module) is the part that must happen
first. **That is a training-and-content engagement with a published deadline**, which is rarer in
this industry than it sounds.

🟢 **And the delivery substrate is permissive.** **Sunbird** — the open-source stack anchoring
**DIKSHA**, developed and maintained by the **EkStep Foundation**, described by a 2026 *British
Journal of Educational Technology* evaluation as a public–private partnership upgraded toward a
**Personalised Adaptive Learning** experience — is **MIT across the estate**. p740 promoted two
components with their grants byte-read:
[`sunbird-telemetry-sdk`](https://github.com/project-sunbird/sunbird-telemetry-sdk) (MIT,
`7dde06716f25`) and
[`sunbird-ml-workbench`](https://github.com/project-sunbird/sunbird-ml-workbench) (MIT,
`4ff07e32ea3b`, holder `EkStep`).

⚠️ **One discrepancy to carry rather than smooth over.** The publisher's own description is
*"a micro-services stack of more than 100 building blocks"*; the GitHub organisations expose **`77`
repositories under `project-sunbird` and `58` under `Sunbird-Ed`**, and `p739` measured all `77` as
MIT. **The "100+ building blocks" figure is architectural, not a repository count** — do not quote
it as one.

uncorrected machine transcript is not publishable, and the correction interface is the expensive

#### 🆕 `p737` (2026-11-10) — the attitude numbers `p736` called unobtainable, and the Anglophone markets are the restrictive ones

🟢 **`p736` declared a gap: "no APAC classroom-adoption percentages obtainable at usable quality."
`p737` closes it partially, and the caveat must travel with the numbers.** The **Ipsos Education
Monitor 2026** measures **support for *banning* AI in schools**: **`23 %` in Indonesia rising to
`31 %` in South Korea**, with **Australia and New Zealand higher than either**, and support **rising**
in **Japan, Australia and South Korea**.

⚠️ **This is a ban-support series, not an adoption series** — it does not say what share of
classrooms use AI, and it must not be restated as if it did (`T322`). 🟢 **But it answers the
question a regional pitch actually turns on: how much public permission exists.**

🔵 **Two consequences that invert the usual framing of this region.** First, **APAC is not one
market on this axis, and the Anglophone APAC markets are the *more* restrictive ones** — a pilot in
Australia or New Zealand faces more public opposition than one in Indonesia, and the opposition is
growing. Second, **where ban-support is rising, the deliverable is the safeguard rather than the
capability**: the consent surface, the parental story and the opt-out are what make a deployment
survivable, which is `P196` adapted to the regional noun (TEQSA's **institutional action plan**).

🟢 **Regulatory position, firmed up and dated.** **South Korea's AI Basic Act entered into force
`22 January 2026`** — the region's first comprehensive AI statute. **Vietnam's Law on AI is in force
from `1 March 2026`**, with longer transition windows for systems already operating and **education
among the sectors given an extended period**. **India** has governance guidelines plus **binding
labelling rules for synthetic content from `20 February 2026`**. **China** regulates by targeted
instrument; **Japan and Singapore** remain voluntary-framework and toolkit-led (AI Verify);
**Australia** relies on existing law plus guidance. ⚠️ **No APAC jurisdiction was found with an
education-specific AI law** — education appears as a sector carve-out or an extended transition
inside general AI statutes.

🟡 **Supply finding, and it is thin but non-zero.** `T305` ("APAC supply is no longer only CJK") has
now gone **two consecutive passes unconfirmed**, and `p736` recorded every one of its APAC rows as
CJK or Korean. `p737` files **two Indian rows under MIT** —
`ELEVATE-Project/mentoring-bap-service` (`7★`) and `ELEVATE-Project/user` (`3★`), teacher mentoring
built on India's Beckn/DPI protocol stack. 🔵 **The architecture is the finding rather than the star
count: mentoring as a protocol-mediated market, with separate consumer and provider services, is how
a national system reaches teachers across thousands of institutions without one platform owning the
relationship** — the shape every ministry-scale APAC engagement eventually needs (`T328`'s
companion finding, `T305` partially confirmed). ⚠️ **The rest of the Indian DPI estate did not
qualify:** `org:tekdi`, `org:Samagra-Development` and `org:Shikshalokam` returned **`0` fileable
rows between them** — the top repositories carry **no licence at all**, or were last pushed in 2024.
**An unlicensed national-scale estate is a real obstacle, and it is stated here rather than glossed.**


#### 🆕 `p736` (2026-11-10) — three divergent regimes, a regulator that mandates a plan, and institutional publishers shipping production pipelines

| Jurisdiction | Instrument | Status / what it requires |
|---|---|---|

| **China** | targeted regulation | Sector instruments rather than a horizontal act |
| **Japan, Singapore** | light-touch | Principles and guidance |

#### 🆕 `p735` (2026-11-10) — the region finally yields an adoption number, the institutional calendar is the channel, and the supply is no longer only CJK

measurements are survey-grade* — and that is progress worth recording.

**The institutional calendar, which is the actual procurement channel.** Unlike EMEA (a statute) and
North America (state bills), APAC's AI-in-education agenda moves through convened bodies and dated
programmes:

| Body / programme | What it is | When |
|---|---|---|

| **Acer Edu Summit Asia Pacific** | vendor-led device/infrastructure channel | 2026 |
| Teacher-training rollout | **`34,000` leading teachers** trained through 2026 | 2026 |

training-record deliverable sized to a `34,000`-teacher rollout (`P187`), is selling into a

**Demand drivers.** The fastest-emerging region and, uniquely, the **largest open-source
supplier** in this industry — the two biggest education agents on the shelf (DeepTutor, HKU;
OpenMAIC, Tsinghua) are both APAC academic projects. Adoption is uneven and connectivity is
a real constraint; Times Higher Education (April 2026) reported patchy uptake with virtual
tutor adoption at **30%**. The APAC EdTech market is highly fragmented — one paid report
counts **>3,000 players**.

**Regulation.** The **UAE** introduced **25 generative-AI prohibitions** for schools in
February 2026 (age suitability, privacy, academic integrity, exams) — the most prescriptive
national rule set found. Ipsos' *Education Monitor 2026* found notably **lower public support
for banning AI in schools** across Asian markets, i.e. permissive public sentiment.
Institutional coordination is the stated bottleneck: investment needs to be "more coordinated"
to unlock regional potential. The World Bank ran a Global EdTech Policy Academy on AI in
Seoul, 31 Aug – 4 Sep 2026.

**Opportunity.** (1) **Productise APAC academic research** — DeepTutor and OpenMAIC are
permissively licensed (Apache-2.0, MIT) research artefacts at 57k and 43k stars with no
commercial wrapper; hardening them for enterprise is the single highest-leverage play in
this KB. (2) **National-exam-aligned tutoring**, where the corpora are already open
(GAOKAO-Bench, gaokaomath 1952–2026). (3) **Offline-first delivery** via Kolibri (MIT) for
low-connectivity systems. (4) Gulf-state compliance packaging against the UAE rule set.

##### 🔴 New at p723 — a cited Philippine "national AI framework" does not exist, and the APAC adoption denominator is missing for a seventh pass

- 🔴 **The claim:** a quarterly industry note states that the Philippines' Commission on
  Higher Education issued **"Memorandum Order 21, a national framework for AI in teaching,
  research and operations."** Searched this pass: **no such issuance was found.** What the
  record shows instead is a policy *in formation* — CHED **"eyeing a comprehensive national
  AI policy"** (March 2026); a **CHED RAISE 2026** summit (February 2026) at which
  institutions, student representatives and industry partners signed a digital commitment to
  a *proposed* framework; an August 2026 CHED push for **ASEAN regional cooperation** on AI
  under its ACHIEVE agenda; and new CHED technical panels planned for AI and data analytics.
  The 2026 CMOs that do exist cover other subjects entirely — **CMO 18 s.2026** is student
  affairs and services, **CMO 05 s.2026** is health and well-being.
- 🔵 **Why this is worth filing rather than dropping.** The Philippines is at the stage
  where the framework is being *written*, which is a materially different and better
  commercial position than a jurisdiction that already has one: **contributing to the
  reference implementation is available here and is not available in Korea, Vietnam or
  Australia.** A pass that had accepted "MO 21" as issued would have scoped a compliance
  engagement against a non-existent instrument and missed the actual window.
- 🟢 **Supply:** [`Samson-Ho/GSAT-Tutor`](https://github.com/Samson-Ho/GSAT-Tutor) (7★,

### LATAM

#### 🆕 `p768` — 🟢 the region with the **most school-specific instrument on the register**, a public federal registry to verify it against, and a supply that is large, Portuguese, and almost entirely grant-less

🟢 **Brazil holds the only instrument on this register that names school transport in the statute and attaches the consequence to the right to operate.**

| Instrument | What it sets |
|---|---|
| **CTB (Lei 9.503/1997) Art. `105`** | 🟢 the **cronotacógrafo is mandatory, school transport named explicitly** |
| **CTB Art. `136`** | 🟢 a **`semiannual` safety inspection of every vehicle used to transport schoolchildren**, 🟢 **as a condition of the authorisation issued by the traffic authority** — so a lapse costs the right to carry children, not a fine |
| **CONTRAN Resolution `938/2022`** | 🟢 minimum technical requirements for the tachograph, in force since **`1 April 2022`** |
| Calibration (*aferição*) | 🟢 **publicly verifiable at `cronotacografo.rbmlq.gov.br`** — a federal registry the deliverable can check an expiry date against |
| **MP 1.343/2026** | 🔴 would allow tachograph records as evidence of speeding; reported passed and awaiting sanction in July 2026, **final status unconfirmed** |

🔵 **And the enforcement posture is unusually public:** **Ipem-SP**, a state metrology institute, publishes back-to-school guidance telling **parents** to check the device's certificate before hiring a school van. **The buyer here has a public-facing accountability the other three regions do not** — which makes a verifiable compliance record a marketing asset, not only a legal one (`P349`).

🔴 **The region's open-source supply is the largest this base has ever measured on a register, and that is a trap.** `gestao de frota` returns **`812`** repositories and `gestion de flota` **`482`** — against `fleet compliance management` at `151` in English. 🔴 **Ranked by stars the Portuguese and Spanish clusters are coursework and capstone projects at `1`–`7★`, overwhelmingly carrying no grant at all.** The usable rows are small and few: `OneBus/OneBus-API` (**MIT**, `5★`), `RamomRicarto/sistema-gestao-frota` (**MIT**, `4★`), `XAndresViverosX/FleetManager` (**MIT**, `3★`), `tecno-consultores/RoSGrid` (**GPL-3.0**, `2★`, the register's only MCP server). 🟢 **The lesson is stated as a rule rather than a complaint: volume in a non-English query predicts nothing about grants; the data owner does** (`T690`, `768-N`).

🔴 **And the orthography defect is a LATAM problem first.** `tacografo` returns **`57`** repositories, `tacógrafo` returns **`28`**, and they are different result sets — **GitHub does not fold diacritics**, so the correct Portuguese and Spanish spelling reaches the smaller bucket (`T689`, `ACTION p768-A`).

**AI-in-education context for the region:** adoption is ahead of governance on both measures. The **Digital Education Council's 2026 LATAM survey** reports **`92%` of students and `79%` of faculty** actively engaging with AI; **UNESCO IESALC** surveyed `200` institutions across `19` countries and found **`87%` using AI but only `26%` with a formal AI strategy**; in Brazil **`53%` of school administrators use AI while only `22%` report school guidelines**. A **Universidad de los Andes** study counts **`716` AI-related regulatory instruments and proposals across `23` countries**, **more than `80%` initiated since 2023**. Brazil's legislature is considering an EU-style framework; **Argentina** submitted a bill reported to commit to keeping AI unregulated; **Colombia** adopted CONPES 4144 in February 2025; **Uruguay** was the first in the region to sign the Council of Europe's AI framework convention (2025). **UNESCO launched a regional Observatory on AI in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean in April 2026** with CAF, CENIA, Cetic.br/NIC.br, ECLAC, Fundación Ceibal, Fundación Santillana, Tecnológico de Monterrey and ProFuturo.


#### 🆕 `p767` — 🟢 the region with the **most codified instrument on this register**, which inverts this base's regional default — and the region whose supply exists, is school-shaped, and has no grants

🟢 **`T678`: on this register LATAM holds the most specific instrument and North America the least.** That is the opposite of this base's usual gradient, and it changes what a LATAM engagement is: **here you encode levels, where in the United States you have nothing to encode.**

**ABNT NBR 16246-3 — *Avaliação de risco de árvores*** (first edition 2019) defines **three assessment levels**:

| Level | Method (search-sourced) |
|---|---|
| **Level 1** | Limited visual analysis — permitted *on foot, by vehicle, by drone or other form of aerial inspection* |
| **Level 2** | 🟢 **360° external visual analysis with hand tools** — the level a school estate will actually buy |
| **Level 3** | Advanced instrumentation — tomography, radar, penetrometers |

The series runs **Part 1** (pruning of trees, shrubs and other woody plants in urban areas, which itself requires a visual inspection of every target tree before work), **Part 2** (arboricultural safety, in preparation), **Part 3** (risk assessment), **Part 4** (planting and transplanting, in preparation).

🟢 **And a municipal regulator has already narrowed the national standard** — the same shape `p766` found in São Paulo for playgrounds (`T668`): **Niterói's municipal arboriculture manual directs that Levels 1 and 3 are not to be applied locally and that assessment should preferentially be at Level 2.** Capivari (SP) cites NBR 16246-1 in its own management guide. 🟢 **Make the permitted level set a per-municipality configuration, not a constant** (`P342`).

🔴 **Caveats, stated rather than buried.** ABNT normative text is **copyrighted and was not read**; every level description above is search-sourced. A claimed **March 2025 revision of NBR 16246-3** appears only on a vendor blog and **is unconfirmed against ABNT** — state the edition as *2019, revision status unconfirmed*. 🔴 **No tree-inspection instrument was found for Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Colombia or Peru** in the sources read; Brazil is the only LATAM jurisdiction on this register with a national standard.

🟢 **The most useful single artefact in this region is the one with no licence.** `inventario-arboreo-escolar` is **the only *school* tree inventory on GitHub in any language** — exactly this register's buyer and exactly its asset. **Read it as a requirements document; take no code** (`P342`).

🔴 **The most interesting is the one with a non-`main` default branch.** `ArborRisk` is tree **risk** analysis plus register, built by an AI coding agent (its default branch is `claude/arborisk-github-deploy-fsowc6`, its evidence file is a `CLAUDE.md`), and it specifies **ISA-type reports applied in Argentina** — **the North American method crossing into a jurisdiction whose region has its own standard.** 🔴 Every root-path probe on this address returns nothing, because the branch is not `main`: a concrete case for deriving `default_branch` rather than guessing it (`T671`).

🔴 **And the one that looks most like the product forbids being used.** `neocizee/arboladoMun`, a Django REST backend for a municipal tree register, carries *"Proprietary License … All Rights Reserved"*: no commercial use, no modification, no derivative works, **no production use** — while GitHub indexes it `NOASSERTION`, the same value it shows for genuine Apache-2.0 and genuine AGPL-3.0 payloads. **Second consecutive register with this exact shape** (`T682`, `767-A`).

**Education-market context for this region (attribution applied):**
- 🔵 **Adoption is high and governance is absent — the sources agree on this and it is the region's defining gap.** The **Digital Education Council's AI in Higher Education LATAM Survey 2026**, run with **Tecnológico de Monterrey**, reports **`92%` of students and `79%` of faculty** actively engaging with AI, from `7,319` faculty responses across `29` institutions.
- 🔵 A **UNESCO IESALC** survey covering `200` institutions in `19` countries found the gap between adoption and institutional governance especially wide in the region; a UNESCO IESALC / UNU-IAS working paper maps adoption across teaching, research, community engagement, administration and governance and calls for stronger governance and digital-literacy investment. Times Higher Education's coverage summarises adoption as *"neither uniform nor evenly distributed"*, with notable gaps between private and public universities.
- 🔵 One survey quotation states plainly that **there is a lack of formal policies for the use of AI in universities in Latin America.** 🔴 **No national AI-in-education regulatory framework was found for Brazil, Mexico or Argentina** in the sources read — an informed gap, not an absence of interest.
- 🔵 The **IDB** has catalogued **`193`** AI initiatives across the region and reports that Latin America is building hybrid, context-sensitive systems rather than importing models wholesale. **EdTech Hub and Fundación Ceibal** announced a partnership to help regional education systems respond to AI.
- 🔴 MarketsandMarkets publishes regional AI-in-education estimates; **treated as market-research figures and not relied on here.**


#### 🆕 p766 — 🟢 the LATAM instrument **exists and is specific** — ABNT NBR 16071 **Part 7** — and a municipal regulator has already published that the national standard is defective

**Register: playground-equipment inspection** (`ACTION p765-E`). This pass expected to declare a LATAM gap and **found an instrument instead**, which is the opposite of this register's pattern elsewhere.

**ABNT NBR 16071** is a multi-part Brazilian standard — Part 1 terminology, Part 2 safety requirements, Part 3 impact-absorbing surfaces, Part 5 play-area design, Part 8 inclusive playgrounds — and **Part 7 (`NBR 16071-7`, 2012 edition) is specifically *inspection, maintenance and use***. That is the direct counterpart to EN 1176-7. 🔵 **Honest limits, both recorded:** 2021 editions are cited for some parts, so **Part 7's current edition is unconfirmed**; and the press claim that Part 1 is *mandatory* for residential condominiums is journalism, not legal text, and is not relied on here.

🔴 **And the sharper finding: a regulator has published that the standard does not work.** São Paulo's **Resolução CPA/SMPED 033/2025** establishes complementary municipal requirements **because** NBR 16071 Part 8 (inclusive playgrounds) *"possui diversas inconsistências o que dificulta sua aplicação"* — it has several inconsistencies that impede its application. **A municipality documenting that the national standard is unusable, and legislating around it, is a procurement event**: it creates a per-municipality compliance surface that nothing in open source addresses (`T668`, `P339`).

🔴 **Supply against this instrument is nil, measured and stated.** `NBR 16071` is **`0`** across this entire base. `search/repositories` returns **no repository** naming NBR 16071, and **no new work in LATAM on this register was found on either the repository or the code channel this pass.** The register's only permissive agent is EMEA, its only permissive platform is APAC, and LATAM has **neither** — while holding one of the four clearest statutory instruments. **This is the widest instrument-to-supply gap this register shows in any region.**

**Market context:** adoption is high and governance is not. The UNESCO/CEPAL **Observatorio de IA en Educación** for Latin America and the Caribbean reports **`92%`** of higher-education students using AI tools regularly (Google's August 2026 figures: **`92%`** of university students, **`79%`** of teachers — a commercial source). A regional survey covering **`200` higher-education institutions across `19` countries** (August–October 2025) supplies the institutional-governance baseline. Against that, the region *"carece de un marco regulatorio unificado"* on AI in higher education, and ProFuturo/OEI find basic-education adoption *"desigual y limitada"* relative to other regions. The IDB published an October 2026 report, linked to PISA 2025, on whether Latin American schools are ready for their students' AI use, and runs the regional **"IA Presente"** call.


#### 🆕 p765 — **two real artefacts on this exact register**, Chile's is the only legible national instrument, and the building-level census does not exist in any of the three largest systems

**Register: school-estate safety and statutory compliance.** This is the first pass in which LATAM contributes **working code** on the register rather than only demand-side figures — and the first in which the demand side comes back largely empty, which is recorded as a measurement rather than passed over.

🟢 **The supply side: two artefacts, both permissive, both byte-read.**

| Repository | ★ | Grant, byte-read | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`Aikenort26/geovisor-asbesto`](https://github.com/Aikenort26/geovisor-asbesto) | `1` | **MIT** · `1,232 B` · `642b1cca083e` — **plus `CC BY 4.0` on the geographic data in `public/data` and `public/tiles`**, stated in Spanish in the payload's own tail | A **public asbestos geoviewer for Cartagena de Indias, Colombia**, carrying a national public-investment (`BPIN`) code in its own description. Index: `NOASSERTION`. 🔴 **For an asbestos geoviewer the data *is* the deliverable, so the CC BY 4.0 attribution obligation is the operative term, not the MIT grant** |
| [`Sergiorsantana/rota-segura`](https://github.com/Sergiorsantana/rota-segura) | `1` | **MIT** · `1,072 B` · `29b0c50c3abf` | Computes fire-escape routes for an arbitrary building (Brazil) |

🔵 **Also placed here by language rather than by origin**: [`AnabasaSoft/MantPro`](https://github.com/AnabasaSoft/MantPro) is a Spanish-language GMAO/CMMS with Android apps (🔴 AGPL-3.0, `34,523 B`, `0d96a4ff68ad`), which makes it the readiest copyleft reference implementation for a Spanish-speaking engagement.

🔴 **The demand side, searched in Spanish and Portuguese, and reported as found — including where it was not found.**

| Country | What was found | Grade |
|---|---|---|
| **Chile** | 🟢 **Decreto 548 MINEDUC**, approving norms for the physical plant of educational premises, **amended by Decreto 393 (2009) and Decreto 40 (2021)**. Establishments seeking any state certification **must** comply with educational-infrastructure norms; MINEDUC's `roaf.mineduc.cl` publishes the infrastructure scope for official recognition. MINEDUC also publishes a **self-diagnostic infrastructure-condition checklist** | 🟢 the only legible national instrument found in LATAM. 🔴 **The checklist is guidance, not a mandatory inspection** |
| **Brazil** | 🔴 Only **state-level laws on metal detectors and bag searches** (Acre, Rondônia). **This is physical security, not estate safety**, and does not belong to this register | 🔴 **No federal school building-safety inspection regime was found** |
| **Mexico** | 🔵 NOM-002-STPS-2010 on extinguishers, emergency exits and refuge spaces, and a SEP civil-protection committee under *Acuerdo 535* — **both blog-sourced and unverified against the DOF**. Plus an **old draft** Mexican standard (Secretaría de Economía / CAPFCE) on minimum requirements for supervising educational physical-infrastructure works | 🔴 **not a current 2026 instrument**; recorded as a draft, not as law |

🔴 **And the gap stated explicitly, so the silence is not read as coverage: no building-level school estate census was found for Brazil, Mexico or Chile.** `p764` could place `MXN 58,415M` against Mexico's 2026 infrastructure line and `14.67` lakh schools against India; **this register's equivalent — how many school buildings exist, their condition and their compliance status — returned nothing in any of the three.** A Chilean parliamentary research note of June 2026 compares school *physical security* across the US, England, Brazil and Mexico, which is the adjacent register and not this one.

🟢 **The opportunity that follows from exactly that.** Chile has the norm and a self-diagnostic checklist and no system to collect it; Colombia has a municipality that already publishes an asbestos register as open data under MIT + CC BY 4.0. **The deliverable is the collection layer between the two: ODK Central (Apache-2.0) for capture, a permissive work-order core, and the Chilean checklist encoded as the interval table that `repos/foundations.md` records as missing everywhere.** 🔵 **The Colombian geoviewer is the proof that a LATAM public buyer will publish this data openly when it has somewhere to put it.**

#### 🆕 p763 — a statutory return that allocates money for ~`40` million students, with a `2026-12-11` deadline, and a supply side of `12` repositories whose maximum is `3` stars

**Register: the education data warehouse and the statutory return.**

🟢 **Brazil has the best-documented statutory return on this register anywhere, and it is a funding instrument.** The Censo Escolar da Educação Básica 2026 runs through **Educacenso** under **Portaria Inep nº 217/2026**, and the declared structure must reflect the school as it stood on the reference date **`2026-05-27`**.

|---|---|
| Reference date (structure and staffing as declared) | **`2026-05-27`** |

| Declared data opened for checking in Educacenso | `2026-08-31` |
| Checking period extended to | `2026-09-11` |
| Deadline for corrections and complements online | `2026-10-23` *(secondary-sourced)* |

| *Indicadores de rendimento* published | `2027-05-14` |

🟢 **The `2026-12-11` transmission to the FNDE is why this register has a budget in LATAM**: the census is what the federal funding allocation is computed from, for roughly `40` million students. The return is annual, dated, and has no retry.

🔴 **And the supply side is a measured nil, with the denominator stated.** `censo escolar inep microdados` returns **`total_count 12`**; the **maximum star count in the entire result set is `3`**; the entries are predominantly undergraduate analyses of published microdata. The only repository naming itself a pipeline, [`kevinleandrogomes/censo-escolar-pipeline-etl`](https://github.com/kevinleandrogomes/censo-escolar-pipeline-etl), has **`0★`** and **no licence payload at `17` paths and no manifest declaration**.

🔴 **And the Spanish-language probe returns nothing at all.** `educacion datos abiertos ministerio escuelas` → **`total_count 0`**. Not a thin result set — zero. The Spanish-speaking half of the region has no discoverable open estate for ministry education data under its own vocabulary (`T613`).

🟢 **Globant's reading: this is the sharpest demand-to-supply gap this pass measured in any region.** A dated, funded, annual statutory return for `40` million students, against twelve repositories with three stars at the top and no licensed tooling. The components that would serve it are all NA- and EMEA-authored and all permissive (`P311`), so the build is a composition, not a research problem.

🔵 **Adoption context:** the Digital Education Council's 2026 LATAM survey reports `92%` of students and `79%` of faculty engaging with AI, from `7,319` faculty across `29` institutions. UNESCO IESALC published a September 2026 working paper mapping university AI use. The figure that **~`30%` of LATAM universities have published AI-use policies** is attributed to a single conference speaker whose name varies between articles and is carried as weak. UNESCO has a cooperation agreement with Chile's **CENIA** including **Latam-GPT**; EdTech Hub and **Fundación Ceibal** announced a partnership in September 2026; the IDB published a 2026 Argentina piece on regulation and financing.

🟢 **LATAM is the strongest demand region for this register by a wide margin, and the figures are government and institute data rather than vendor surveys.**

Position control against funded lines (`P308`) is not an efficiency project here — it is the budget's control surface |

| Mexico — higher education teaching staff | ~`460,000`, of whom **`70%`** are *profesores de asignatura* | SEP | An overwhelmingly hourly-contracted workforce — which is a scheduling and position-control problem before it is an HR problem |

| Honduras | `6,000`+ teachers left the public system in one year | El Heraldo | Attrition measured at national scale in a smaller system — the shape where a single engagement can cover the whole country |
| LATAM higher education — AI engagement | `92%` of students, `79%` of faculty | **Digital Education Council LATAM survey 2026** (with Tecnológico de Monterrey) | Carried from previous passes. Adoption is not the gap |

🔴 **The declared supply nil, and it is complete.** No LATAM-authored open-source artefact for any part of this register was found: no teacher-workforce system, no payroll or position-control tool, no credential-verification component, no school-staffing agent. **The region with the best-measured demand on these shelves has no measured supply.** That asymmetry is the opportunity and it is stated as a nil rather than filled with a nearest neighbour.

🔴 **And a regulatory nil.** No LATAM instrument governing AI in employment decisions was found — nothing analogous to NYC Local Law 144 or Illinois HB 3773. 🔵 **The commercial reading is two-sided:** the absence lowers the compliance cost of a `P308` engagement today, and it means a client has no external standard to point at when challenged. **The audit discipline from `P307` is worth building in voluntarily**, because the alternative is building it later under a regime that does not exist yet.

🟢 **The engagement, concretely.** `P308` — model the funded establishment rather than the headcount, project retirement and attrition per school, per subject, per certification, and keep the record in the ministry's existing payroll system, which for FONE is non-negotiable because it is a federal transfer with its own reporting obligations.

#### 🆕 `p760` (`2026-11-11`) — 🔴 LATAM is a **declared supply nil** on this register, and the displacement it would serve is the largest in the hemisphere

🔴 **Supply nil, declared with the queries that produced it.** `refugee education` and `education in emergencies` return **no Spanish- or Portuguese-language address at any star count** on the `search/repositories` channel, `2026-11-11`. 🔴 **The Venezuela displacement is the largest in the Americas and its education response has no open-source artefact of its own** (`T581`).

🔵 **Written down because an unrecorded nil looks exactly like coverage** — and it prices the region honestly: **LATAM on this register is a build, not an integration**, which is a larger and better-defined engagement than the APAC equivalent rather than a smaller one. The same verdict `p759`'s `T562` reached on the wellbeing register, from the same cause.

🟢 **LATAM remains the best-measured *demand* region on this page, and the figures are unchanged and still the strongest sell on these shelves:**

- 🟢 **`92%` of students and `79%` of faculty actively engaging with AI**, on a named **`7,319`-faculty** sample across **`29`** higher-education institutions (Digital Education Council LATAM survey `2026`).
- 🟢 **UNESCO IESALC across `200` institutions in `19` countries: `87%` using AI, `74%` in teaching, `26%` with a formal AI strategy, `55%` with no AI budget, `4%` public-university dedicated funding.**
- 🔴 **Roughly `30%` of LATAM universities have a published AI policy** — a panellist figure this base has not been able to verify against the survey report itself, and it is published with that caveat attached.

**New this leg:**

- 🟢 **UNESCO and Chile's CENIA are partnering on ethical AI in education across Latin America**, including **Latam-GPT**, an open large language model built for the region. 🔵 **For this register that is the single most important LATAM development**: a regional open base model is exactly what a Spanish- and Portuguese-language build needs, and its absence was the reason `p759` priced LATAM as a data-and-fine-tuning programme.
- 🟢 **Fundación Ceibal and EdTech Hub launched a partnership** to help education systems across Latin America and the Caribbean respond to AI; the IDB published on AI in education in Argentina and the region, including regulation and financing; ECLAC's **eLAC** digital agenda is the cooperation platform.
- 🔴 **No binding regional regulatory framework for AI in education was returned by this leg**, and the gap is recorded rather than filled from a vendor source.

🔵 **The LATAM sell is unchanged and it is the gap, not the growth rate: adoption already happened, without governance and without budget.** 🟢 **What is new is that the base model problem now has a named regional answer, which converts the LATAM build from greenfield to a fine-tuning programme over Latam-GPT.**

#### 🆕 `p751` — the scheduling and assignment register, placed in LATAM

🟢 **LATAM is the region where this register is already *operating at national scale*, and that makes it the strongest reference story in the pass.** **Chile's Sistema de Admisión Escolar (SAE)** allocates school places nationally using an adaptation of the **Gale–Shapley deferred-acceptance** mechanism, extended to Chilean law and Ministry requirements — retaining the current seat of a student who changes school, and favouring sibling assignment to the same school. The adaptation is not cosmetic: under the modified stability notions **a stable assignment may not always exist**, so the published approach breaks ties **at the family level**. A 2026 working paper characterises SAE as strategy-proof deferred acceptance with unrestricted preference lists and **full publication of the algorithm, the rules, the data and a simulator**.

🔴 **And the implementation is not open source (`T446`).** The organisation that held the Ministry contract (`2022–2024`) for maintaining the assignment code, [`ConsiliumBots`](https://github.com/ConsiliumBots), has **`7` public repositories and the assignment algorithm is not among them**. The only permissively licensed one is [`school-choice-dashboard`](https://github.com/ConsiliumBots/school-choice-dashboard) (**MIT** · `1,070 B` · sha256₁₂ `550db3b76ed5`, `0★`, last push `2025-05-20`) — **monitoring, not mechanism**. 🔵 **So the pattern is public and the code is not.** That is the opposite of the usual LATAM gap and it is unusually favourable: *the hard part — a defensible, published, legally-adapted mechanism — is documented in the open literature, and the implementation is a build.* The permissive building block is [`daffidwilde/matching`](https://github.com/daffidwilde/matching) (**MIT**, `170★`) — 🔴 **`13` months stale, and one of only `3` repositories matching `school assignment deferred acceptance`.**

🟢 **Demand is measured and the governance gap is measured with it.** A **UNESCO Observatory on AI in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean launched April 2026 at ECLAC in Santiago**. It reports that in countries such as Chile and Brazil **more than `50%` of teachers already use AI tools while fewer than `10%` of institutions have formal guidelines**. On 2024 figures: **`56%` of secondary teachers in Brazil and `55%` in Chile** had used AI in the previous year against an **OECD average of `36%`** — LATAM teachers are ahead of the OECD, not behind it. In Brazil **`53%` of school administrators use AI and only `22%` report school guidelines**. 🟢 **The `50%`-use / `10%`-guidelines spread is the engagement:** governance, audit and oversight scaffolding for AI that is already in the building.

🔵 **Regulation: the most developed framework in the region, and a status this base will not overstate.** **Brazil's PL 2338** is described as the region's most developed framework, with tiered risk categories and civil liability, with political signals pointing to a vote in **late 2026**. **Chile's** bill status is disputed in the sources read this pass — one says it cleared the lower chamber in October 2025 and sits in Senate second reading, another lists it as **Boletín 16821-19, pending**. **Peru's Ley N° 31814** (published `2023-07-05`) is identified as the first enacted national AI statute in Latin America. 🔴 **`escuela horario open source` returns `0` repositories** — the Spanish-language supply leg for this register is an outright nil, recorded as an informed gap rather than left as silence.

#### 🆕 `p750` (2026-11-10) — the wellbeing and safeguarding layer: Brazil has the region's binding instrument and it names AI review explicitly; the university tier has the problem and no measurement

🟢 **Brazil's ECA Digital is the strongest instrument in the region for this register, and unlike most
LATAM AI policy it is law with a regulator attached.** **Lei 15.211/2025**, in force since
**`2026-03-17`** (date fixed by **Lei 15.352/2026**), regulated by **Decreto 12.880/2026**, enforced by
the **ANPD**. What it does that matters here:

- It builds a **shared-responsibility model** across families, platforms, public authorities **and
  educational institutions** — i.e. the school is a named duty-holder, not a bystander.
- It targets **digital dependency and the mental health of minors**, including the inducement,
  incitement or instigation of behaviours causing **physical or mental harm**, and preventive measures
  against content encouraging **self-harm and suicide**.
- 🔴 **It requires periodic review of AI tools, with expert participation**, to ensure suitability for
  children and adolescents, with the ability to **disable non-essential functions**. 🟢 **That is a
  recurring, billable assurance obligation written into a statute** — the LATAM analogue of KCSIE's
  annual review, and the first one this base has found in the region.
- Digital and media education in the curriculum from 2026 — though the Lemann Foundation notes that duty
  already flowed from **BNCC Computação**.

⚠️ **Scope caution:** the law does not address schools in every one of its `41` articles; the school-facing
duties come from the shared-responsibility provisions plus the regulating decree. Quote the decree, not a
summary.

**The higher-education demand signal is the strongest in the region and it is a retention story.**

| Finding | Source quality |
|---|---|
| **`92%` of students and `79%` of faculty** in LATAM higher education actively engaging with AI (`7,319` faculty, `29` institutions) | Digital Education Council with **Tec de Monterrey**, 2026 — the firmest LATAM AI figure this base holds |
| Mental-health deterioration is associated with **higher dropout risk**; prevalence of mental disorders among low-performing university students exceeds general-community rates; **selective prevention targeting first-year students** is the recurring recommendation | Peer-reviewed regional literature (Redalyc, Veritas) — 🟢 the most-replicated regional finding |
| **`30–50%`** of LATAM university students do not complete their studies | ⚠️ **UNESCO-attributed via a consultancy; primary source not reached this pass** |
| Dropout rates of **`25–35%`**, linked to emotional difficulties | ⚠️ **Single journal source, methodology not verifiable** |
| Only **`30%`** of LATAM universities have published AI-use policies | ⚠️ **Single-source, carried from `p748` and still uncorroborated** |

🟢 **Institutional programmes to name in a proposal, both dated 2026:** the **Universidad de El Salvador**
launched an institutional *Ruta para la Prevención, Detección y Atención de la Conducta Suicida*, with
protocols covering students, faculty and staff — 🔵 **a university-wide protocol is exactly the artefact an
AI triage layer must route into, and it now exists as a reference**; and Mexico's **Universidad Latina de
América** ran a Mental Health Week (`2026-10-05` to `2026-10-09`) focused on early-warning signs and
emotional exhaustion.

**Regional AI-in-education actors for the register:** **UNESCO IESALC** with **UNU-IAS** (2026 working
paper mapping AI across teaching, research, administration and governance, and describing adoption as
*"neither uniform nor evenly distributed"*, with public/private gaps); **UNESCO + Chile's CENIA**
(cooperation on ethical AI in education, including **Latam-GPT**); **EdTech Hub + Fundación Ceibal**;
the **IDB**, whose agenda includes AI-supported teacher accompaniment and the regulation-and-financing

🟢 **The LATAM play, in one line:** *the statutory hook is Brazilian and recurring (`Decreto 12.880/2026`
AI review), the budget holder is a university retention office, and the channel is SMS/WhatsApp* —
which is why [`rapidpro/rapidpro`](https://github.com/rapidpro/rapidpro) (**AGPL-3.0**, `912★`, UNICEF

#### 🆕 `p749` (2026-11-10) — the alternative-format layer: the statute is the strongest in any region, the enforcement machinery is the weakest, and the university layer is thin

🟢 **Brazil has the region's clearest instrument, and on paper it is more sweeping than the US or EU
rules.** The **Lei Brasileira de Inclusão (LBI, Lei 13.146/2015)** guarantees digital accessibility across
websites, applications and online services, and **for education it requires that educational content and
platforms be accessible at *all levels* of education** — a scope statement broader than ADA Title II,
which reaches only public entities. Companion standards: **eMAG** (the government's WCAG-derived
guidelines) and the **ABNT NBR 17225** technical standard, named in a 2026 academic source. Federal
universities are required to eliminate barriers, provide assistive resources and operate
**núcleos de acessibilidade**. ⚠️ **Sources disagree on the WCAG baseline** — one cites 2.0, another
2.1 AA — so pin it per contract (`P249`'s step 3 applies here too).

🔴 **The rest of the region is government-facing, not education-facing.**
**Argentina**: **Ley 26.653** with standards set by **ONTI provision 6/2019** — aimed principally at
**government** websites. **Mexico**: a **Norma Mexicana** obliging **federal agencies** to WCAG 2.1 AA;
🔴 **nothing found this pass on Mexican *university* obligations**. **No confirmed 2026 change** was found
to either the Argentine or the Mexican instrument.

🔴 **The honest gap, stated plainly: the university-specific accessibility layer is thin across LATAM
outside Brazil, and most of the available sourcing is vendor compliance marketing rather than primary
law.** Primary texts — **Planalto** (BR), **Infoleg** (AR), **DOF** (MX) — were not reachable for
verification through this session's channels and should be read before anything is promised in writing.
⚠️ **Recorded as a measured gap rather than left silent**, because silence here reads exactly like coverage.

**The structural asymmetry that should drive the pitch.** 🟢 **LATAM's adoption numbers are the highest
of any region and its governance is the weakest** — the Digital Education Council's February 2026 survey
found **`92%` of students** and **`79%` of faculty** actively using AI (faculty component: `7,319`
respondents across `29` institutions), while only about **`30%` of Latin American universities have
published any AI-use policy**, and UNESCO IESALC's survey of `200` institutions across `19` countries found
the adoption-versus-governance gap **most pronounced in this region**. 🔵 **Accessibility conformance is the
easiest governance win to sell into that gap:** unlike AI policy, it has a statute behind it (the LBI), a
measurable pass/fail, and a deliverable a rector can point to.

**Supply — 🔴 nothing in this tier is LATAM-published, and the Portuguese/Spanish alt-format layer is
the regional gap.** All `18` rows originate in North America or Europe. 🟢 **But the permissive core is
language-agnostic**: `daisy/ace`, `w3c/epubcheck`, `daisy/MathCAT` and `eleventypub` work on
Portuguese and Spanish content unchanged, and `liblouis` (**LGPL-2.1**) already carries braille tables that
can be extended for regional needs. 🔵 **The buildable product is a Portuguese/Spanish alt-format
pipeline** — `P246` plus `P247`'s local-model alt text, which also sidesteps the data-residency objection
that LATAM public institutions raise. Regional actors to engage: **UNESCO IESALC**, **Fundación Ceibal**
(with EdTech Hub), **Tecnológico de Monterrey's Institute for the Future of Education**, **ECLAC/eLAC**,
and Chile's **CENIA**, whose UNESCO partnership covers **Latam-GPT**, an open LLM for the region.

#### 🆕 `p738` (2026-11-10) — 92% / 79% / 30%, and the reason this region reads thin on a GitHub-sourced base

🟢 **The region now has the sharpest adoption-versus-readiness triple in any region, on a named

Council**'s *AI in Higher Education LATAM Survey 2026*, run with **Tecnológico de Monterrey** and its
**Institute for the Future of Education**, reports:

| Measure | Figure |
|---|--:|
| Students actively engaging with AI | **92%** |
| Faculty actively engaging with AI | **79%** |
| Believe their institution has responded effectively | **30%** |

🔵 **The commercial reading is the inverse of the usual one. Nobody needs to be sold adoption —
adoption already happened without anyone's permission. `30%` is the sellable number**, and what it
names is institutional: an operative policy rather than a published one, a model-choice record, an
assessment-integrity position, and a faculty capability programme. 🔵 **Put the `79%` in the
proposal explicitly**, because it kills the *"our professors will resist"* objection before it is
raised; a separate DEC reading characterises that faculty use as **high adoption, conservative
usage**, which is precisely the population a capability programme converts rather than persuades.

**Corroboration, and one complication worth carrying into a bid.** A **UNESCO IESALC** working paper
(**September 2026**) finds adoption *"neither uniform nor evenly distributed"*, with a significant
**public-versus-private university gap** — so a regional offer needs two price points, not one. A
2025 UNESCO regional survey of **200 institutions across 19 countries** finds the
adoption-governance gap especially pronounced in LAC. The **IDB** has catalogued **193 AI
initiatives** across the region, which is the best available map of who is already doing what.
**EdTech Hub and Fundación Ceibal launched a partnership in September 2026** to help LAC systems
respond to AI — a named, open door for a studio with regional delivery capacity.

🔴 **And this pass closed the question of why LATAM reads thin on this base while reading first in
the world on adoption. It is not language and it is not the wrong publishers: the institutions are
not on GitHub.** `p738` ran **`14` publisher legs** at Latin American ministries, agencies and
universities — the leg type that produced *every* fileable row in this pass and in `p737`.

European ministry has already open-sourced its school platform, the work is integration into someone
else's estate. **Where a LATAM ministry has published nothing, the institutional artefact itself is
unbuilt** — the governance framework, the model-choice record, the teacher-capability programme, the

#### 🆕 `p737` (2026-11-10) — the adoption–governance scissors measured again at school level, and it is wider than in higher education

🟢 **`T319` measured the gap in universities (UNESCO IESALC: `87 %` of institutions using AI,

  programme, which is the point: **the infrastructure precondition is what distinguishes it**, not
  enthusiasm.
- **ECLAC/CENIA's ILIA 2026** covers **`20` countries** and names the region's biggest gaps as
  **compute capacity, enterprise AI adoption and the *implementation* of national strategies** —
  implementation, not authorship. 🔵 That is the single best one-line argument for a services
  engagement in this region.
- **Governance counterparties now exist to anchor a proposal.** UNESCO launched the **Observatory on
  AI in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean on `14 April 2026`**, with **CAF, CENIA,

engagement: the school district.** A `22 %`-governed estate with `53 %` usage needs a usable policy,
a teacher training record and a data boundary — **the same artefact as the higher-education
engagement, at lower cost and higher volume**, and a district is dozens of schools under one
secretariat with one decision to make. 🔵 **Lead with the client's own numbers (`53 / 22`, `75 %`):
this is not a pitch to adopt AI, it is a pitch to govern what teachers are already doing**, which is
a far easier conversation with a secretariat. Pair it with one visibly useful capability — in Brazil,
ENEM essay marking via `matheussilvano/mooose` (Apache-2.0).

#### 🆕 `p734` (2026-11-10) — the supply side is now measured too, and the region's flagship open-AI estate is unbuildable

🔴 **The headline finding of this pass for LATAM, and it is a measurement rather than an
impression.** Every regional leg this base runs names the **Latam-GPT** programme — UNESCO's
cooperation agreement with Chile's **CENIA** cites it as the regional open model. `p734` enumerated
the organisation: **`8` repositories, `7` with no licence field at all, `6` archived, and `0` that
are both live and permissively licensed.** The single MIT repository is archived; the only live code
repository carries no licence. Most recent push to any code repository: **`2025-07-09`** (`T291`).

🟢 **Combined with the demand side, this defines the engagement precisely.** LATAM has the **highest
measured usage in this base's files** — **`92 %` of students and `79 %` of faculty** actively
engaging with AI across `29` institutions (Digital Education Council, co-produced with Tec de
Monterrey) — and **`30 %`** of universities with any published AI-use policy. A UNESCO **IESALC**
working paper (September 2026) maps AI across five university dimensions including governance and
finds adoption *"neither uniform nor evenly distributed"*; an earlier UNESCO-affiliated survey of
**`200` institutions across `19` countries** found the same gap (`T296`).

🔵 **So: highest usage, lowest governance coverage, and no regional platform to build the governance
on.** The deliverable is therefore the **governance artefact itself** — an approved-tools register,
a data-residency posture, and a PII boundary for Spanish and Portuguese student data — assembled
from components the region does not supply. That is **`P181`**, and it is why an archived `1★`
repository earned a row on `repos/foundations.md`: the **Latin-American national-ID regular
expressions** in `latam-gpt/anonymization-filter` are the one piece nobody should write twice, MIT
is irrevocable, and it should be vendored and owned rather than depended on.

🟢 **Institutional actors are organising, and they are the channel:** **UNESCO–CENIA** (Chile) on
ethical AI including Latam-GPT; **EdTech Hub with Fundación Ceibal** (Uruguay) from September 2026;
**ECLAC's eLAC** agenda as the cooperation platform; **IADB** on evaluation at scale.
⚠️ **Declared gap, fourth consecutive pass:** no national AI-in-education statute was found for
**Brazil, Mexico or Chile**. The Mexico-focused source asserts a need for regulatory alignment
without naming an instrument. Searched and missing, not unsearched.

**Ceibal** (Uruguay); UNU-IAS.

`profesores`, `estudiantes`, `colegio`) enumerated a deduplicated pool of **`326` repositories**,

education technology.** This base's earlier passes recorded "no LATAM supply", which was wrong in a
misleading direction — the supply exists and is substantial; it is a *different kind of thing*.

purchase: it is **governance and assessment design on top of tooling the institution already uses**,
which is precisely `P174` (auditable mastery, frozen rubric, no new tenant) and `P175` (schedule

portability across jurisdictions is worth more than depth in one.

**Demand drivers.** The sharpest adoption/governance gap in the world, which is itself the
opportunity. A Digital Education Council survey with Tecnológico de Monterrey across 29
institutions found **92% of students and 79% of faculty** actively using AI — while
**only 30% of LATAM universities have published any AI policy** (Bossio). A UNESCO IESALC
survey of 200 institutions across 19 countries found the adoption-governance gap most
pronounced here. Compute and adoption inequality is widening within the region.

**Regulation.** **No binding national AI-in-education law was found in force in 2026** in any
LATAM country — searched and explicitly not found. Governance is arriving through
institutions and multilaterals instead: UNESCO + Chile's **CENIA** on ethical AI, including
integration of **Latam-GPT**, an open LLM built for Latin America and the Caribbean;
**EdTech Hub + Fundación Ceibal** partnership (September 2026); IADB publications on
teacher accompaniment; ECLAC's **eLAC** digital agenda. Mexico analyses call for regulatory
alignment and curriculum redesign.

**Opportunity.** (1) **Institutional AI governance** — writing the policies 70% of
universities lack is fast, well-defined, and reaches a defined buyer. (2) **Latam-GPT
integration** as a sovereignty-aligned alternative to US-hosted models, which is a
differentiator no North American competitor can match. (3) **ENEM/national-exam tutoring**,
where open structured content already exists (`enem-api`, 366★). (4) Offline-first and
low-bandwidth delivery (Kolibri, MIT). (5) Moodle and Chamilo are the incumbents here, both
GPL — so customisation is legally straightforward, unlike the AGPL North American stack.

**Supply note.** Searching Spanish education words is a dead leg (it returns teaching-demo
clones); searching the national exam is productive. Recorded so the next pass does not
repeat the mistake.

#### 🆕 p765 — the cross-region law of this register: **the code is permissive, the law is not, and which half you can obtain is decided by jurisdiction**

**Register: school-estate safety and statutory compliance.** One finding governs every region above and it is not visible in any licence file.

🔴 **On a statutory-compliance register the software is the cheap half.** `61` licence payloads were byte-read this pass and the substrate is permissive almost throughout — `25` MIT payloads, `11` Apache-2.0, the field-capture layer Apache-2.0 without exception. **The three components that are *not* usable are the three that encode the law:**

| Component | What it is | Grant | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`buildingSMART/IDS`](https://github.com/buildingSMART/IDS) | The computer-interpretable grammar in which *"this fire door shall carry an inspection date and a certificate reference"* becomes machine-checkable | **CC BY-ND 4.0** | 🔴 A national or client **profile of the specification** is refused. 🟢 `.ids` files you author are not derivatives |
| `1EdTech/caliper-js` | A standards body's reference implementation | 🔴 **moved to private repositories** | 🔴 `422`; cited `11` times on this base. **A restricted grant can be worked around; a private repository cannot** |
| [`TowerScout/TowerScout`](https://github.com/TowerScout/TowerScout) | The only artefact addressing the built-environment legionella pathway, used by real health departments, and the only one on this register that says `school` | **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0** at `LICENSE.TXT` | 🔴 **NonCommercial.** Index said `NOASSERTION` |

🔴 **The jurisdictional asymmetry is the thing to put in a proposal.** US federal regulation is a work of the United States government and carries no copyright, so the corpus can be ingested and redistributed — which is why the one artefact on this register with **no vendor in its data path** is American. England splits: HSE guidance is Crown copyright on open terms, the British Standards it points to are paid BSI products. Saudi Arabia's SBC is copyrighted, and the MIT server built to serve it ships **without the code it exists to serve**, by its own README. **The same agent is buildable in North America, half-buildable in England and not buildable from open sources in the Gulf — and the repository licence tells you none of this** (`T639`, `T637`).

🟢 **The shape of the deliverable is the same in every region, which is the commercially useful part.** England's *Manage Your Education Estate* annual return, New York's Fire and Building Safety Report, Florida's certification to the State Fire Marshal, Tamil Nadu's district audit report to the Directorate: **the output is a filed statutory return with a named signatory and a deadline, not a dashboard.** One artefact, five jurisdictions' interval tables.

🔴 **And the gap is identical everywhere: nothing models a statutory interval.** A statutory duty is a recurring date with a competent-person attribute and an evidence artefact attached. Every candidate on this register models a **work order** — a task without a legal deadline. `topic:asbestos` returns `5` repositories worldwide and `topic:legionella` returns `12`, against `topic:compliance`'s `10,822`, which is the software-compliance register (`T629`). **`5 : 10,822` is this register's structural fact: the word is crowded, the subject is not.**

🔴 **Cross-region instrument warning, carried from this pass's own defects.** Plain-language search on this register does not return a noisy answer, it returns **another discipline**: `legionella` is `24/30` microbiology, `fire risk assessment` is `22/30` wildfire, `playground inspection` is `29/30` software sandboxes. **None of `153`, `174` or `46` is a supply figure for this register** (`T628`). And `raw.githubusercontent.com` returning `200` does **not** mean an address is current — it follows renames silently where the search channel does not, which is how this base came to cite `openedx/edx-platform` `49` times while already carrying its live successor `147` times (`T635`, `T636`).

#### 🆕 `p759` (`2026-11-11`) — the direction of travel is governance and purpose-built tooling, and one mandated leg is now a known hazard rather than a thin channel

**This pass's `AI education industry trends 2026` leg, net of its defect:**

- 🟢 **From experimentation to governance.** 1EdTech frames `2026` as the year AI in education shifts from experimentation to **governance** — explicit policies, data boundaries, oversight. HolonIQ expects **selective** acceleration, with institutions favouring tools that can show instructional value.
- 🟢 **From general-purpose to purpose-built.** The movement away from generic assistants toward education-specific platforms is named as the defining trend, with the **OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook** reportedly recommending the same. 🔵 **On this register that is decisive**: a general-purpose chatbot cannot be made to satisfy `T548`'s input boundary or `T549`'s refusal rails, and a purpose-built pipeline can.
- 🟢 **AI as embedded infrastructure**, spanning admissions, advising and administration, with agentic AI moving into everyday workflows.
- 🟢 **Skills and credentials:** a skills-driven ecosystem driven by employer expectations, with verified digital credentials as the endpoint.
- 🟢 **Assessment integrity:** AI-aware rubrics that state when AI use is permitted, required or prohibited, and how it must be disclosed.

🔴 **And the leg's defect, for the second consecutive pass.** It again returned *"an April 2026 deadline for large public institutions to meet updated ADA accessibility guidelines for all web content, including vendor apps."* 🔴 **That deadline does not exist** — DOJ's Interim Final Rule of `2026-04-20` moved ADA Title II web-accessibility compliance to **`2027-04-26`** (entities serving ≥`50,000`) and **`2028-04-26`** (smaller entities and special districts), WCAG 2.1 Level AA unchanged. 🟢 **`ACTION p758-A`, adopted one pass ago for exactly this, fired on its first opportunity.** 🔵 **The finding is the reproduction rate, not the date: two passes, same leg, same superseded figure, different secondary sources — this is the steady state of the trade press on this obligation** (`T551`, `ACTION p759-B`).

**Market size — unchanged and still not quotable as a point estimate.** This pass returned **~`$10.6B`** for `2026` from one source and **~`$12.3B`** for `2026` from another (attributed to HolonIQ) — a **~`16%`** spread on the same year, consistent with the `~8%`–`5×` range this page has measured since `p657`. 🔵 **Quote the range and the direction, never a single figure**; and on this register prefer the structural ratios (`<10%` of LATAM institutions with guidelines against `>50%` teacher use) over any TAM.

#### 🆕 `p758` — the market numbers still disagree, and the direction of travel is from pilots to infrastructure

⚠️ **Market size: the published figures conflict and are recorded as a range, not reconciled.** For the AI-in-education market in 2026 the legs returned **`$10.4B`**, **">`$12.5B`"** and **`$12.3B`** (HolonIQ). 🔵 **All are vendor or market-research sources; the base's standing practice is to carry the bracket and refuse the point estimate.** ⚠️ No figure here was primary-verified (`T540`).

🟢 **The one direction every source agrees on: AI in education has moved from experiment to infrastructure**, and from standalone tools to embedding in admissions, advising and administration. 🔵 **This is the single most useful framing for an engagement conversation**, because it moves the discussion from "which tool" to "which system of record" — and the systems of record in education are open (Opencast, BigBlueButton, Moodle, Open edX), which is where a services firm has leverage that a product vendor does not.

🟢 **Purpose-built over generic.** The **OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook** urges purpose-built educational AI designed to produce durable learning gains, and multiple sources describe a move away from general-purpose assistants. 🔵 **Read commercially: the generic assistant layer is being given away at state and platform scale** (see the North America block), so the defensible work is the vertical, estate-specific, measured kind.

🔴 **The governance gap is the global constant, not a regional quirk.** Roughly **a quarter of faculty** report their institution has a formal AI policy, and most US public schools are reported to lack formal student-facing AI policies — against adoption figures of **`86%` of students across `16` countries** and **`83%` of K-12 teachers** using generative AI. ⚠️ Survey-sourced, mixed quality. 🔵 **Every region this pass measured shows the same shape, which is why the governance offer travels better than any product offer.**
