#### 🆕 `p757` (`2026-11-11`) — 🟢 the whole research-integrity screening market is **proprietary**, and that is the clearest open-source opening this base has measured

🟢 **The global finding is a market structure, and it is global because the publishers are.** Research integrity is now an operational function with named instruments at scale — and **every one of them is closed**:

| Instrument | Owner | Status | Scale claim |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Check Integrity** | Elsevier | 🔴 proprietary | reported expanded to **~`2,000` journals** (March `2026` press release) |
| **Geppetto** (AI-generated text), **SnappShot** (images) | Springer Nature | 🔴 proprietary | publisher toolkit |
| **RobotReviewer** | academic (`ijmarshall`) | 🟢 open — but **`GPL-3.0`** and **dormant since `2022-07-18`** | `180★` |

🔵 **That table is the opportunity in one line: the function is being bought, the tools are closed, and the only open artefact is copyleft and four years cold.** ⚠️ A secondary analysis explicitly cautions that **claims of universal AI screening across major publishers are not independently substantiated** — so sell the capability gap, not a market-size figure.

🔴 **Scale of the problem, with source confidence attached.** More than **`400,000`** papers published in the last 20 years are suspected to have originated from **paper mills** (review literature). ⚠️ A blog attributing to Retraction Watch an audit finding **~`1` in `277`** PubMed-indexed papers from early `2026` citing a **nonexistent** paper is **not confirmed against its primary source and must not be quoted**. 🟢 **The policy side is firmer:** major publishers prohibit listing AI as an author, require disclosure of tool use and hold human authors responsible; **ICMJE issued updated recommendations in January `2026` with a dedicated section on AI in publishing** — a series this base held **`0`** mentions of.

🔴 **The finding a research-integrity proposal must survive, and it is a published negative.** A `2026` review of AI-in-publishing policies found those studies **describe policy design, not policy effectiveness**, and that **similar growth in detected AI-assisted writing appears at journals both with and without AI policies.** 🔵 **Read plainly: writing the policy does not change the behaviour, which is precisely why the billable artefact is detection-and-provenance infrastructure rather than another policy document.** A Frontiers editorial pushes the other way and belongs in the same brief: institutions should **not deploy AI screening without documented bias, security and data-governance assessments** — so the deliverable is a screening pipeline **plus** its own evaluation dossier.

🟢 **The permissive global substrate that makes this buildable, all byte-read this pass.** [`ResearchObject/ro-crate`](https://github.com/ResearchObject/ro-crate) + [`ro-crate-py`](https://github.com/ResearchObject/ro-crate-py) (`Apache-2.0`) for provenance packaging; [`datalad/datalad`](https://github.com/datalad/datalad) (`MIT`, corrected this pass from `NOASSERTION`) for versioned data; [`ror-community/ror-api`](https://github.com/ror-community/ror-api) (`MIT`) for organisation identity; [`openaire/iis`](https://github.com/openaire/iis) (`Apache-2.0`) for output-to-grant linking; [`asreview/asreview`](https://github.com/asreview/asreview) (`Apache-2.0`) for screening at corpus scale.

🔴 **And the global licence warning that applies to every region (`T524`).** The register's most-starred agent, [`SakanaAI/AI-Scientist-v2`](https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist-v2) (`7,495★`, plus `14,979★` on the byte-identical v1), is indexed `NOASSERTION` and is governed by a bespoke RAIL-derived licence whose **clause `3.3` requires its use restrictions to be reproduced as an enforceable provision in Globant's own downstream agreement**, and whose **clause `3.2(e)` constrains the content of any manuscript it generates.** 🔵 **It is usable and it is commercial — it is simply the one component in this register whose cost includes Legal's time.**

#### 🆕 `p756` (`2026-11-11`) — 🟢 the cheapest supply in this market is the inventory you already own: `968` rows swept returned `565` grants and `141` unpublished permissive education repositories

🟢 **The finding of this pass is a sourcing-economics result, and it is global because the mechanism is.** This base's own index of record carried **`968`** repository addresses whose licence had never been read. Sweeping them cost **`968` addresses / `~5,000` requests** on a single channel and returned **`565` readable grants (`58.4%`)**, of which **`412` are permissive** and **`141` are education-named and had never been published on any shelf** (`T509`, `T516`).

🔵 **Against every search leg run this pass, the backlog won.** The mandated global agent leg returned generic agent lists with almost nothing education-specific — **a nil**. The backlog returned **ETS's automated-scoring harness**, an **LTI grade-return service**, two **national curriculum graphs**, a **public-domain sixteen-state curriculum ontology** and a **national government's live production service**, all permissive. 🟢 **Price the implication into every engagement: a licence-and-provenance audit of the client's existing estate is cheaper than a build, and routinely finds supply the client already owns** — `P283` packages exactly that, with the instrument preserved at `ingest/p756-unstated-sweep.sh`.

🔴 **The counter-finding is the expensive half, and it should be said out loud.** `45` of the `565` (`8.0%`) are **non-commercial, source-available or proprietary** — `PolyForm Noncommercial` ×`13`, proprietary/all-rights-reserved ×`10`, bespoke non-commercial ×`8`, `CC-BY-NC` ×`6`, `Elastic-2.0` ×`2`, `BUSL-1.1` ×`2` (`T510`). 🔴 **The share is small and the placement is terrible:** it clusters on the ready-made artefacts a team reaches for first — a finished eval **dataset** (Khan Academy's), a finished **platform** ([`canyongbs/advisingapp`](https://github.com/canyongbs/advisingapp), Elastic-2.0, un-hostable), a finished **MCP server** (`AStheTECH/mewcp-google-classroom`, commercial integration *"strictly prohibited"*). 🔵 **And the boilerplate is spreading by copy-paste** — three byte-identical PolyForm payloads (`4,563 B`, `ffcca38841ad`) across unrelated owners.

🔴 **Governance read, from this base auditing itself.** `98` of the `968` rows were **desynchronised** — the shelves had already published a grant the index called unread. `90` confirmed the shelves; **`4` were wrong licence cells, in both directions** (one MCP server shelved **MIT** is **GPL-3.0**; one shelved **AGPL-3.0** is only **GPL-3.0**), `3` were **dead citations**, and `1` had no source in any channel (`T513`). 🔵 **Report unread backlog and desynchronisation separately: the first is a procurement finding, the second says your record of truth is wrong — and the second decides what gets bought next.**

🔵 **Market framing unchanged and still the honest one:** quote the **under-digitisation ratio and the governance gap**, not a TAM. `T519`'s LATAM figures are the cleanest instance this base holds — **`87%` adoption, `26%` strategy, `4%` public funding** — and the same shape, adoption ahead of governance, is reported for higher education globally.

| Series | Claimed CAGR | **Implied by its own endpoints** | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|

🟢 **The structural trends that matter to this register, as opposed to to edtech generally.** Sources converge on three: **AI has moved from pilots into core systems**, bringing new demands on reliability, **agent permissions** and assessment design; **agentic AI is moving into campus operations** and multi-step administrative work rather than only answering questions; and **governance and interoperability have become purchasing criteria** — buyers now ask not only where data is stored but what models see and how decisions are made. 🔵 **All three describe this register precisely:** timetabling, exam diets, room allocation and place assignment *are* campus operations, they *are* decisions that must be explained, and they are bought by registrars and ministries who will ask exactly those questions.

⚠️ **Adoption statistics in this area are weak and should be handled as such.** Figures such as "`84%` of high-school students use generative AI" come from aggregator pages that mix measured results with forecasts, and several `2026` roundups carry inconsistent publication dates. 🔵 **This base cites them only with the caveat attached, and prefers the UNESCO/OECD teacher-use figures in the LATAM block, which name their year and their comparator.**

🟢 **The global supply fact, in one line, and it is the thesis of the pass:** *the solver substrate for every education scheduling problem on earth is permissive and actively maintained — `13 / 13` general-purpose solvers read this pass carry Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD or MPL grants, with `or-tools` at `14,359★` pushed the day of this pass — while the education-specific agent layer above it does not exist (`9` repositories against `991` for the generic equivalent) and what little exists is copyleft.* **The gap between those two facts is the product.**

#### 🆕 `p749` (2026-11-10) — the alternative-format layer: one structural fact holds in all five regions, and it is the sales argument

🔴 **The cross-regional fact: the standard written into law lags the standard the W3C actually
recommends, everywhere.** WCAG **2.2** has been the W3C Recommendation since 2023. What the binding
instruments cite:

| Region | Instrument | Cited standard |
|---|---|---|
| **North America** | ADA Title II web/mobile rule (DOJ 2024, dates extended 2026) | **WCAG 2.1 AA** |
| **EMEA** | EN 301 549 **v3.2.1** (OJ-cited) / **v4.1.1** (published `2026-09-02`, not yet harmonised) | WCAG **2.1**-aligned |
| **APAC** | `JIS X 8341-3:2016`, under revision; Australia DSS; India IS 17802 | **2.0 / 2.1**, revision aiming higher |
| **LATAM** | Brazil LBI + eMAG + ABNT NBR 17225; AR Ley 26.653; MX Norma Mexicana | **2.0 / 2.1 AA** (sources conflict) |

🟢 **The architectural recommendation falls straight out and it is the same in every region: build to
WCAG 2.2, certify against whatever the local instrument names.** The delta between 2.1 AA and 2.2 AA is
small; the cost of re-auditing an estate when a citation updates is not. 🔵 **This single rule makes an
accessibility deliverable durable across jurisdictions**, which is exactly what a global client with
campuses in several regions is buying.

🔴 **The second global fact: the two tasks every institution needs have `0` open-source agents.**
`alt text generation llm accessibility` → **`0`** repositories.
`captioning lecture accessibility open source` → **`0`**.
`course accessibility checker lms` → **`1`** at `0★`. Meanwhile `a11y mcp server` → **`69`** and
`pdf accessibility remediation` → **`85`**. 🟢 **`T424` explains the split, and the explanation is the
commercial case:** wiring a rules engine to an agent is free to run and needs no human in the loop, so
open source does it; generating alt text for tens of thousands of images or captions for thousands of
lecture hours has a real unit cost **and** an irreducible human-review obligation, because a confidently
wrong alt text is worse for a blind student than a missing one. 🔵 **That is a services business, not a
repository** — which is precisely why it belongs to Globant rather than to a maintainer.

🟢 **The third global fact: the licence gradient is clean and it is architecturally decisive** (`T423`).
Across `18` rows measured this pass with **zero crossovers**: the checker, validator and format-spec layer
is **permissive `10 / 10`** (MIT ×`4`, Apache-2.0 ×`3`, BSD-3-Clause ×`3`), and the assistive-technology
runtime is **copyleft `8 / 8`**. 🟢 **Globant can own, extend and ship the entire checking and conversion
layer outright**; it must call, deploy or package the braille and speech runtime (`P248`). No engagement in
this register needs a licence negotiation, provided that boundary is drawn on day one.

**Market sizing — stated with its uncertainty.** Digital accessibility *software* is roughly
**`$0.85B`–`$1.0B`** in 2026 across five publishers, with the broader market including services near
**`$1.75B`**; forecast CAGRs span **`~6%` to `~20%`**, a spread wide enough that the midpoint is not

`κ ≤ 0.079` in `12 / 12` measured model×condition cells — negative in `6` of `12` — and misstates
the monthly amount by `$276`–`$486`.** Measured from a **pre-registered** study (hash frozen before

🟢 **And the single most useful sentence to carry into a client meeting:** feeding the model the

gain was base-rate guessing on an imbalanced binary, not agreement. **Evaluate on κ, or the demo
will sell you.**

parameter local models** (Phi-3.5-mini, Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-3-4b) on **SNAP**; the repository is
`0★` and single-author; it is **not** a measurement of frontier models and must not be quoted as

an aid determination must be reproducible on appeal, and a sampled model is not reproducible even

pedagogical control**. 🔵 This converges with the Council of the EU's "support, not replace"
language on the EMEA block above: **two independent institutional sources arriving at the same
design constraint.** For a studio that constraint is a feature specification — human-in-the-loop by
default, teacher override as a first-class surface — and it is the same architecture the
`talk2yourdata` row on [`../agents/top.md`](../agents/top.md) implements for data queries.

**Adoption — carried with its caveat.**
A Microsoft 2025 report puts generative-AI use among education organisations at **`86%`, the highest
of any industry**. ⚠️ Secondary, and a 2025 reading quoted in 2026.
🔴 **Declined again, consistent with this base's standing refusals:** a `53% → 88% → 94%`
(2024→2026) student-and-teacher series that no source traces to an original instrument, and the
*"86% of students across 16 countries"* and *"83% of K-12 teachers"* figures that `p739`-era passes
already traced to a **single aggregator with no primary instrument named.** **Recorded so no
successor mistakes them for new evidence.**

**Supply — the two Global-placed estates added this pass.**
🟢 **`DHIS2`** (`BSD-3-Clause`, `252` repositories) and **`UNICEF–ITU Giga`** (`32` repositories) are
both Global-placed and both were at `0` mentions on this base before this pass.
🔴 **Giga's grant follows its layer and a buyer must be told which half they are getting:**
**Apache-2.0** on the models and analysis (`3 / 3` byte-read), **AGPL-3.0** on the hosted services
(`4 / 4`) — `T389`, `7 / 7` with zero crossovers. **`P233` is built on that boundary and `P234` is
the sweep that detects it anywhere else.**

🟢 **First proctoring/e-assessment sizing this base holds.** Six independent `2026` bases:

| Online exam proctoring (MarketReportsWorld) | **`$0.835B`** | `$3.58B` by 2035 | `17.4%` |
| Online exam proctoring (Business Research Insights) | **`$1.07B`** | `$8.09B` by 2035 | 🔴 `25.27%` — outlier |

| Exam & assessment software (Market Growth Reports) | **`$1.12B`** | `$2.76B` by 2035 | `11.9%` |

proctoring is roughly `7–14%` of AI-in-education**, and against the agentic series (`$2.37B`,
Mordor) it is **of the same order as the entire agentic segment**.

🔴 **The CAGRs are the honest disagreement.** Five of six fall in **`10–19%`**, and they split
cleanly by definition: the three *"proctoring software/solutions"* series sit at `10–12%`, the
three *"exam proctoring"* market series at `17–19%`. The `25.27%` outlier is a single source.
⚠️ **Which series a proposal cites should be chosen by scope, not by size** — software-only or
market-wide — and the choice stated.

🔵 **And the number that is not in any of these reports is the one `T386` measured.** Every series
above prices a market served almost entirely by four US proprietary vendors. The open-source agent
supply for that same market is **three repositories under `5★`**, with **zero** MCP servers for
QTI, the interchange format all of it runs on. **A `$0.8–1.6B` market growing at `10–19%`, under a
dated statutory mandate, with essentially no open composable layer** — that is the clearest
build-vs-buy opening in this knowledge base, and `P226`–`P230` are the recipes.

🟢 **Globally reusable, region-neutral supply:** the `1EdTech` standards estate is Apache-2.0 and
MIT throughout (`lti-1-3-php-library`, `basiclti-util-java`, `openbadges-validator-core`,
`OpenCASE`, `cert-schema` MIT `1,096 B` `06d87bf42a0a`), and Learnosity publishes Apache-2.0 SDKs
in `7` languages. 🔴 **`T381`: the standards layer is permissive and every deployable platform in
this tier is copyleft** — so the cross-region build target is the spec library, everywhere. `P229`.

the broad-market CAGRs disagree by `15.6` percentage points (`25.9 %` ↔ `41.5 %`) on overlapping

#### 🆕 `p743` (2026-11-10) — a tier-sized blind spot, and the three facts from it that travel to any region

🔴 **The finding is about this base before it is about the market.** `11` publisher addresses probed against every shelf, both trending logs and a `3,382`-row address ledger: **`10 / 11` novel, `0` on a live shelf, `0` in the ledger** (`evidence/tier-novelty.2026-11-10-p743.tsv`). The eleventh, `ilios/ilios`, was discovered and byte-read by an earlier pass and never promoted — a backlog defect, not a blind spot, and recorded as the former. CERN/Invenio, Harvard IQSS/Dataverse, Samvera, Islandora, PKP, SciELO, LA Referencia — roughly **`800` repositories across seven publishers**, none of which had ever been addressed in `742` passes. **Cause: every discovery leg ever run here asked for the word *education*, and this tier says *research data*, *institutional repository*, *scholarly publishing* instead (`T363`).** Before any later pass declares supply exhausted, it should change the noun.

🟢 **Three facts from this tier that sell in every region:**

1. **Permissive is the norm here, not the exception.** Of `16` foundations rows filed this pass, `11` are MIT, `3` BSD-2-Clause, `4` Apache-2.0 and `1` GPL-3.0 — the inverse of the LMS layer, where Moodle is GPL-3.0 and Open edX and Canvas are AGPL-3.0.
2. **The permissive-edge seam is now `7` publishers deep with `0` counter-examples (`T365`).** Islandora, PKP and Opencast join H5P, Instructure, Pix and openHPI. *Enumerate a publisher's components before writing off a copyleft estate* is the single most reusable sales fact this base holds.
3. **Fork-to-star inversion identifies deployed infrastructure.** `invenio-rdm-records` carries `128` forks on `23★`; `invenio-app-rdm` `207` on `187`; `pkp/ojs` `1,039` on `1,051`. **Rank institutional software on forks, not stars** — stars measure attention and forks measure deployment.

🔴 **And one standing caution, re-measured.** `2` subjects were refused this pass for having no locatable grant at `14` probed paths, one of them an **AI-agent-skills collection published by Harvard** at `48★` ([`harvard-lil/lawskills-hub`](https://github.com/harvard-lil/lawskills-hub), `T366`). Institutional provenance plus an on-topic description is exactly the combination that reaches a client deck unread. ⚠️ **`T328` still binds every regulatory claim on this page:** primary-law hosts are unreachable from this session, so instruments are corroborated across independent secondary sources and disagreements are published rather than resolved.

#### 🆕 `p742` (2026-11-10) — the market-size spread is unchanged, and this pass adds a licence-structure fact that applies in every region

🟡 **No new market-size series this pass, and that is deliberate** — `p695` and `p705` established that this sector's figures are vendor-commissioned with incompatible methodologies, and the legs returned the same irreconcilable set again: **~`$10.6B` (2026) → `$42.48B` (2030)** against a **`$9.58B`** base growing **">`30%`/yr"**, plus the Technavio `$3.37B` "market opportunity" at a different scope. 🟢 **The honest published position is unchanged: roughly `$10B` today, high-30s-to-low-40s CAGR, no agreement beyond that.** Re-buying it costs a leg and yields nothing.

🟢 **What is genuinely new and region-independent is a structural fact about the supply, `T360`:** in education OSS the licence seam follows **host-platform linkage**. Measured on `109` repositories of one Open edX operator — **`12 / 12` `xblock`-named repositories AGPL-3.0, `12 / 12` `theme`-named repositories MIT, zero crossovers** — and independently on a Moodle project carrying **MIT at depth 1 and GPL-3.0 at depth 3** that the index reports as `MIT`.

🔵 **Commercially this is the most portable thing in the pass.** It means the answer to *"can we build on this?"* is not a property of the repository but of **which layer you intend to touch**, and it is decidable before any code is read:

| Layer | Typical grant | Studio action |
|---|---|---|
| Themes, schemas, validators, Dockerfiles, deployment | **permissive** | **take it** |
| Plugins, XBlocks, runtime extensions | **inherits host copyleft** (AGPL / GPL) | **reimplement, or run as a separate service** |
| Anything else in a public-sector estate | **frequently no grant at all** (`65 / 109` here) | **ask; assume nothing** |

🟢 **The third row is the one that will surprise a buyer:** the single largest licence state in a real public-university estate was **no grant at all**. `P213` is the pattern; `P102`'s licence-drift gate is the control.

🟡 **Cross-cutting evidence note, carried:** the OECD's 2026 framing — AI helps learning only when pedagogy stays in control — and the edtech-analysis finding that **only `45%` of the most-used tools have published research meeting an ESSA evidence tier**. 🔵 **That `45%` is a procurement wedge in every region**, because it makes "show me your evidence tier" a question the buyer can ask and most vendors cannot answer.


#### 🆕 `p741` (2026-11-10) — the market figures still do not reconcile, and 2026's cross-regional theme is governance over experimentation

🔴 **The market-size spread is unchanged and still irreconcilable from secondary sources**, so it is
shown rather than averaged: **`~$10.6B` in 2026 rising to `~$42.5B` by 2030** (Research and Markets,
via an aggregator); **`$12.3B` for 2026** (HolonIQ, via a vendor blog); **`$136.79B` by 2035**
(Azumo); **US-only `$2.01B` (2025) → `$32.64B` (2034)** (vendor blog). ⚠️ **These use different
market definitions.** `725-F` applies in full: **secondary-source-only, and the disagreement is the
honest answer.**

🟡 **Two adoption figures that belong together because they contradict the obvious conclusion.**
**`83%` of K-12 teachers report using generative AI tools** (Azumo), while **only `15%` of students
with Khanmigo access actually use it** (VoxBooster). 🔵 **Teacher adoption is not student
adoption, and a proposal that cites the first number to justify a student-facing product is citing
the wrong one.** The sellable implication is the one `p737` and this pass both reach: **the
teacher-facing workload product has demonstrated pull; the student-facing product has a documented
engagement problem.**

🟢 **The cross-regional theme for 2026 is consistent across independent sources and it is
governance.** 1EdTech — **the standards body whose estate this pass read** — frames the year as AI
in education moving *"from experimentation to governance"*, with coordinated policy-guided
ecosystems replacing isolated use cases, and expects **digital credentials to rise as employer
expectations shift toward a skills-driven ecosystem.** Independent commentary converges: AI shifting
*"from a feature to infrastructure"*, a move away from generic tools toward **purpose-built
education platforms** (echoed by the OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook), **disciplined
adoption** of bounded and measured use cases, explicit institutional rules on when AI use is
allowed/required/prohibited and how it must be disclosed, and **teacher workload** as the durable
driver.

🔵 **Why this matters for how the shelves are sold.** Governance, credentials and purpose-built
platforms are each directly served by substrate this base already holds and byte-read: the
`Apache-2.0` LTI/Open Badges/CLR estate and the `MIT` conformance suites (`P209`), the xAPI and
Ed-Fi record layers from `p740` (`P205`, `P206`), and the copyleft-boundary architecture for a
client's existing assessment engine (`P211`). 🟢 **The pitch "we can show you the licence of every
component" is not a technicality in a governance year — it is the product.**

#### 🆕 `p740` (2026-11-10) — what is true in every region: the grant is not where the index says, and the licence text quotes itself

🟢 **One finding holds in all four regions and it changes how every row on these shelves should be
read.** p740 byte-read **`36` licence payloads (`36 / 36` classified)** and found **three distinct
defects in the obvious way of classifying them** — each caused by licences naming other licences:

1. 🔴 **`GPL-3.0` cannot be told from `AGPL-3.0` by keyword**, because `GPL-3.0`'s **section 13 is
   titled "Use with the GNU Affero General Public License"** and names it three times. The working
   discriminator is `AGPL-3.0`'s own section 13 heading, **`Remote Network Interaction`**:
   `7 / 7` decided this pass, **`2` corrections toward `GPL`**. `T344`.
2. 🔴 **`MPL-2.0` contains the string `GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE`**, because that is how it defines
   a *"Secondary License"*. Four payloads misfiled before correction. `T345`.
3. 🔴 **The `Apache-2.0` operative-text digest is not universal**: `7 / 8` payloads normalise
   identically and the eighth — the xAPI specification publisher's own —
   **drops the `(a)`–`(d)` labels from section 4's redistribution conditions**. The verdict is
   unchanged and **a digest gate rejects it**. `T349`.

🔵 **The commercial reading, in one sentence a partner can use:** *the `GPL`/`AGPL` line is the
line that decides whether we may host a modified system for you without publishing our source, and
until this pass this base was one `grep` away from getting it wrong in both directions.* 🟢 **The
fix costs nothing — order the classifier by specificity, not by alphabet** — and every pattern on
[`../compose/patterns.md`](../compose/patterns.md) that quotes a copyleft verdict written before
`p740` should be re-checked against the discriminator before it reaches a client.

🟢 **A second global finding, and it is the one that recovers value.** *No licence file* is **not**
*no grant*. p740 found grants in three places a path probe misses — **per-file headers** (the whole
Moodle, WordPress and Drupal plugin world works this way), **ecosystem-conventional filenames**
(`MIT-LICENSE` for RubyGems), and **a `COPYRIGHT` file named only in the README**. That reclassified
**four repositories from unbuildable to usable on this pass alone** (`T347`), including a `30★`
state-ministry AI gateway. ⚠️ **Conversely, one repository survived all three checks and still has
no grant** — `EsupPortail/esup-myia` — which is what a genuine absence now looks like.

🔴 **And one shape to check for on every content-bearing repository, everywhere.**
[`openstax/exercises`](https://github.com/openstax/exercises) carries **three grants in one
repository**: `AGPL-3.0`-or-later code, `MIT/X11` vendored components, and **every
non-programmatic asset "All Rights Reserved"** with derivations forbidden from using them
(`T348`). **The code a client can have; the items they assumed they were buying they cannot.**
Read the `COPYRIGHT`/`NOTICE` text for an asset carve-out **before the SOW is signed**, not after.

#### 🆕 `p737` (2026-11-10) — the compliance artefact is the same everywhere, and the sandbox under the grader was the real gap

🟢 **Cross-region reading 1 — one artefact, four nouns, and this is now evidenced in all four
regions.** What every instrument asks for is a **register of AI systems in use, with purpose, owner,
data and a human-oversight step**, plus a **training record**. The EU calls it technical
documentation (live Article 50 duties now, conformity apparatus `2 December 2027`); North Carolina
calls it a district policy (`30 June 2027`); TEQSA calls it an institutional action plan; LATAM
ministries call it a register. 🟢 **`P196` builds it once and relabels it**, which is why it is the
most portable engagement in this base — and why it is the best-qualified lead generator: its week-1
inventory enumerates every AI surface the institution runs, which is the input to every other
pattern here.

🟢 **Cross-region reading 2 — the gap that was actually blocking delivery was never an agent.**
`p737` aimed `12` discovery legs at the agent shelf and filed **`0` rows**: `9` of the `12` returned
only repositories this base already holds, and the English-language AI-education agent namespace is
**saturated against this base**. What was missing, in every region at once, was **a permissive
sandbox that executes student code** — because an LLM can read code but only an execution harness
can say it compiles and passes the tests. `openHPI/codeocean` (**BSD-3-Clause**) and
`openHPI/poseidon` (**MIT**) close it, and `P192` is region-neutral in a base where almost nothing
is. 🔵 **The generalisable lesson for how this base spends its budget: when the agent shelf
saturates, the remaining value is in the substrate the agents stand on** — and substrate is
published by institutions, which is why `org:` legs produced **all `14`** of this pass's rows and
the `9` mandated prose legs produced **`0`** (`T326`, 41st consecutive nil).

🟢 **Cross-region reading 3 — a licence heuristic worth applying before writing off any copyleft
platform.** Four unrelated publishers now show the same split: **permissive components over a
copyleft core.** H5P (GPL-3.0 core, MIT content types), Instructure (AGPL-3.0 Canvas, MIT
`instructure-ui`/`ims-lti`), Pix (AGPL-3.0 core, **MIT `pix-ui`**), openHPI (BSD-3-Clause
application, **MIT `poseidon`** orchestrator — the *more* reusable layer carrying the *more*
permissive grant). 🔵 **Instruction: when a platform's core is copyleft, enumerate the publisher's
component repositories before concluding the estate is unusable** (`T327`). `4` instances, `0`
counter-examples so far — a heuristic on four cases, not a law, so check the payload every time.

⚠️ **Cross-region limitation, and it bounds everything above.** `WebFetch` to hosts outside this
session's network allow-list fails at **DNS resolution** (`2 / 2` attempted), so **no pass running
here can verify a regulatory claim against primary text** — EUR-Lex, the Official Journal, state
legislatures and ministry portals are all unreachable. Every date in this section rests on
**corroborated secondary readings**; the EU high-risk date is confirmed from three, the Article 50
date is published **as a conflict**, and one US state mandate is **refused** for want of a second
source (`T321`, `T324`, `T328`). 🟢 **A declared conflict is a usable finding; a single-sourced date
presented as settled is not.**


#### 🆕 `p736` (2026-11-10) — what is true in every region, and the one component that is permissive everywhere

🟢 **The framing shift is global and three independent sources state it the same way:** **1EdTech**
— *"AI in education is shifting from experimentation to governance"*; **HolonIQ** — **"selective AI
acceleration"**, institutions deliberately choosing where to invest; **Campus Technology's**
industry panel — AI becoming **embedded infrastructure across admissions, advising and
administration** rather than a set of pilots. One source reports teams now holding AI *"to the same
reliability standard as login or grade sync"* (`T320`).
🔵 **The positioning sentence of this pass, and it is worth quoting verbatim in a deck:** the
**OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook** is reported to recommend **moving beyond general-purpose
AI tools toward purpose-built educational AI designed to produce durable learning gains.** That is
the argument against the generic-chatbot pilot almost every institution has already run.
🟢 **Globally true and newly held: identity is the one layer of an institution's education stack
that is already permissive.** Every LMS on these shelves is copyleft — Moodle GPL-3.0, Open edX /
Canvas / Frappe AGPL-3.0, Sakai ECL-2.0 — while **`apereo/cas` (`11,393★`) and its client libraries
are Apache-2.0** (`T314`). **`P189`** therefore works in every region, and it is the only entry
point on these shelves with no licence argument attached.
🟢 **Second globally applicable route: `P190`.** H5P's **core is GPL-3.0 and its content types are
MIT** (`T315`), and H5P is already installed inside Moodle, Canvas, Open edX, WordPress and
Drupal — so a permissive, drop-in interactive content type reaches students in **all four regions**
with no fork, no LTI registration and no infrastructure. Almost nothing else on these shelves is
region-neutral in that way.
🟡 **Market size, as a range with its sources named, never as a number:** **≈ `$10.6 B`** for 2026
up from `$7.52 B` in 2025 (Research and Markets, via secondary citation) against **`$12.3 B`**
(HolonIQ) — **≈ `16 %` spread on the same year**, narrower than the factor-of-five spread `p664`
recorded. A widely circulated US-only projection of `$2.01 B` (2025) → `$32.64 B` (2034) is
**low-confidence vendor-blog material and should not be quoted.**
🔵 **The credentials axis is where the money visibly moved this quarter:** **Pearson agreeing to
acquire Workera** (AI-skill verification) and **Instructure building an AI study coach into
Canvas** — both consistent with `T297`'s reading that the revenue is in services and credentials
while the learning-evidence base stays thin. `P179`'s credential-anchored upskilling track is the
pattern that sells into it.
⚠️ **Standing caveat for this whole page (`725-F`, `T246`):** secondary sources only;
`unesco.org`, `iesalc.unesco.org`, `eur-lex.europa.eu` and `digitaleducationcouncil.com` are
unreachable from this environment, so no figure here is primary-confirmed and none should be
presented as such.


#### 🆕 `p735` (2026-11-10) — one finding holds in all four regions, and it decides what to sell

🟢 **Adoption is settled everywhere; governance is settled nowhere.** Put the four regional readings
side by side and the pattern is unambiguous:

| Region | Adoption | Governance / readiness |
|---|---|---|
| **North America** | institution-wide implementation **`66%`** | **~`100`** state bills in 2026; **`≥15`** states legislating — volume, not settlement |
| **EMEA** | **`67%`** of teachers using AI; **`76%`** of students expecting to | **`80%`** of teachers say it is arriving faster than schools can manage; Annex III duties dated **`2 Dec 2027`** |
| **APAC** | virtual tutors **`30%`**, uptake "patchy" | agenda moves through convened bodies; **`34,000`** teachers in training |
| **LATAM** | **`92%`** students / **`79%`** faculty | only **`30%`** say their institution responded effectively; **no formal AI policies** |

🔵 **The structural reading, and it is the one to carry into any engagement: the binding constraint
has moved off the model and onto the institution.** Nobody is being asked whether AI works in
education; they are being asked to show who approved which tool, against which review, trained
whom, and on what record. 🟢 **So the deliverable that sells in `2026` is a governance artefact —
a register, a review record, a training log, an audit trail — and the model is an implementation
detail inside it.** This pass's patterns are shaped to produce exactly those: `P185` (EU Annex III
admissions), `P186` (the LTI delivery path that leaves the LMS licence untouched), `P187` (the
training record), alongside `P181` (LATAM governance front door).

🟢 **Two supply developments make that sellable rather than merely true.** **(1) Sovereignty is now
answerable with first-party components:**
[`intel/university-curriculum-enabling-tool`](https://github.com/intel/university-curriculum-enabling-tool)
(Apache-2.0) runs locally with no outbound model call, and
[`hypothesis/lms`](https://github.com/hypothesis/lms) documents per-geographic-region deployment as
a standard operation. **(2) The integration problem has a permissive answer:** LTI is the only door
into an institution's LMS, and every LMS on this base's shelf is copyleft — Moodle GPL-3.0, Open
edX / Frappe / Canvas AGPL-3.0. A readable LTI implementation means the AI layer ships **beside**
the LMS instead of deriving from it, which removes the licence objection that has ended more
proposals in this base's history than any technical one.

⚠️ **What the demand legs are good for, stated plainly after `39` passes of evidence.** The four
mandated prose legs produced **`0`** novel repository addresses again this pass (`4 / 4` already
held) — but they produced every number in the table above. 🔵 **Read them for demand and never for
supply**; `735`'s entire supply came from the `api.github.com` sweep (`T298`).


#### 🆕 `p734` (2026-11-10) — the spread holds, the evidence base is the gap, and three heavily-sold categories are fading

🔴 **Sizing unchanged in shape.** Roughly **`$10.6B` (2026) → `$42.48B` (2030)** on the figure this
base has carried since cycle 2. ⚠️ **One new figure, filed with its scope flagged rather than
merged:** Hyde Park Capital puts global **EdTech** at **`$238.4B`** for 2026 — that is all of
education technology, **not** AI-in-education, and the two must not be compared. Adoption stays the
firmest number: **`86 %`** of education organisations using generative AI, the highest of any
industry.

🔴 **The real gap is evidence, and it is quantified.** Only **`45 %` of the most-used tools have
published research meeting an ESSA evidence tier** — in a sector whose buyers increasingly must
justify procurement. 🔵 **Consequence for proposals: an outcomes claim now needs an evidence plan
attached, and with `55 %` of incumbents unable to produce one, a measurable-outcome design is a
differentiator rather than a cost** (`T297`).

🔴 **Three categories reported fading** — **blockchain credentialing**, **full-classroom VR**, and
**the chatbot-as-tutor pitch** — with the sector's focus shifting *from policing academic integrity
to managing cognitive load*. 🟢 **Where spend is going instead matches this base's shelf:**
skills and credentials (**Instructure's Canvas Career**, a skills-focused AI LMS, **GA January
2026**), **industry-aligned microcredentials**, and **in-flow-of-work learning** (HolonIQ, January
2026). The **OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026** warns AI helps learning **only when pedagogy
stays in control**.

🔵 **Read with `p733`'s `P179` and the certification shelf at `p732`: lead with the credential, not
the tutor.** `T297` is the demand-side justification for those artefacts, and the fading list is the
warning about what not to lead with.

🟢 **One global supply note that changes which licences matter.** `p734` filed
[`google/moodle-on-gcp`](https://github.com/google/moodle-on-gcp) (**Apache-2.0**) — a first-party
hyperscaler deployment kit for **Moodle**, which is GPL-3.0 and the most-deployed LMS in the world.
It deploys Moodle without deriving from it, so **the operations layer is permissive even though the
application is not**. That is the cleanest answer this base has to "can we build on Moodle", and it
is now a pattern (**`P182`**). ⚠️ Secondary, vendor-commissioned sourcing throughout; `725-F` holds
— `eur-lex.europa.eu`, `www.unesco.org`, `www.iesalc.unesco.org` and `digitaleducationcouncil.com`
remain unreachable from this session, so figures are recorded precisely enough for a reader with
access to settle them in one lookup.

governance**, not student-facing product — three jurisdictions converging on the same deliverable

Standards and framework bodies to align deliverables to: **OECD** (*Digital Education
Outlook 2026*), **UNESCO** (teacher AI competency framework; IESALC for LATAM), **Council of
Europe** (AI and Education Compass), **ESSA evidence tiers** (US procurement gate),
**EU AI Act** (the strictest binding regime, and therefore the sensible global design target).

Building to EU AI Act high-risk standards produces a product sellable in all five regions.
Building to the loosest regional standard produces one sellable in one.

**🔴 Added at p723 — one global number contradicts this base's own `T209`, and the
contradiction is the useful part.** `T209` records that *detection is being abandoned as a
control* and that spend is moving to assessment redesign. A 2026 statistics roundup reports
the opposite motion on the ground: **AI-detection tool use in higher education rose from 38%
to 68% in a single year.**

🔵 Both can be true, and reading them together is what makes them actionable:
**institutional *policy* is moving away from detection while institutional *purchasing* is
still moving toward it.** Detection is the control a worried administrator can buy this
quarter; assessment redesign is the control that works and takes two years. For an engagement
this means the buyer may well be mid-detection-rollout while the pedagogy leadership has
already written detection off — so an assessment-redesign proposal lands as a *replacement
for a tool they have just paid for*, and has to be positioned as such rather than as a
greenfield improvement.

⚠️ Sourcing caveat, consistent with how this page treats figures: the 38% → 68% pair comes
from a vendor-adjacent statistics roundup citing a primary survey it does not fully identify.
It is filed as a **signal of direction, not a measured rate**, and the `T209` policy-side
evidence is better sourced than this purchasing-side figure.


**🟢 `p724` — a new product category that is region-neutral: lecture-capture-to-notes.** Two independent
permissive implementations appeared within three weeks of each other, in different languages
(`mizorewww/course2md`, **`508★` MIT**, Rust; `drpwchen/lecture-to-notes`, **`117★` MIT**, Python), against
the same problem: **the lecture recording is the artefact every institution already has and none of them can
search.** 🔵 **Why this is a market fact and not a tooling note:** the input requires no curriculum, no
integration and no data migration — the recordings already exist — so it is the shortest path from a signed
engagement to something a faculty member can see working, in any region. And because `lecture-to-notes` runs
ASR, OCR and slide-semantics **locally** and calls an LLM only at the final prose step, it is deployable
under the data-boundary constraints (`T229`) that disqualify most hosted tutoring products in EMEA higher
education. **Two implementations, two cost profiles, one pitch.**

**🟡 `p724` — market sizing: no movement, and the disagreement is the finding.** Re-read this pass:

primary report read, still vendor-commissioned methodology, still not averaged here.** The demand-side
reality check also re-verified and is the number worth quoting to a client: **only ~15% of students with
Khanmigo access actually use it**, and **roughly two-thirds of higher-education institutions still have no
formal AI policy** — i.e. **the constraint on this market is adoption and governance, not model capability.**

🟢 **The 2026 base BRACKETS tightly — `USD 9.58B` to `11.40B`, a spread of about `1.2×`** — which is the narrowest agreement this file has recorded on a current-year base. 🔴 **The forecasts do not agree at all:** the 2033-ish endpoints cluster near `USD 57B` while Precedence projects `136.79B` by 2035, and the CAGRs run from `16.8%` to `41.5%` — Coherent's `16.8%` is **arithmetically inconsistent** with its own `11.40B → 57.25B` over seven years, which needs ~`26%`. **Cite the base, never the CAGR.** Total edtech for context: `~USD 380B` (Fortune Business Insights via Emerline) to `~USD 404B` (Searchlab), growing `13`–`17%`.

🔴 **The counter-signal, and it should go in any deck that quotes the growth figures:** HolonIQ data reports **edtech VC funding fell to `USD 2.4B` in 2025, down `89%` from the 2021 peak**, with AI-enabled startups taking most of what remained. A `34%` CAGR forecast and an `89%` funding collapse describe the same industry; the reconciliation is that spend is moving from new entrants to **incumbent institutions buying services** — which is a consulting market, not a product market, and is the better reading for a studio.

## Market size — and why the numbers disagree

### 🆕 Re-measured at p705 — the `2026` figures finally BRACKET, and that is new

🟢 **For the first time this base can quote a `2026` range tight enough to plan against.** This pass's legs returned **`$11.40B`** for `2026` (Coherent Market Insights) and **~`$12.3B`** for `2026` (X-Pilot, attributed to **HolonIQ**) — a spread of **~`8%`** on the same year.

🔵 **Why the `2026` convergence is plausible where the 2030s are not:** `2026` is nearly observed, and both figures are current-year estimates rather than compounded forecasts. The divergence has always been in the growth assumption, and a current-year estimate barely compounds.

🔴 **p655 makes the disagreement worse, and that is now the most useful fact in this table.** Five further estimates were read this pass and the 2026 figure for the *same* named market — "AI in education, global" — now spans **$9.58B to $11.40B**, with CAGRs on it spanning **16.8% to 41.5%**. Two sources attach a 16.8% and a 41.5% CAGR to dollar figures two billion apart. **Stop quoting a headline number.** The two readings that are actually usable in a conversation are the *segmented* ones, because their scope is stated: **higher education at $4.09B (2026)** and **K-12 at $0.70B (2026)** — a 6:1 split that matches where this KB finds real procurement, and which no aggregate figure reveals. The **agentic** sub-segment at **$2.37B (2026)** is the one worth tracking year on year: it is ~23–25% of the broad market on any of the above readings, and it is the only slice whose definition matches what Globant actually builds.

**These do not reconcile**, and the disagreement is informative rather than noise. Note in particular that **two sources quote the same dollar figures with incompatible growth rates (25.9% and 16.8%)** over near-identical horizons, which means at least one is arithmetically wrong — a useful reminder that these are marketing documents, not research. Further: "AI tutors" ($3.6B) and "AI-powered education tools" (>$17B) differ by roughly 5× because one counts a product category and the other counts every tool with an AI feature. Do not quote a single market size to a client without naming the scope. Treat the AI-tutor figure as the addressable one for tutoring engagements.

### 🔧 CORRECTED at p695 — `p664`'s "three sources, three CAGRs" is ONE source counted twice, and one of its two CAGRs is arithmetically impossible

🔴 **Read this before using the p664 table below.** It presents three rows as three sources and concludes that "the spread is now a factor of five on the same year, and the sources have stopped converging." **Two of its three rows are the same series, and the CAGR it attributes to that series cannot be the CAGR of the endpoints it prints in the same row.**

**The arithmetic, reproducible from the figures already on this page.** The series is Coherent Market Insights, **$11.40B (2026) → $57.25B (2033)** — seven years:

| Claim as published | Check | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `p657` row: **~25.9%** | `(57.25 / 11.40) ^ (1/7) − 1 = ` **`25.93%`**; compounding back gives `11.40 × 1.2593⁷ = ` **`$57.25B`** | 🟢 **correct — it is the implied CAGR of the stated endpoints** |
| `p664` row: **16.8%** on the same `$11.40B → $57.25B` | `11.40 × 1.168⁷ = ` **`$33.81B`** — **`40.9%` below** the terminal printed in its own row. `16.8%` needs until **2036** to reach `$57.25B`, or a 2026 base of **`$19.31B`** | 🔴 **impossible as published** |
| `p664` row: *"A second aggregator, same segment — 25.9%"* | `25.9%` is `p657`'s own implied-CAGR arithmetic on the **identical** Coherent series | 🔴 **not a second source — it is this page's own calculation re-labelled** |

🔵 **What follows, and it cuts the other way from how p664 reads it.** Strip the duplicate and the impossible rate, and the p664 table holds **two** real series, not three: Coherent at **25.9%** and the Europe-only estimate at **31.9%**. **The independent spread is narrower than this page has been publishing, not a "factor of five."** The `2026` base spread (`$9.58B`–`$12.3B`, a `28%` range) and the `3×` disagreement in the terminal years are both real and are unaffected by this correction — they rest on genuinely different publishers.

🔴 **Channel limitation, stated rather than hidden.** `coherentmarketinsights.com` is outside this session's allowed network domains, so the vendor's own published CAGR could **not** be read this pass and it is unknown which of `16.8%` or `25.9%` it prints. **The defect does not depend on that:** a row cannot carry endpoints and a growth rate that contradict each other, whoever published them. Where the vendor itself prints `16.8%` alongside `$11.40B → $57.25B`, the vendor's table is the thing that is internally inconsistent and the correct action is to quote the endpoints and mark the rate as unreconciled.

🟢 **Standing guidance is reinforced, not weakened.** `p664`'s conclusion — *do not put a market level in a client deliverable from this file, quote the structure instead* — survives intact. **It was simply argued from a number that was partly this page's own echo.** `T77` predicted this: a knowledge base's own novelty measurement is a channel, and it decays toward optimism; here a self-citation was re-read as independent corroboration one pass later.

## Structural read of the market

Three facts shape every engagement:

1. **Usage has decisively outrun governance.** 86% of education organisations use generative AI, and most lack a policy. One 2026 benchmark reports 54% of K-12 students and 92% of university students using AI. The buying trigger in 2026 is frequently *governance*, not capability — institutions already have AI in the building and no control over it.
2. **Agent deployment is still rare.** The Bridges 2026 survey of K-12 and college leaders found relatively few districts and colleges running AI agents in day-to-day operations, with leaders explicitly wary of giving agents access to sensitive student data. The gap between "using chatbots" and "running agents" is where the integration work is.
3. **The evidence base is thin, and buyers know it.** A July 2026 scoping review of 474 studies found the field fragmented, with pedagogical design poorly connected to technical capability. A 2025 study found AI tutors adapt worse in real time than human tutors. Expect pilots with measurement attached, not big-bang rollouts.

##### 🆕 p682 — the leg returned **one** fact this page did not hold, and it is a funding rule that creates a reporting obligation

🟢 **New, and it is the only genuinely new regional fact of this pass: `Workforce Pell`.** The US Department of Education's **final rule** creates the **Workforce Pell Grant Program**, extending Pell eligibility to **short-term programmes for the first time**. Dates, as the rule states them: provisions **generally effective `2026-07-20`**, with **optional early implementation from `2026-07-01`** at each institution's discretion. Scope: programmes of roughly **`150`–`599` clock hours** (about **8–15 weeks**), offered **only by accredited institutions**, with **governors in consultation with state workforce boards** designating the high-demand industries and approving programmes. 🔵 **Eligibility widens in a way traditional Pell does not:** it can reach students who **already hold a bachelor's degree**, and awards are **prorated by programme length**.

🟢 **Why this belongs in a market file and not only in a policy note — it is an engineering requirement with a date on it.** A Workforce Pell programme keeps its eligibility only by passing **completion, outcome and earnings tests per programme**, and a programme with zero or negative value-added earnings **loses eligibility**. That is **per-programme, longitudinal, auditable outcome reporting** — completion, credential attainment, and earnings linkage — demanded of exactly the institutions (community colleges, technical colleges, continuing-education arms) whose student-records estate is thinnest. 🔵 **This base already holds the layer that answers it:** the xAPI/LRS shelf ([`yetanalytics/lrsql`](https://github.com/yetanalytics/lrsql), `144★`, and [`adlnet/xAPI-Spec`](https://github.com/adlnet/xAPI-Spec), `955★`), the interoperability shelf ([`Ed-Fi-Alliance-OSS/edfi-oneroster`](https://github.com/Ed-Fi-Alliance-OSS/edfi-oneroster), [`jdolny/OneRoster.NET`](https://github.com/jdolny/OneRoster.NET)) and the early-warning row `p681` placed here ([`Saidkhusayn/student-dropout-early-warning`](https://github.com/Saidkhusayn/student-dropout-early-warning), MIT). **The buying trigger is a statutory deadline, not an AI ambition** — which is the most durable kind this file records.

🔵 **What Canada actually is, commercially:** a large federal *capability* commitment with no binding regulation behind it and provincial policy ranging from an outright suspension (Quebec) to nothing at all (Nova Scotia). That is the opposite of the US profile on this page — there, mandates without guidance; here, funded ambition without mandates. The offers are therefore different, and a single "North America" proposal template will mis-fit one of the two countries.

🔵 **Why the DC item matters more than its legal weight.** A non-binding district policy is not a market. But *grading, discipline and IEP decisions* is the same prohibition shape as Annex III, arrived at independently — which is the first evidence this base has that the US and EU are converging on **which uses are unacceptable** even while diverging completely on instruments. A deliverable designed against Annex III is therefore more portable into North America than the regulatory divergence suggests. Note this is a **reversal of direction** from T8 (regulation is diverging by region): divergence holds for instruments, convergence is appearing in prohibited uses.

**Opportunities:**
- 🟢 **Canada's AI-literacy commitment is a curriculum sell, not a compliance sell.** One million post-secondary students and 3,000+ educators is a delivery problem with public money attached and no regulation to satisfy. This is the one North American opportunity on this page where the deliverable is teaching material and teacher capacity rather than controls — and `patchy631/ai-engineering-hub` (MIT, 41.1k★) is a permissive base for exactly that. See `compose/patterns.md` **P10**.
- 🔵 **Provincial fragmentation is the Canadian version of the policy-to-implementation gap**, with one twist: in Quebec the current posture is *suspension*, so the sellable work is the evidence and governance case that would let a directive be lifted, not a deployment. Do not pitch classroom AI into Quebec as though the Ontario or Alberta conversation applies.
- **Policy-to-implementation gap as a service.** Ohio-style mandates require a policy with no guidance on content, and Maryland requires a district AI coordinator role that districts have no one to fill. Globant can productise the compliance artefact *plus* the technical controls behind it, repeatable across districts.
- **Canvas-first agent pilots.** Canvas dominates North American HE. `canvas-mcp` (MIT, 317★) reaches real course data with no migration — the shortest credible path to a funded pilot.
- **"No AI replacing teachers" as a design constraint, not an obstacle.** Idaho's bar makes teacher-augmentation framing legally safer than autonomy. `Instructional Agents` (MIT) automates course *preparation* — exactly the defensible side of that line.
- OATutor (MIT, UC Berkeley) carries domestic academic provenance, which matters in public procurement here.

Price that as the entry engagement and the platform work as phase two.
- 🟢 **p655 — the gap between teacher use and institutional policy is the live risk, and it is wide.** 60% of US teachers report using AI tools (Gallup, 2,200+ educators), while a joint Child Trends / US Department of Education analysis finds **most US public schools still have no formal AI policy for students**. Higher education is further along: ~70% of institutions across North America and Europe have guidance or are drafting it. Shadow adoption at 60% with no policy is a liability conversation, and it is the one a superintendent will take a meeting about.
- 🟢 **p655 — two instructive procurement constraints to design against, not around.** The **DC** OSSE policy for 2026-27 **bans AI from grading and discipline decisions outright**; **New York's A 9190** would restrict classroom AI to grade 9 and above with carve-outs for diagnostics and special education. The vehicle is reported as the **Digital Omnibus, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744**. ⚠️ **Verify against EUR-Lex before putting any of these dates in a client document** — every source here is a law-firm or vendor summary, and they disagree with each other.

**Why it bites in education specifically:** the Act lists AI used in **education access and assessment** — admission decisions, student evaluation, exam scoring — as high-risk. 🟢 **The practical consequence is a build constraint, not a filing exercise:** an automated-assessment feature needs logging, human oversight and documented accuracy *designed in*, and the December 2027 date is the window in which to do it, not a deferral.

**Beyond the EU, the picture is uneven and should be described as uneven:** very few countries in the region had **binding** national AI-in-education regulation as of 2026; most operate on guidance, pilot frameworks, or silence.

| Jurisdiction | Instrument |
|---|---|
| **UK** | Department for Education **generative AI product safety standards for education (January 2026)**; **Ofqual** resources on AI and coursework integrity (March 2026) |
| **Gulf states** | 🟢 Moved unusually fast on formal AI governance relative to infrastructure — **Dubai's KHDA has issued explicit guidance to private schools**. The anomaly worth noting: governance ahead of deployment, the inverse of every other region in this file |
| **OECD** (policy, not jurisdiction) | 2026 Digital Education Outlook recommends moving **beyond general-purpose AI tools toward purpose-built educational AI** |

**Market slice:** European AI-in-education put at **`USD 2.64B` in 2026**, forecast `USD 8.0B` by 2030 at **`31.9%` CAGR**. ⚠️ Single secondary compilation; treat as directional only, and note it is consistent with roughly a quarter of the global 2026 bracket recorded above.

#### 🆕 Added at p717 — THE AI ACT DEADLINE MOVED, and the common sales pitch is now `13` months out of date

🔴 **High-risk education obligations were deferred from `2026-08-02` to `2027-12-02`.** Multiple compliance sources describe the Digital Omnibus amendment (one names it **Regulation (EU) 2026/1744**) moving the Annex III date. 🔴 **Guides still citing August 2026 as the education deadline are stale**, and several are still being published — which is itself the opening: clients are being sold urgency against a date that no longer exists.

🟢 **What did NOT move, and this is the live obligation:**

- **Emotion recognition in education has been prohibited since `2025-02-02`.** Already in force. Any deployed proctoring or engagement-monitoring feature touching affect inference is a live exposure, not a future one.

**In-scope as high-risk:** admission decisions, student evaluation, exam scoring, proctoring and behaviour monitoring. Educational chatbots and pedagogical content generators are covered by the transparency track. An institution that **buys** an Annex III system becomes a **deployer** with its own separate obligations — so there are two distinct buyers for the same compliance work, the vendor and the school.

🟢 **The 18-month window is the actual product.** `2027-12-02` is far enough out that remediation is a programme rather than a panic, and near enough that budget exists: conformity-assessment readiness, technical documentation, logging and human-oversight design for grading and admissions systems already in production.

#### 🔴 p713 — EMEA: **THE EU AI ACT'S HIGH-RISK DEADLINE FOR EDUCATION HAS MOVED BY ~16 MONTHS, AND EVERY ENGAGEMENT PLAN DATED TO `2026-08-02` IS NOW WRONG**

🔴 **This is the single most consequential regional finding of the pass, and it is a correction rather than an addition.** Education AI is **high-risk under Annex III** of the EU AI Act — a system that evaluates learners or influences access to qualifications falls in scope. The date those obligations bite has been **postponed**:

| obligation | previously | now |
|---|---|---|
| stand-alone **Annex III** high-risk systems (where education AI sits) | `2026-08-02` | 🔴 **`2027-12-02`** |
| AI **embedded in regulated products** | — | 🔴 **`2028-08-02`** |
| **Article 4 AI-literacy duties** for staff | — | 🟢 **already in force since February 2025** |
| prohibition on AI-generated **NCII / CSAM** | — | 🔴 **`2026-12-02`** |

🔵 **Provenance, stated because it decides how much weight to put on it.** The postponement comes via the **Digital Omnibus** amendment, reported against a **May 2026 political agreement**; two independent sources in this pass carry it, one of them a law firm's global AI regulatory update. 🔴 **One source in the same pass still publishes the old `August 2026` date.** The primary record is the Official Journal, and **`ACTION TN` registers verifying the amendment there before this date is used in a client-facing document.** Until then, treat `2027-12-02` as *well-sourced but not primary-verified*.

🟢 **Why a postponement is an opportunity rather than a reprieve.** Three things are true at once and they point the same way:
- the **compliance deadline moved out** by ~16 months,
- the **AI-literacy duty is already live** (Feb 2025) and the **NCII/CSAM prohibition lands `2026-12-02`**, inside the next 12 months,
- the **OECD 2026 Digital Education Outlook** recommends moving **beyond general-purpose AI tools toward purpose-built educational AI**.

🔴 **So the near-term obligations are the ones nobody is planning for, because attention was fixed on the high-risk date that just moved.** An institution that deferred everything to `2026-08-02` has deferred its Article 4 literacy obligation too — and that one was never postponed.

🟢 **The engagement (`P114`), and the instruments are permissive:** build the high-risk **technical dossier** on the regulator-adjacent open stack rather than buying a compliance product — [`aiverify-foundation/aiverify`](https://github.com/aiverify-foundation/aiverify) (Apache-2.0) for the test harness, [`moonshot-cicd`](https://github.com/aiverify-foundation/moonshot-cicd) (Apache-2.0) to re-run it on every change, [`aboutcode-org/scancode.io`](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode.io) (Apache-2.0, **sponsored by the European Commission and NLnet NGI0**) for provenance, [`openedx/codejail`](https://github.com/openedx/codejail) (Apache-2.0) for the execution-isolation claim. **The extra 16 months is build time for a dossier that is produced by the pipeline rather than written once by a consultancy.**

#### 🟢 p711 — EMEA: **the compliance clock SPLIT — high-risk education slipped to `2027-12-02` while transparency bound on `2026-08-02`. That gap is a ~13-month build window**

🔴 **`0` repositories from the mandated EMEA leg; `EMEA 24` did not move.** The region's finding this pass is entirely regulatory, and it is the most consequential single item of p711.

The EU **Digital Omnibus on AI** moved the deadline for stand-alone **Annex III high-risk** systems — education sits there whenever AI touches **admissions, assessment or proctoring** — from `2026-08-02` to **`2027-12-02`**; AI embedded in regulated products moves to `2028-08-02`.

| duty | applies from | moved? |
|---|---|---|
| **Article 4** AI literacy — every organisation using AI, therefore every school | **`2025-02-02`** | 🔴 no — already binding |
| **Article 50** transparency — chatbot disclosure, synthetic-content labelling | **`2026-08-02`** | 🔴 no — already binding |
| **Annex III high-risk** education systems (admissions, assessment, proctoring) | **`2027-12-02`** | 🟢 yes, from `2026-08-02` |

🟢 **Read commercially, this is a window, not a pause** (`T178`): roughly **13 months** in which a high-risk education system is buildable without the full Annex III conformity burden, **while disclosure, labelling and staff AI literacy are enforceable today**. 🔴 **The deployer carries the duty even when the tool is third-party** — so a school buying a vendor's agent does not buy out of the obligation, and that is the sentence to put in front of a university client.

🟢 **The one EMEA supply event is an upgrade rather than a row:** [`fborrasumh/planificaia-docente`](https://github.com/fborrasumh/planificaia-docente) (Universidad Miguel Hernández de Elche, Spain) was re-found independently, confirmed byte-identical, and its row enriched with the mechanism that makes it matter — **the model proposes, the code verifies** (`711-B`, `T180`). For an Annex III conversation, a deterministic validator plus a named human decision-maker is the architecture that the assessment use case needs.

🟡 Institutional posture: schools are reported **mostly in pilot and pre-compliance mode**. Ireland stood up an **AI Office under its AI Regulation Act 2026**. Policy is coordinated through the Digital Education Action Plan alongside the AI Act, per a **European Parliament briefing (March 2026, `784574`)**. UNESCO's generative-AI guidance (late 2023) and the OECD AI Principles (updated 2024) remain the soft-law baseline.

#### 🟡 p701 — EMEA: the high-risk deadline that guidance is still being published against **may have moved by 16 months**, and that discrepancy is the region's most actionable fact

🔴 **Two incompatible dates for the same obligation were in circulation when this pass read them, and both are being published as current.** Education AI is an **Annex III high-risk** category under the EU AI Act. #### 🔵 p690 — EMEA: the leg nilled, and this pass's finding is that **Europe's public-sector education software reads as unlicensed to every scanner**

🔴 **The demand leg returned nothing new.** Held: the Digital Omnibus amendments (adopted June 2026, in force **27 July 2026**) moving stand-alone **Annex III** high-risk obligations to **2 December 2027** and AI embedded in regulated products to **2 August 2028**; the 7 May 2026 Council/Parliament political agreement behind that `16`-month delay; the Commission's 2026-updated ethical guidelines for educators via the European Digital Education Hub; the AI Continent Action Plan naming education for AI uptake; UNESCO's `68` countries regulating AI in education (up from `14` in 2021); the UK's light-touch, existing-regulator posture. 🔴 **Dubai's KHDA guidance to private schools remains secondary-source only** — a standing EMEA debt, unchanged. 🔴 **No African datapoint was returned by this leg at all**, against a shelf that holds four named African programmes from `p677`; that is a leg failure, not an absence of activity.

🟢 **The novel EMEA finding of this pass is a supply-side legal fact with direct procurement consequence.** `p690` audited every shelved subject against GitHub's own `spdx_id` and found that **all `11` [`Opetushallitus`](https://github.com/Opetushallitus) repositories — the Finnish National Agency for Education's production learner stack — return `NOASSERTION`, i.e. *no detectable licence*.** The grants are real and short: [`koski`](https://github.com/Opetushallitus/koski) `LICENSE.txt` **`653 B`**, *Licensed under the EUPL, **Version 1.1** or ...*, © 2015; [`ataru`](https://github.com/Opetushallitus/ataru) `LICENSE.md` **`296 B`**, *EUPL **Version 1.2** or ...*, © 2025. The same holds for [`kouta-backend`](https://github.com/Opetushallitus/kouta-backend) (`295 B`), [`oph-design-system`](https://github.com/Opetushallitus/oph-design-system) (`650 B`), `ehoks`, `eperusteet`, `eperusteet-ylops`, `ludos`, `suorituspalvelu`, `varda` and `organisaatio`.

🔵 **Why this is an engagement and not a curiosity.** The EUPL is the licence European public bodies publish under, and it is the one family on this shelf that **no automated composition-analysis tool will attribute**. A client's licence gate does not report *copyleft, price it* — it reports **`unknown licence`**, which is the output that stops a review dead, because unknown cannot be risk-assessed. 🟢 **Three separate things can therefore be sold into an EMEA public-sector or university engagement, and none of them require writing an agent:** (i) a **licence attestation** over the estate that resolves every `unknown` to a named family with payload evidence; (ii) the **EUPL reciprocity boundary** priced properly — the EUPL's own definition of *Distribution or Communication* reaches making the Work available over a network, so the boundary is not GPL's; and (iii) the **version split**, which this pass measured and which matters: `koski` is **EUPL-1.1**-or-later and `ataru` is **EUPL-1.2**-or-later, and they are not the same instrument. See `690-P` in [`compose/patterns.md`](../compose/patterns.md).

Paired with [`DavidLMS/learnmcp-xapi`](https://github.com/DavidLMS/learnmcp-xapi) (MIT) writing every interaction to an xAPI store, a studio can show *what was said, why it was said, and that the record exists*. ##### 🆕 p686 — The AI Act high-risk deadline MOVED, and selling urgency off the old date is now selling a date that does not exist

🔴 **This is the most consequential correction of the pass.** Education AI is Annex III high-risk under the EU AI Act, and the widely-quoted compliance date was **2 August 2026**. The **Digital Omnibus amendment, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744**, moved it: **2 December 2027** for stand-alone Annex III systems and **2 August 2028** for AI embedded in regulated products. Vendor material published earlier in 2026 — including sources returned by this pass's own search leg — still quotes August 2026. 🟢 **What did NOT move: the prohibition on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM takes effect `2 December 2026`**, i.e. **inside the next month**, and it binds any deployment with a generative image surface pointed at minors. For a schools engagement that is the live deadline, not the high-risk one.

🟢 **Commercially this is a reprieve that changes what to sell.** An extra `16` months removes the compliance-panic trigger, so EMEA education AI reverts to being bought on instructional value. The OECD's **2026 Digital Education Outlook** says the same thing from the demand side: move **beyond general-purpose AI** toward purpose-built educational systems. Market figure found: **$2.64 B** for European AI-in-education in 2026 — single vendor source, uncorroborated, flagged.

🟢 **The permissive-licence asymmetry is sharpest in this region, and p686 sharpened it further.** European institutional procurement rewards sovereignty and self-hosting, while the dominant LMS estate is copyleft — Moodle GPL-3.0, Open edX AGPL-3.0. **OpenOlat (Apache-2.0, `10,982 B`, `6dbc5b605ed0`, re-verified byte-exact at p686) is the only major institutional LMS that permits a closed commercial derivative**, and it is **Swiss** — `frentix GmbH` is named in the repository's own README, which is how this base places it EMEA rather than by owner attribute. For any EMEA engagement needing a proprietary layer on an open LMS, OpenOlat is the only lawful base. Leading K-12 integrators cited: **Finland, Estonia, Netherlands**.

🟢 **Gulf:** the regional guide finds Gulf states moving faster on formal AI governance than on infrastructure — the **UAE national AI strategy** and **Dubai's KHDA** issuing explicit responsible-AI guidance to private schools. A KHDA-aligned governance artefact is a procurable deliverable for the Dubai private-school segment, which is large, fee-paying and centrally regulated.

🔴 **AFRICA IS A MEASURED GAP, NOT COVERAGE.** The EMEA leg returned **no substantive Africa-specific adoption or regulation material** — the sources resolve to EU plus Gulf and stop. This base therefore holds **no** African education-AI intelligence, and the `A` in EMEA is currently unearned on this shelf. **An EMEA engagement scoped to Africa cannot be served from this KB today.** Closing it needs country-level legs (Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Egypt) rather than another regional one, and the EU-first framing of every source returned is itself the reason the gap persists.

Finland has answered both in public, in production: the reference implementation of a statutory personalised-learning object (`ehoks`) and of a machine-readable national curriculum (`eperusteet`) are readable, and the licence the ministry chose is the one an EU procurement office recognises in **23 languages**. 🔴 **It also sets the licence expectation an EMEA bid may have to meet: EUPL, not MIT** — and because the EUPL counts online availability as distribution, a vendor SaaS built by forking it inherits the obligation. **Regulatory posture:** the most binding regime in the world, and the timeline just moved. The **Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)** deferred high-risk obligations for stand-alone education AI from 2 August 2026 to **2 December 2027**. Guides still citing August 2026 are out of date. High-risk covers **admissions, learning-outcome evaluation, student level placement, and exam/behaviour monitoring**. **Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026** — a school running a student-facing chatbot owes disclosure *now*. **Emotion recognition in schools has been prohibited since February 2025.** Article 4's AI-literacy duty was softened from "ensuring a level of AI literacy" to "taking measures". Schools are **deployers** under the Act.

That is a precise, actionable finding: the partnering motion for Africa is co-development with existing product teams, not adoption of an African open-source stack, because there is not yet one to adopt. The high-risk delay is therefore a **window, not a reprieve**: the transparency duty lands first, and the institutions that will face the 2027 obligations are procuring now. An xAPI statement log in an Apache-2.0 LRS is the cheapest artefact that satisfies an Article 50 enquiry and pre-positions for Annex III evidence — and it stays in the institution's own database, which is the sovereignty answer EMEA buyers ask for first. ##### 🟢 New at p668 — two of the three EU obligations are already live, and that is the sales fact most guidance still gets wrong

- 🔴 **Re-verified at p668 and unchanged from `T7`/`T15`: the deadline that moved is the *only* one that moved.** The Digital Omnibus (**Regulation (EU) 2026/1744**) shifted stand-alone Annex III high-risk education systems — admissions, student evaluation, exam scoring — from `2026-08-02` to **`2027-12-02`**, with AI embedded in regulated products at `2028-08-02`. But **Article 50 transparency applies from `2026-08-02`** and **Article 4 AI literacy has applied since `2025-02-02`**. 🟢 **So a school that reads "the deadline moved to 2027" and stands down is already non-compliant on two counts today** — and that misreading is in circulation, because multiple vendor compliance guides still publish the August 2026 high-risk date.
- 🔵 **The deployer is the school, even when the tool is someone else's.** Schools carry deployer obligations for third-party tools, and vendors carry conformity duties, so `P37`'s week 6–8 artefact has two buyers in the same engagement. Enforcement splits: the Commission's **AI Office** supervises general-purpose model providers; national authorities take most of the rest.
- 🟢 **`T50`'s one permissive system of record matters more here than anywhere.** EMEA public-sector procurement is where a GPL-2.0 or AGPL-3.0 system of record most often *is* the incumbent, and `P32` already covers not inheriting the EUPL from a ministry stack. `P37` extends the same move to the SIS.

### APAC

#### 🆕 Added at p721 — the region supplied EVERY agent filing this pass, and the compulsory-curriculum mandates explain why

🟢 **APAC filed `3 / 3` of this pass's agent rows** (`good-learning`, `HiNote`, `Morrow`) and now holds **`91 / 345`** — the largest region on the shelf. The supply is not an accident: it tracks national mandates that create a domestic user base before any export market exists.

| Country | Mandate / rule | Date |

| **China** | Compulsory national AI curriculum, **from age 6**; one of only two countries running one since the 2025-26 school year | in force |
| **UAE** | The other compulsory national AI curriculum | in force |
| **India** | AI and computational thinking **compulsory from Class 3**, tied to the IndiaAI Mission and teacher training | **2026-27 academic year** |
| **South Korea** | **AI Basic Act** in force | **22 Jan 2026** |
| **Vietnam** | AI law in force | **1 Mar 2026** |
| **China** | Anthropomorphic-AI rules issued 10 Apr 2026 | **effective 15 Jul 2026** |

🔵 **Adoption, with the caveat attached:** one report characterises the region as *"adoption breadth is extraordinary but depth remains shallow"*; India is described as APAC's fastest-growing AI market at **`38.9%` CAGR**. Public opinion is notably more permissive — **only `26%` in India support banning AI in schools against `39%` globally** (Ipsos). 🟡 UNESCO's read is that the region is **uneven**: China and Singapore have established AI-in-education policies while others are still meeting basic educational needs.

🔵 **Opportunity:** this is the **source region for components, not just a target market**. Every APAC agent filed this pass is MIT and built as a *skill on a host harness* rather than an application — **so the cheapest route to a North America or EMEA tutor product is to localise an APAC skill, not to build one.** 🔴 **The gate is language, not licence:** `good-learning`'s prompts, rubrics and output templates are Chinese-primary, so localisation is a translation-and-pedagogy task of real size, and it is the thing a client is actually paying for.
