#### 🆕 Added at p717 — the region split into THREE DIFFERENT MARKETS, and one of them went backwards

🟢 **China — a mandate, and it is the largest single education-AI demand event anywhere.** Ministry of Education guidelines (May 2025) make AI instruction compulsory **from roughly age six, across all school grades**. Reported shape: **at least `6` hours a year** for lower grades, **one hour a fortnight** for higher grades, formalised as a named subject — *"Artificial Intelligence and Technology"* — for the **2026–2027** year. 🔴 **Two hard constraints that invert the usual product:** primary pupils are **barred from using generative AI independently**, and teachers are **barred from substituting AI tools for core instructional duties**. So the buyable thing is **curriculum, teacher training and assessment of AI literacy** — not a student-facing chatbot, which is the thing most vendors are selling.

🔴 **South Korea — a REVERSAL, and it is the most useful negative datapoint in the region.** AI textbooks were slated as mandatory from 2025; lawmakers then **stripped them of "textbook" status and reclassified them as "supplementary materials"**, moving the adoption decision to individual principals. Reported uptake before the change was **under `30%` of `6,339` elementary schools**. 🟢 **Read it as a procurement lesson, not a market exit:** a national mandate that arrives before teacher capability and evidence does not convert, and the spend reappears as **`6,339` separate school-level decisions**. That is a channel problem, and it is a different engagement from a ministry programme.

🟢 **Japan — permissive and cautious at once, which favours pilots.** The AI Basic Plan was adopted **December 2025** with a **second-phase plan on `2026-07-14`**; regulation **promotes AI without penalties**. MEXT holds a **neutral stance** and is watching school pilots. Its guidelines (2024, updated 2026) steer generative AI to **lesson preparation, administrative drafting and communication, with teacher judgement of output required** — i.e. the Japanese buyer is the *teacher workload* case, not the student tutor case.

**Regulatory baseline for the rest of the region:** South Korea has a general AI law in force; China regulates **by type of service**; India has **no dedicated AI law** and works through its data-protection statute, sector regulators and voluntary guidance, with **AI-content labelling rules effective `2026-02-20`**; Vietnam is named by one source as holding the region's only comprehensive AI statute. 🔴 **Sources conflict on who is "first"** (one puts South Korea ahead, another Vietnam) — treat the ranking as unsettled.

**Sentiment, for pricing resistance:** Ipsos Education Monitor 2026 finds **weak support for banning AI in schools** — about **`26%` in India**, **`29%` in Japan** (up from `21%`). UNESCO records **China, Japan, South Korea and Singapore** already building AI-focused curricula.

🔴 **Gap, stated:** beyond the China mandate, the leg found **no 2026 education-specific ministry directive text** for India or Japan — only secondary coverage. The China figures are news and commentary, **not the directive itself**.

Anchored on **NEP 2020** and **NCF-SE 2023**, delivered through a **NCERT–CBSE coordination committee** with KVS, NVS and the state/UT boards; **NCERT has constituted a textbook development team for Grades 11–12**, where AI stays optional; **CIET-NCERT** ran a *"Leveraging AI for Transforming School Education"* educator training series in **January 2026**. 🟢 **Demand — Singapore, and this is the region's governance template.** MOE's **Student Learning Space (SLS)** has carried **Learning Feedback Assistants** since **December 2023**: a *Language Feedback Assistant* for English writing mechanics and a *Short Answer Feedback Assistant* that suggests grades and generates content feedback, with a mathematics variant offering hints and suggested marks. **The guardrails are the part worth copying:** a September 2026 MOE reply states the Learning Assistant requires **teacher activation** and lets a teacher **cap the number of interactions**, and teachers review or adjust automated feedback before it reaches a student. On the workforce side, MOE's **Teacher AI Literacy Professional Learning Roadmap** (**August 2026**) sets **one compulsory AI module by end-2026** and two more strongly recommended by end-2027; pupils use education-specific AI tools from **Primary 4** under supervision, which the education minister has described as deliberately low-exposure. MOE also states it is still investigating these tools' effect on learning.

APAC's two anchor countries both buy at **national-platform** level: the unit is a state board deploying shared DPI, or a ministry extending one national learner surface. That changes the deliverable from *integrate with their LMS* to **extend their platform without forking it**, and it is the first region where this base holds the platform's own source under a permissive grant. The leg was run (`AI education APAC 2026 adoption regulation players`). **Already held:** South Korea's **AI Basic Act** in force 22 January 2026 with a guidance-first grace period through 2026; **Vietnam Law 134/2025/QH15** effective 1 March 2026 and **Decision 33/2026/QD-TTg** naming automated assessment in education as high-risk; Australia's **TEQSA** requirement that providers file institutional generative-AI action plans; China's registration and content-labelling regime with penalties up to ¥50M; and the EU-spillover argument for APAC ed-tech selling proctoring or admissions tools into Annex III scope. **Nothing new: `0` facts added.** 🔵 **Recorded as an informed nil.** APAC remains the region where this base is strongest on supply (**8** of the 15 placed agent rows) and where the regulatory picture is a patchwork by design — three postures (comprehensive risk-based, targeted, light-touch) across one commercial region, which is a per-jurisdiction compliance cost, not a regional one.

**Regulatory posture:** no longer merely fragmented — **APAC now has a binding, horizontal, risk-tiered AI statute that names education explicitly**, and this KB did not hold it until p651.

🔴 **South Korea — the AI Basic Act (Law No. 20676), in force 22 January 2026.** The world's second comprehensive AI statute after the EU AI Act. Its **"high-impact AI" category covers AI used for student assessment in early-childhood, elementary and secondary education** — named in the statutory definition, not inferred from a sector list. Operators must determine whether their system qualifies before deployment (and may request a determination from MSIT), and must make efforts to assess the system's impact on fundamental rights before putting it into a product or service. **MSIT has signalled a grace period of at least one year before administrative fines**, so the enforcement edge falls around **January 2027**, with the interim focused on guidance through a new integrated support centre. A promotion-focused amendment commences 21 July 2026. *(Enactment date 21 January 2025 per the official text; one secondary source says December 2024 — rely on the official text. Grace-period length is reported as "at least one year"; confirm with MSIT before relying on it contractually.)*

🔴 **Vietnam — the dated hook p651 left open is closed, and it names education in a decision, not an inference.** The **Law on Artificial Intelligence (No. 134/2025/QH15)**, passed 10 December 2025, in force **1 March 2026**, sets a three-tier risk framework. The operative instrument is **Decision 33/2026/QD-TTg**, effective **15 August 2026**, which promulgates the list of high-risk AI systems: **46 systems across six sectors, of which education accounts for three.**

The primary education entry covers AI used to **automatically run examinations or assessments, assess learning outcomes, and rank learners** — and it is scoped: it applies **only where the results serve as the official basis** for assessing learning outcomes or ranking learners within the national education system. That scoping clause is the commercially important part. A formative or practice tool falls outside it; the same model wired into the system of record falls inside.

**Transition:** systems already operating before 15 August 2026 have until **1 September 2027** to comply in education, healthcare and finance (other listed sectors: 1 March 2027).

*(Law and decision numbers, dates and the education entry's wording are from law-firm and compliance summaries plus a reproduction of the decision text; the primary Vietnamese text was not read at first hand. Two further entries reported by one commentary — systems that monitor and analyse learner behaviour, and self-study tools generating content from uncontrolled sources — **could not be confirmed against the decision text and are not published here as fact.**)*

**Singapore** relies on governance toolkits rather than a statute: new AI governance guidance covering **generative and agentic** AI, with MAS consulting on AI Risk Management Guidelines. No education-specific rule.

🔴 **A claim about Australia was tested this pass and does not verify.** A widely-repeated summary states that **TEQSA requires all higher education providers to submit institutional action plans addressing generative-AI risks** — which would have been the most education-specific regulatory action in the region. **No such submission mandate was found.** What exists is guidance and a standards hook: TEQSA published *"Assuring quality learning in a gen AI-integrated future"* on **24 June 2026**, maintains a Gen AI Knowledge Hub for providers, staff and students, and frames academic-integrity risk through **Threshold Standard 5.2** rather than a new instrument; prior key documents are a 2024 report on gen AI strategies and a 2025 guide to enacting assessment reform. Australia's posture is therefore unchanged from what this page already says — existing law plus sector guidance — and the contradicting claim is recorded as rejected rather than quietly dropped.

🟢 **Two genuinely procurement-grade Australian assets surfaced while testing that claim**, and they are the kind of thing this page has been declaring absent in APAC: a **Zenodo dataset (October 2026) recording the public student generative-AI disclosure rules of all 220 providers on the TEQSA National Register**, and an **AJET study (July 2026) analysing how 39 universities align with TEQSA's gen-AI principles.** A census of every provider's published rule is exactly the artefact that lets an engagement open with the client's own position already mapped.

**China** regulates by service — Generative AI Regulation (2023), Deep Synthesis (2022), Recommendation Algorithm (2022); companion-service rules effective 15 July 2026; the amended Cybersecurity Law adds the first AI clause (Article 20). **India** has no dedicated AI law and governs via the DPDP Act and 2025 Rules plus voluntary MeitY guidelines; amended IT Rules on **synthetic-content labelling took effect 20 February 2026**. **Japan**'s AI Promotion Act (May 2025) is deliberately non-binding, with a government AI Basic Plan adopted by Cabinet in July 2026. **Australia and Hong Kong** apply existing law and sector guidance rather than a standalone AI act.

#### 🔴 p715 — LATAM: **the supply question moved from "is there any?" to "is it USABLE?", and on the region's largest publisher the answer is no**

🔴 **The mandated LATAM leg returned `0` repository addresses for the `35th` consecutive pass.** The one row filed this pass came from an **owner probe**, which is not in the mandate — full method in [`../agents/trending.md`](../agents/trending.md) `715-D`.

🔴 **The headline is a licence finding with direct commercial consequence for LATAM engagements.** [`EL-BID`](https://github.com/EL-BID), the **Inter-American Development Bank** — the largest publisher of public-sector development software in the region — holds **`79` repositories and `0` permissive grants** (`68` `NOASSERTION`, `8` ungranted, `3` `GPL-3.0`). The `NOASSERTION` mass is the bank's own **"IDB Open-Source Software License" (effective December 2025)**, and despite the name it is **not an open-source licence**: §11 permits termination *"in its sole discretion"*, §12 then requires the code destroyed or returned and makes continued use of derivatives conditional on **written IDB authorisation**, §4 is viral, §10 has the user indemnify the bank for exercising the granted rights, and §15 forces **AAA arbitration seated in Washington DC**.

🔴 **Read this as a sourcing constraint, not a curiosity.** IDB-funded education software — `IADB-education-1`, `edu-brazil-poc`, `IDBx-Data-Engine`, `SmartReader`, `escola-no-lugar-certo`, `matricula-digital` (Tacna, Peru) — is **off-limits as a base layer for commercial client work**, because a revocable grant plus a destroy-on-termination clause cannot sit under a client's production system. 🟢 **The opportunity that replaces it:** these are *reference implementations of problems LATAM ministries are already funding* — school siting, digital enrolment, mass document analysis. **Read the IDB estate for the requirement, build the implementation clean.** That is a legitimate, well-specified engagement thesis, and it is strictly better advice than *fork it*.

🔴 **Two institutional nils, with distinct causes, stated so silence is not mistaken for coverage.** **Tec de Monterrey** — named by this base's own intel for four passes — publishes `40` repositories of which `22` are **per-student coursework** on the slug `C.MTY.TC1031.607.2613.A<enrolment-number>`, `21` MIT, `0★`: real, live, permissive, worthless as substrate. **Plan Ceibal**, the region's most-cited education-technology agency (~`700k` students), has one searchable org, `ceibal-tatu`, **last pushed `2015-12-03`**, `35` repositories, almost entirely GPL/LGPL Sugar-era packaging, `1` MIT. The bare `Ceibal` org has **no public repositories to search**. 🔵 **So part of why this column is thin is that LATAM's flagship agency stopped publishing code eleven years ago** — a fact about supply, not about search.

🟢 **The one genuine addition, and the opportunity it marks:** [`CENIA-DEV/multilingual-translator-app`](https://github.com/CENIA-DEV/multilingual-translator-app) (**Apache-2.0**, Chile, pushed `2026-11-04`) is Spanish ↔ **Rapa Nui** translation with a self-hostable PyTriton server and a published NLLB checkpoint. 🔵 **Endangered- and indigenous-language education is an underserved, fundable LATAM niche with almost no permissive supply** — Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay and Mexico all run intercultural bilingual education mandates, and this is the only Apache-2.0 substrate this base has found addressing one.

🔵 **Demand-side figures re-confirmed, not new:** DEC/Tec de Monterrey 2026 — `92%` of students and `79%` of faculty actively using AI across `29` institutions (>`30,000` responses); UNESCO IESALC — `87%` of institutions across `19` countries using AI in at least one area, adoption driven by faculty and students rather than institutional policy. **ILIA 2025**: `85%` of countries have an AI strategy in place or in development, **but only Brazil and Colombia allocate budget**; Brazil, Chile and Uruguay lead the index; all `20` countries offer postgraduate AI programmes and more than half have AI in school curricula. 🔴 **Still no current binding national AI-in-education law anywhere in the region** — re-confirmed, and now the sharpest contrast in the market map: LATAM has the **highest measured adoption** and the **least binding regulation** of the four regions.

🟢 **The region's product this pass is a method, and it is the pass's headline.** `711-C` concluded that the five-value region vocabulary *"CANNOT EXPRESS Spanish-language, country unknown"* — the shape of most LATAM supply. **It can, and the expression is a standard code the repositories already ship.** [`JhostinAleck/brightspace-mcp`](https://github.com/JhostinAleck/brightspace-mcp) (MIT, `1,070 B`, `15★`) commits `src/shared-kernel/output/i18n/catalogs/es-419.json`. **`es-419` is the UN M.49 code for Latin America** — "Spanish, Latin America, no country" is precisely what it means — and `America/Bogota` is the sample timezone in `17` of the repository's files. **`es-419` → LATAM, with no inference, no name-guessing and no prose.**

🔧 **The guard that makes it reliable: place on the catalogues a project SHIPS, never on the locales it PERMITS.** This repository's config schema also lists `pt-BR` and `fr-CA`, and matching on those would have filed one artifact in three regions at once. It ships catalogue files for `en-US` and `es-419` only.

🔵 **Why this is worth more to this base than the row is.** LATAM supply is overwhelmingly Spanish-language work by individual authors who declare no location — the condition `20 / 27` of this pass's probed owners were in. **Every internationalised project in that population carries its own region key in its i18n directory.** The channel is cheap (`gh api -X GET search/code -f q='es-419 repo:…'`), server-side, and immune to the name-inference error this base has repeatedly warned against.

**Demand side — the strongest regional intel of the four legs, and it is adoption rather than regulation.** The Digital Education Council's 2026 LATAM survey, run with Tecnológico de Monterrey across **`29` universities**, reports **`92%` of students and `79%` of faculty actively engaging with AI** — faculty rising but still behind students. 🔴 **And the gap is stated rather than glossed: no current binding national AI-in-education law was found anywhere in the region this pass.** A UNESCO IESALC/UNU-IAS working paper maps university practice including governance, and a comparative Ibero-American study of higher-education AI rules exists but was reachable only as a bibliographic record. Infrastructure remains the hard constraint — connectivity and digital literacy, not model access.

🔵 **The engagement shape that follows from `92% / 79%` with no statute: governance and enablement, not a build.** The AI is already in the institution; what no university in the survey has is a defensible position on how it is used. That is consistent with this base's standing LATAM reading (`P110`), and `712`'s contribution is that **the region's own supply can now be found and placed**, so a LATAM engagement can start from LATAM-authored components.

#### 🟢 p705 — LATAM: **the first properly DENOMINATED evidence this base has held for any region**, and it describes a governance gap, not an adoption gap

🟢 **UNESCO IESALC, launched at Digital Learning Week `2026`, surveyed ~`200` institutions across `19` countries.** This is the pass's best source on any region: a named institution, a stated sample, and percentages with a denominator rather than a vendor's projection.

| Measure | Value |
|---|--:|
| Institutions using AI in **at least one area** | 🟢 **`87%`** |
| Using AI in **teaching and learning** | 🟢 **`74%`** |
| Holding a **formal AI strategy** | 🔴 **`26%`** |
| With **no specific AI budget at all** | 🔴 **`55%`** |
| **Public** universities with dedicated AI funding | 🔴 **`4%`** |

🔵 **Read the gap, because it is the entire commercial thesis for the region: `87%` are using it and `26%` have decided how.** Adoption is explicitly **bottom-up** — driven by individual academics, researchers and students rather than institutional strategy. The schools layer tells the same story: in **Chile and Brazil more than `50%` of teachers** already use these tools while **fewer than `10%` of institutions** in the region have formal guidelines.

🟡 **And read the constraint honestly, because it is the thing that kills LATAM proposals: `55%` have no AI budget and public universities sit at `4%` dedicated funding.** 🔴 **A region can have `87%` adoption and still have no money to buy anything.** The sellable work is therefore **governance and enablement** — strategy, guidelines, teacher capability, procurement framing — not platform licences; and it is disproportionately **privately funded or donor/multilateral funded**, which changes who the buyer is.

🟢 **The policy layer now has a permanent address: UNESCO's regional Observatory on AI in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean launched in Santiago, Chile on `14 April 2026`** at the ECLAC-hosted forum, to guide public policy and capacity-building. 🔵 **Named players for this region:** UNESCO **IESALC**, **UNU-IAS**, **ECLAC**, **CENIA** (Chile — working with UNESCO on ethics and education) and **Tecnológico de Monterrey** (UNESCO agreement on AI in education, **`March 2026`**). 🟢 **Tec de Monterrey is the single most actionable name on this page for LATAM** — a major private institution with a signed multilateral agreement is both a reference client and a credential.

🟡 **External regulatory pressure is real and arrives from outside the region.** The EU AI Act reaches LATAM firms selling into Europe, and the commentary this pass returned warns that companies failing to certify compliance **"may be excluded from tenders and global supply chains"** — a law-firm framing, so read as interpretation. 🔵 **For Globant that is a service, not a threat: EU conformity readiness for LATAM-built edtech**, and it pairs with the Annex III classification boundary recorded under `### EMEA` above.

#### 🟢 p704 — LATAM: three education-specific bills are moving in parallel, two of them novel to this base — and Mexico is a measured hole

🟢 **Novel at `p704`: Brazil now has a legislative *pipeline* for AI in education, not a single bill**, and this page can brief it with stages and dates:

| Instrument | Stage read at `p704` | What it would do |
|---|---|---|
| **`PL 2338/2023`** (horizontal AI frame) | Approved by the Senate **`2024-12-10`**; national AI governance system supervised by the **ANPD**; its principles include AI education and public awareness | The frame everything else sits inside |
| **`PL 3399/2026`** (Senate) 🆕 | Reported in **Senate plenary as of `2026-07-01`**, still processing | Adds **AI literacy** and countering synthetic disinformation to the *National Digital Education Policy* |
| **`PL 2397/2026`** (Senate, Sen. Jader Barbalho) 🆕 | **Filed `2026-05-14`**, awaiting committee assignment | **National ethical standards for AI use in public and private schools** |
| **`PL 3379/2023`** (Chamber of Deputies) | `PL 1837/2026` attached to it **`2026-06-09`** | Adds AI teaching to secondary education under the national education guidelines law |

🟡 **None of the four is law, and the two novel ones are at the earliest stages.** Published as a **pipeline to brief**, not a deadline to sell against — a client told "Brazil requires this" would be misled.

🔵 **The commercial read, and it is different from EMEA's.** Brazil is legislating **AI literacy and school-level ethics standards** — curriculum and governance obligations — while the EU legislates **system risk classification**. 🟢 **That means the LATAM deliverable is a teaching-and-governance artefact, not a conformity file**: AI-literacy curriculum, disclosure practice, an ethics policy a school can adopt, and teacher capability. `P95` is closer to the LATAM ask than `P96` is, which inverts the usual assumption that compliance work leads.

🟡 **Held, not new:** the Digital Education Council–Tec de Monterrey survey (**`92%` of students, `79%` of faculty** across `29` universities), UNESCO's **Regional Observatory on AI in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean** (launched April 2026), the **UNESCO–CENIA** agreement (Chile, February 2026), UNESCO IESALC/UNU-IAS five-dimension university mapping, and the infrastructure constraint that bounds all of it.

🔴 **Mexico: nilled explicitly, and this is the region's most consequential gap.** The LATAM leg returned **no** Mexican instrument — the only Spanish-language legislative material it surfaced was Brazilian. Mexico is the region's second-largest education market and this page still holds **zero** Mexican AI-in-education instruments. 🔵 **Named so it is not mistaken for coverage**, and with the fix specified: run a Spanish-language leg at Mexico directly (`SEP`, `Cámara de Diputados`), because an English-token `LATAM` query demonstrably resolves to Brazil.

Two different organisations announcing the identical amount one month apart in the same region is more likely one story recounted twice — plausibly Google.org **funding** the Raspberry Pi Foundation — than two independent commitments. **Do not sum them, and verify each against its own announcement before either appears in a deliverable.** This is `p695`'s correction discipline applied to funding rather than to market size: one source counted twice is the commonest defect in this category.

**Opportunities:**

##### 🟢 New at p656 — the cheapest fix for the PoC-to-P&L gap is a statement log, and it is permissive

🔴 **This page's sharpest LATAM finding is a governance and evidence gap, not a technology gap:** high usage against formal AI strategy at a small minority of institutions, and under a third of proofs-of-concept reaching P&L. p656 shelved the components that make a LATAM pilot *defensible*, which is the binding constraint on whether it survives into a budget cycle.

🟢 **Why this fits LATAM specifically, on three counts.** First, **licence**: Moodle (GPL-3.0) and Chamilo (GPL-3.0) dominate the regional installed base, and an LTI 1.3 launch is a separate work — so [`tsugiproject/tsugi`](https://github.com/tsugiproject/tsugi) (Apache-2.0) or [`dmitry-viskov/pylti1.3`](https://github.com/dmitry-viskov/pylti1.3) (MIT) puts a Globant-owned tool inside the ministry's Moodle **without forking it and without inheriting GPL**. Second, **infrastructure**: [`yetanalytics/lrsql`](https://github.com/yetanalytics/lrsql) runs on SQLite or a single PostgreSQL instance — no cloud analytics contract, no egress, which is both cheaper and the data-residency answer. Third, **the sale**: a per-learner statement log is what converts "the pilot felt good" into a cohort delta a finance director will fund. **P5** has sold governance-and-measurement in this region without naming a component; **P17** names them.

⚠️ **Scope the dependency honestly, because it is thinner than it looks.** `lrsql` is the **only** live, maintained, permissively-licensed LRS in existence. If a client already runs `LearningLocker/learninglocker` — plausible, at 584 ★ and years of installed base — it is **GPL-3.0 and dormant since 2024-05-30**; the recommendation is migration, not extension, and that is a line item.

🔴 **No new LATAM-specific repository was found this pass.** The two permissive rows shelved at p656 with identifiable provenance are both EMEA (Newcastle University, France Université Numérique). Searched `topic:xapi`, `topic:lti`, `topic:scorm` and `topic:accessibility topic:education`; **no LATAM-origin project surfaced in any of the four.** Recorded as a measured absence rather than left as silence — and consistent with this page's standing finding that the region's AI-education activity is deployment and policy rather than published open source.

##### 🟢 New at p657 — the one live component of the measurement layer is Brazilian, and spoken assessment is the region's best-fitting new opportunity

**Supply.** [`douglasrizzo/catsim`](https://github.com/douglasrizzo/catsim) — **BSD-3-Clause**, 153 ★, pushed **2026-11-01**, tag `0.9.1`, default branch 🔴 **`dev`** — is the **only maintained component in the entire permissive psychometric-measurement layer** (**T31**), and it is Brazilian. This KB has repeatedly recorded LATAM as a consumer of open education software rather than a producer; **the single most load-bearing row in the layer added this pass is LATAM-origin**, and that is worth stating plainly in a regional pitch.

**Adoption, and it is the best-measured region in this KB.** UNESCO IESALC, across **~200 higher-education institutions in 19 countries**: **87% use AI in at least one area, and only 26% have any formal framework.** The Digital Education Council's **LATAM 2026 survey** (with Tecnológico de Monterrey and its Institute for the Future of Education): **92% of students and 79% of faculty actively engage with AI.** In schools: **75% of Uruguayan public-school teachers** report using these tools (Ceibal); in Brazil, **65% of internet users aged 9–17** use AI tools and **53% of school administrators** use AI while **only 22% report that their school has guidelines** (Cetic.br).

**Regulation.** Universidad de los Andes (Bogotá) counted **716 AI-related regulatory instruments, rules and legislative proposals across 23 countries and territories, more than 80% initiated since 2023** — volume without convergence. The regional argument is for **common definitions, risk categories, audit principles and mutual recognition** rather than a single statute. **UNESCO launched its Observatory on Artificial Intelligence in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean on 14 April**, and its recommendations to governments are specific: fold higher education into national AI strategies, fund it, issue national guidance, and **integrate AI literacy and governance into accreditation and quality assurance** — which converts governance work from optional to accreditation-critical. Country bodies to name: **Ceibal** (Uruguay), **Cetic.br** (Brazil), **CENIA** (Chile), plus the **UNESCO–Tec de Monterrey** agreement.

🟢 **The opportunities, in priority order.**
1. **Spoken-language assessment (new, and the best regional fit of anything found this pass).** English-language training is large, funded and measurable across the region, and `OpenPronounce` (MIT) + `wikipron` (Apache-2.0, which supplies Spanish and Portuguese lexicons) replaces a **metered per-utterance cloud API** with a CPU container — a cost argument that lands harder where budgets are tighter. See `verticals/solutions.md` Pattern K and `compose/patterns.md` **P20**.
2. **Governance tied to accreditation.** The 87%-use / 26%-framework gap is the largest adoption-governance gap this KB measures anywhere, and UNESCO's accreditation recommendation gives it a deadline-shaped driver. The cheapest credible deliverable remains an Apache-2.0 statement log (**T28**).
3. **Adaptive assessment on a LATAM-maintained component.** `catsim` plus a calibrated item bank is a defensible, explainable adaptive-testing engagement for a ministry or national platform — and the maintainer is in-region.

⚠️ **The standing caveat has not changed:** this region's constraint is the PoC-to-P&L gap, not enthusiasm. 92% of students using AI is not a budget line; accreditation and procurement are.

### Global

#### 🆕 Added at p721 — the 2026 market bracket RE-MEASURED across six houses, and the figure this base publishes is a SPLICE of two incompatible series

🔴 **Correction to a number this KB has quoted for multiple cycles.** The rotation-log summaries carry *"AI-Edu-$9.58B->$42.48B(2030,41.5%)"*. **Those two endpoints come from two different research houses with different market definitions and different end years, joined into one false series.**

| House | 2026 base | Projection | CAGR |
|---|--:|---|--:|
| **Research and Markets** | **`$10.6B`** | `$42.48B` by **2030** | `41.5%` |
| **Precedence Research** | **`$9.58B`** | `$136.79B` by **2035** | `34.52%` |
| **Grand View Research** | **`$11.4B`** | `$57.2B` by 2033 | `25.9%` |
| **Coherent Market Insights** | **`$11.40B`** | `$57.25B` by 2033 | `16.8%` |
| **Trend X Insights** | **≈`$7.30B`** | `$61.26B` by 2034 | `31.50%` |
| **Technavio** | — | **incremental `+$3.37B`** 2025-2030 | `45%` |

🔴 **The published splice takes Precedence's base and Research and Markets' endpoint and CAGR.** `$9.58B` compounding at `41.5%` does not reach `$42.48B` in 2030 — the series is not merely mixed, it is **internally inconsistent**, which is the same defect class `p695` caught once before on this page.

🟢 **What this base publishes instead, as a bracket rather than a point:** **2026 AI-in-education is `$7.30B` – `$11.40B` across six houses (a `1.56×` spread on the SAME year), with 2030-2035 projections spanning `$42B` – `$137B` and CAGRs from `16.8%` to `45%` (a `2.7×` spread).** 🔵 **Technavio's figure is incremental growth, not market size, and must never be compared to the others** — it is the most likely of the six to be mis-cited.

🟢 **The demand-side reading that is consistent across sources, and is the more useful one:** 2026 is the year AI in education moves **from experimentation to governance**. 1EdTech frames it as governance and oversight becoming essential; the OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook and Teach Better both point to **purpose-built, controlled education platforms displacing generic open tools**; Campus Technology's panel expects AI to become **embedded infrastructure** across admissions, advising and administration; HolonIQ expects **selective** acceleration weighted to demonstrated instructional value; Faculty Focus ties growth to **teacher workload** amid shortages and burnout; and 1EdTech adds **digital credentials and competencies** rising on employer demand.

🔵 **Opportunity:** the convergent signal across all five regions is that **the buyer is now purchasing governance as much as capability** — a tutor that cannot produce its oversight trail, its data-handling posture and its disclosure behaviour is unsellable in North America and EMEA regardless of pedagogical quality. **That is a build requirement, and it is the same one in every region.**

#### 🔵 p715 — Global: **a licence-risk read that applies to every region, and a warning about secondary star counts**

#### 🟢 p708 — Global: what the institutional-agent cohort says about EVERY region, and the one honest instrument warning that belongs on this page

🔵 **p708's mandated market and trends legs nilled for the 47th consecutive time, measured against `18` named markers that were each grepped against the live shelves — `18 / 18` already held** (the full table is `708-B` in [`../agents/trending.md`](../agents/trending.md)). 🟢 **The `2026` bracket on this page therefore survives a seventh independent check unchanged: `$11.40B`–`$12.3B` for `2026`**, with Coherent's `$57.25B by 2033` implying `25.93%` — arithmetic this page already publishes and p708 recomputed rather than copied.

🟢 **The region-independent finding of the pass: the reusable asset in education AI is the AUTHORITY LAYER, not the model, and it now exists in permissively licensed code.** p708's seven filed subjects are institutional agents from four countries, built independently by different authors, and they converge on the same four controls:

| control | where it is implemented, permissively | why a client's gate asks for it |
|---|---|---|
| **Role-aware scope enforced server-side**, not trusted to the client | [`changazo/udesa-mcp`](https://github.com/changazo/udesa-mcp) — *estudiante* / *docente* / *gestor* | a student agent must not be able to request another student's record at all |
| **Compulsory preview-and-approve before any write**, with separate READ and WRITE registries | [`EduardoKrausME/moodle-local_mcp`](https://github.com/EduardoKrausME/moodle-local_mcp) 🔴 GPL-3.0 — read as a **specification** | an agent that posts to a forum or submits an assignment is acting as the user |
| **Pseudonymisation before anything reaches a model** — students arrive under an alias | [`falkenslab/miyagi`](https://github.com/falkenslab/miyagi) 🟢 MIT | California's **`AB 1159`** bars student data from model training; the EU AI Act classifies education as high-risk |
| **Provenance, coverage and warnings on every result**; an error is never returned as an empty result | `changazo/udesa-mcp` | a tutor that silently returns nothing is indistinguishable from one that returns the truth |

🔵 **Credentials never leave the user in any of them** — OS secure store, or the institution's own session, or private single-account OAuth. 🟢 **None of these four is a research problem. All four are shelved, readable and permissively licensed today**, and three of the four are under MIT or Apache-2.0 with no copyleft to negotiate. 🔴 **The fourth, the write-authority model, has its best reference implementation under GPL-3.0 — by construction, because it lives inside Moodle's tree — so it must be re-implemented out-of-tree rather than copied.** That boundary is drawn in full at [`../verticals/solutions.md`](../verticals/solutions.md) `708-V1`.

#### 🟢 p706 — Global: what is true in every region, and the two things that are not region-specific at all

🟢 **Two constraints recurred in EVERY regional leg this pass, which makes them global requirements rather than regional colour:**

1. **Student-data custody is the live adoption brake everywhere** — named as COPPA in North America, as AI Act post-market surveillance and “European LLMs” in EMEA, as sovereignty in APAC, and as ministry-level caution in LATAM. 🔵 **The cheapest architectural answer this pass found is BYOK** — [`its-ahoh/litcode`](https://github.com/its-ahoh/litcode) moves model cost **and** data custody to the learner — with **local-first** and **read-only** integration ([`EdmundD28/moodle-codex`](https://github.com/EdmundD28/moodle-codex)) as the institutional variants.
2. **The system of record, not the model, is the hard part.** Every high-value placement this pass is an agent layer over a system an institution already runs — Wilma, Aula, Moodle, UnB, SLIIT. 🔵 **A studio's reusable asset is the connector, not the prompt.**

🔴 **Market size — unchanged in substance from p705 and restated as a warning:** the `2026` AI-in-education figures returned this pass (~**`$7.5B`** `2025` → ~**`$10.6B`** `2026`, CAGR ~**`40.9%`**) come from **paid vendor reports whose methodology cannot be inspected**, and this base has already documented (`695`) a case of *“three sources, three CAGRs”* resolving to **one source counted twice**. **Treat every figure on this page as a vendor's model, and prefer dated appropriations and funded programmes** — `$169M` US DoE, `$4.6M` Google.org, `$4.6m` Raspberry Pi Foundation — **which are facts with dates attached.**

🟢 **Cross-regional readiness, single instrument (Workday), so the comparison is legitimate:** **EMEA `56%` · Americas `48%` · APJ `45%`** self-reported AI preparedness. 🔵 **Note the inversion worth carrying into a pitch: EMEA reports the highest readiness and carries the heaviest regulation, while APAC reports the lowest readiness and has this base's deepest open-source education supply.**

#### 🟢 p704 — Global: the asset shortage in education AI is not models or repos, it is **readable licences**

🔵 **`p704`'s cross-regional finding came from reading grant files rather than market copy, and it reframes what a studio sells first.** Nineteen subjects were probed at the payload this pass. **Four failed, and each failed differently:**

| Failure shape | Instance | Why it bites a client |
|---|---|---|
| **Source-available masquerading as open source** | [`canyongbs/advisingapp`](https://github.com/canyongbs/advisingapp), `340★`, **Elastic 2.0** | The licence's named prohibition — *“hosted or managed service”* — **is** the studio delivery model |
| **A permissive claim that is simply false** | [`idurar/idurar-erp-crm`](https://github.com/idurar/idurar-erp-crm), `8,944★`, **AGPL-3.0** (a mandated leg called it MIT) | AGPL's network clause reaches the portal's end users |
| **A grant reference that dangles** | [`DMontgomery40/mcp-canvas-lms`](https://github.com/DMontgomery40/mcp-canvas-lms), `104★`, README says MIT, **`10` paths all `404`** | A README grep returns "MIT"; there is no grant at all |
| **A notice with no holder** | [`langx/langx`](https://github.com/langx/langx), `109★`, **BSD-3-Clause**, *“Copyright (c) 2024”* and no name | Symmetric: binds no one, and leaves no one to ask |

🟢 **All four were found with `curl` against `raw.githubusercontent.com` and one batched `gh api search/repositories` call.** Two of the four are **top-decile adopted** in their niches. 🔵 **The generalisation:** in education specifically, "open source" is being asserted by README, by blog roundup and by star count far more often than it is established by a grant file — and the education buyer (a university procurement office, a ministry) is the buyer least equipped to tell the difference and **most** exposed when it is wrong. **A licence-gate pass is therefore the cheapest, earliest, most defensible thing a studio can sell into an education engagement**, and it is specified as `P96`.

🟢 **The second global finding is internal and it changes how this base should be worked.** `12` of `p704`'s `13` verified subjects were already written in [`../agents/trending.md`](../agents/trending.md) and present in **no** live shelf (`704-B`). The mandated legs produced `18` addresses and **`18 / 18` were already held**. **This base's constraint is promotion, not discovery** — a `grep -rlF` against its own backlog outperformed eight web legs by `12` rows to `0`.

🔴 **And one global limit is now named rather than rediscovered:** stars for any repository not attached to the session are available **only** through `gh api search/repositories`; `github.com` HTML returns a `378`-byte interception stub and `api.github.com/repos/…` returns `403` (`704-C`). A repository the search index omits therefore has **no star channel at all** — `704-D` is that case. **Not a transient failure; retrying will not fix it.**


#### 🟢 p703 — Global: **`3` new agent rows, and all three are MECHANISMS rather than platforms — which is where the global gap actually is**

🟢 **Global went `67 / 144` → `70 / 158`, and the three additions share a property worth naming: none of them is a product, and each encodes a piece of pedagogy as configuration.**

- [`VIABLE-Learning-Lab/viable`](https://github.com/VIABLE-Learning-Lab/viable) (MIT code, **CC BY 4.0 data** in `NOTICE`) — a **Harness** that makes any agent read the teaching moment (the goal, how much help is right today, the one misconception that fits) before answering, plus an **Engine** that runs classes on a school's own server against any model. 🔵 **The first artefact on these shelves whose unit of configuration is the teacher's help limit rather than the model**, and a split grant whose data obligation the code licence never mentions.
- [`dylanj7/scholara`](https://github.com/dylanj7/scholara) (MIT) — a tutor built as a **refusal boundary**: it will build an outline skeleton and probe a thesis, and will not write prose a student could paste or compute a maths step, declared per subject. Its author names the real problem precisely — *the hard part of an AI tutor is not the chat interface, it is the refusal boundary* — and published a security review of their own MVP's holes.
- [`NiravRVaghasiya/Polyglot-Swarm`](https://github.com/NiravRVaghasiya/Polyglot-Swarm) (MIT) — a persisted **learner model** (per-skill competence) driving an **FSRS** scheduler driving a conversational tutor: the three primitives this base keeps naming separately, wired into one loop, running fully locally.

🔵 **The global structural reading: model-layer and framework supply is abundant and already held here, so the scarce artefact is pedagogy encoded as something a machine can act on.** `44` rows filed this pass and the ones that will still matter in a year are the ones that answer *how much help, and when* — not the ones that answer *which model*.

**Demand side, with disagreement preserved rather than resolved.** 🔴 **Market-size estimates for AI in education do not agree and this base will not pick one**: one report gives **~$7.52B (2025) → $10.6B (2026) at a 40.9% CAGR**, another frames 2026 as a **$32B** market. Both are secondary; the methodologies have not been seen. What the sources agree on is directional: agentic AI named as 2026's transformation peak, predictive analytics for student retention, AI in institutional operations and administration, K-12 early intervention, course design compressing from months to days — and, as a counterweight, a reported **"human-centric" pivot** with reinvestment in social-emotional learning as AI absorbs more cognitive tasks, plus a flagged **crisis of explainability** as AI takes over curriculum design. 🟡 **Caveat on the whole demand picture, stated: many of these trend pieces are auto-generated posts repackaging the same few primary sources (Deloitte, EdSurge, eSchool News), and this base has read the repackaging, not the primaries.**

**Opportunities.** (1) 🟢 **Compose, don't build.** The highest-value thing p703 found anywhere is [`malkreide/socratic-method-skill`](https://github.com/malkreide/socratic-method-skill) at `55★` — a German-language agent skill, no server, no database, no model choice, droppable into an engagement in an afternoon. **Skills are the cheapest composable unit on these shelves and this base holds almost none.** (2) 🟢 **Explainability is a named concern and `P91` is the answer to it** — floor, repeated-run consistency, agreement with human markers, with no pass threshold so a failure stays visible. (3) **Corpus is solved and should stop being treated as a cost**: [`cyanheads/gutenberg-mcp-server`](https://github.com/cyanheads/gutenberg-mcp-server) puts `78,000+` public-domain full texts behind one tool, so a derivative tutor can quote them in full with no licence negotiation. (4) 🔵 **Sell the transcribe/judge split (`T149`) as the default assessment architecture** — three teams in three languages converged on it independently this pass, which is stronger evidence than any vendor roadmap.

🔴 **Beside it, a measured global nil: no MCP server or agent bridge exists for LibreTexts, OpenStax, the Open Textbook Library or OER Commons.** All four probed, all four nil. The corpora are public and openly licensed, and the access layer is missing — a gap whose hardest part is already solved under MIT.

#### 🆕 p678 — what a studio can take from this pass regardless of region

🔵 **All nine addresses filed this pass are `Global (unplaced)`**, and that is a measured verdict rather than a default: `8` of `8` owner accounts have no `location` set, and `7` READMEs plus every grant payload named no jurisdiction (`678-I`, with both evidence tables linked there). **Unplaced supply is still usable supply** — what it cannot serve is a brief that asks "what is happening in my region".

🟢 **Three findings that travel:**

1. **A platform's licence is not its components' licence.** Open edX is `AGPL-3.0` and its two official mobile clients are `Apache-2.0`; OpenMAIC is permissive and its UI has no grant at all. **Both directions of that error appeared in one pass**, and both are invisible to a repository-level licence badge.
2. **A NOTICE is not a copyleft problem.** `basiclti-util-java` reads `13,185 B` against an `11,357 B` canonical, and the residual decomposes exactly into `1,825 B` of Apache-2.0 subcomponent attributions. A digest gate is **right to flag it and wrong to reject it** (`678-C`).
3. **Forks beat stars for institutional software.** On a 12-point out-of-sample test the `f/★ >= 0.5` boundary held: platform code (LMS clients, LTI libraries, school ERP, Kolibri installers) sat above it, agent code (`MAIC-UI` `0.212`, `wiki-rag` `0.189`) below (`678-D`). **For a platform shortlist, rank by forks per star and apply an `n >= 20` floor.**

🔴 **And one about this base itself:** p678's own intended headline — a mechanism for why two equal-length Apache-2.0 payloads hash differently — **was already held in the tree** and was caught by scoring the claim before drafting it (`678-H`). The base measures well; the standing risk is republishing its own holdings as discovery.

| Binding AI-education rules | State-level, patchy; **no Canadian AI Act (AIDA died Jan 2025)** | **Yes — EU AI Act, risk-tiered**; UK light-touch but has a DfE **product safety standard** (Jan 2026) | **Yes, in two jurisdictions — South Korea** (AI Basic Act, education named in the high-impact definition) **and Vietnam** (Decision 33/2026/QD-TTg: education is 3 of 46 high-risk systems) | Mostly pending (Peru only) |
| Nearest enforcement date | No single federal date; state deadlines vary and several 2026 claims do not verify (see above). Canada: none | **High-risk 2 Dec 2027**; Article 50 transparency live since 2 Aug 2026 | **Korea administrative fines ≈ Jan 2027**; **Vietnam education transition 1 Sep 2027**, high-risk list live since 15 Aug 2026; India labelling live since 20 Feb 2026 | — |
| Market size (2026, directional) | largest | Europe ≈ $2.64B; MEA ≈ $0.56B | ≈ $2.85B, **35.3% CAGR — fastest** | growing; **55% of universities have no AI budget** |
| Institutional readiness | Moderate; 60% of teachers use AI, 55% of schools unrestricted | Moderate–high; ~70% have or are developing guidance | Mixed (China, Singapore have policies; much of the region does not) | **Low — 26% have a strategy, <10% have guidelines** |
| Dominant LMS | Canvas, Blackboard | Moodle, ILIAS; **OpenOlat** in German-speaking HE | Mixed | **Moodle, Chamilo** |
| Open source supply | Modest (OATutor); `canvas-mcp` 317★ serves the Canvas-dominant market | 🟢 **Upgraded at p653: the only region that owns a permissive institutional *platform* — `OpenOlat`, Apache-2.0, 449★ / 32,210 commits, `langchain4j` in-tree.** Agent layer still thin (`feedbacksystem` 24★; Moodle bridges cap at 27★) | **Dominant — DeepTutor, OpenMAIC, AI-Shifu, and now the model layer (OmniEdu)** | Real but **licence-nil** (`Edu-mentor-AI`); no LATAM education agent repo found in any pass |
| Primary sell | Compliance + Canvas agents | Conformity by design; Gulf capability builds; **offline-first in Africa** | **Conformity by design (Korea)** + co-development + labelling | **Governance first, small and fixed-fee** |

🔵 **The single most useful shift in this table at p651:** the EMEA conformity-by-design offer is no longer region-specific. South Korea's AI Basic Act names student assessment in the high-impact category and its enforcement edge (≈ January 2027) falls **before** the EU's (2 December 2027). The same engagement shape now has two jurisdictions and two dates, with Korea the earlier one.

🔴 **And the shift at p652 inverts the assumption underneath this whole page: the EU is now the *last* of three binding education-AI deadlines, not the forcing function.** Ordered:

| Date | Jurisdiction | What falls due |
|---|---|---|
| **≈ Jan 2027** | South Korea | Administrative fines become available after MSIT's signalled grace period; student assessment in early-childhood/elementary/secondary education is high-impact by statute |
| **1 Sep 2027** | Vietnam | Compliance deadline for education systems already operating before 15 Aug 2026 (health and finance share the date; other sectors 1 Mar 2027) |
| **2 Dec 2027** | EU | Stand-alone Annex III high-risk obligations, after the Digital Omnibus deferral from 2 Aug 2026 |

Three consequences, and they are not cosmetic. **(1)** A client selling education AI into all three markets needs one conformity programme with three jurisdictional profiles, sequenced to the Korean date — not an EU programme with APAC bolted on. **(2)** Any proposal that frames December 2027 as "the deadline" is eleven months late for a client with Korean exposure. **(3)** The EU deferral bought European clients runway and bought APAC clients nothing, so the regions that looked least regulated on this page a year ago are now the ones with the nearest dates. **The habit of treating EMEA as the compliance region and APAC as the supply region is now wrong in both directions** — APAC supplies the open source *and* has the earliest deadlines.

### 🆕 Added at p716 — three gaps, each the result of a leg that RAN and returned nothing

🔴 **`G-716-1` — No region-wide APAC AI-in-schools regulatory framework, and no verified list of leading APAC AI-education companies.** The mandated APAC regional leg ran in full and returned neither. The only binding instruments it surfaced were the **UK's** generative-AI school safety standards (January 2026) and the **UAE's** `25` generative-AI prohibitions (February 2026) — **both EMEA**, and both refiled to the EMEA section. 🔵 **The gap is in the CHANNEL, not in the territory:** `p715` established that the first binding instrument in the region naming education as high-risk is **Vietnam's**, which this leg did not surface at all. **An English-language keyword leg cannot see national-ministry instruments published in national languages.** Closing this requires probing ministries directly — China, Singapore, Australia, South Korea, Japan, Vietnam, India — and the keyword leg should not be re-run expecting a different answer.

🔴 **`G-716-2` — The Spanish/Portuguese keyword channel for LATAM repository supply is EXHAUSTED.** `tutor inteligencia artificial educacion license:mit` returned **`0`** results; `educacao inteligencia artificial aluno license:mit` returned **`1`**, last pushed `2025-05-17` and stale by `18` months. 🟢 **Recorded as an exhausted channel rather than as an absence of supply**, because the same pass placed `4` LATAM subjects through a different shape — searching the **institution's own system name** (`e-Disciplinas`, `JupiterWeb`, `SUAP`, `AVA`, `e-FICH`). See `716-D` and `P123`.

🔴 **`G-716-3` — No binding regional AI-in-education regulation in LATAM, and little K-12 policy evidence anywhere in the region's literature.** Mexico shows documented calls for regulatory alignment, institutional reform and curriculum redesign, but **calls are not instruments.** The region's available evidence is heavily weighted toward **higher education**: the two largest instruments this base holds (the DEC/Tec de Monterrey faculty-and-student survey, UNESCO IESALC's `200`-institution study across `19` countries) are both tertiary. **K-12 policy in LATAM is therefore an unmeasured area, not a quiet one**, and any K-12 claim this base makes about the region should be treated as unsupported until a primary source is found.
